bug_categories.description: Replace the OR operator with AND, changing the function from NOR to NAND (~(in1 & in2)).
bug_categories.applicability: The single assign statement uses '|' between in1 and in2; swapping it to '&' is a valid one-token change that produces a different truth table (out=1 for inputs 00, 01, 10 instead of only 00).

bug_categories.description: Remove the output negation so the design behaves as an OR gate instead of a NOR gate.
bug_categories.applicability: The '~' in front of (in1 | in2) is the sole inversion; dropping it makes out = in1 | in2, inverting the output for every input combination.

bug_categories.description: Apply the inversion to only one operand, e.g. out = ~in1 | in2, breaking the NOR equivalence.
bug_categories.applicability: Moving '~' from the whole expression to a single input yields a function that is 1 for in1=0 or in2=1, which differs from NOR on inputs 01 and 10 combinations.

bug_categories.description: Use a different operator class such as XOR (^) or XNOR in place of OR, so the function changes on the 11 input case.
bug_categories.applicability: Replacing '|' with '^' gives out = ~(in1 ^ in2) (XNOR), which outputs 1 for 11 where the correct NOR outputs 0, while still being valid Verilog and plausible as a typo.

bug_categories.bug_type: Input signal substitution / wrong signal reference
bug_categories.description: Use the same input twice, e.g. out = ~(in1 | in1), so in2 is ignored.
bug_categories.applicability: Both operands are simple 1-bit ports; a copy-paste mistake referencing in1 twice makes the output depend only on in1 (a plain inverter) and leaves in2 unused.

bug_categories.description: Force the output to a constant by tying part of the expression to a literal, e.g. out = ~(in1 | 1'b1) or assign out = 1'b0.
bug_categories.applicability: The purely combinational single assign can be replaced or partially replaced with a constant, creating a stuck-at-0 or stuck-at-1 output that ignores one or both inputs.

bug_categories.description: Gate one input with the other or a constant inside the expression, e.g. out = ~(in1 | (in2 & in1)) or ~(in1 | ~in2).
bug_categories.applicability: Inserting an inverter or AND on in2 changes how in2 influences the output (e.g. ~(in1 | ~in2) is 1 only for in1=0,in2=1), making the design a different 2-input function while remaining syntactically valid.

bug_categories.bug_type: Sequential behavior introduced into combinational logic
bug_categories.description: Convert the continuous assignment into a latch-inferring or clocked-style construct, e.g. an always block with incomplete sensitivity or conditional assignment that fails to assign out in some cases.
bug_categories.applicability: Rewriting as 'always @(in1) out = ~(in1 | in2);' (with out as reg) omits in2 from the sensitivity list so out does not update when only in2 changes, producing stale outputs in simulation.

bug_categories.description: Replace the bitwise AND with a bitwise OR so the output is high when either input is high.
bug_categories.applicability: Change 'assign out = a & b;' to 'assign out = a | b;'. The truth table differs for inputs 01 and 10, where out becomes 1 instead of 0.

bug_categories.description: Replace the AND with an XOR so the output is high only when the inputs differ.
bug_categories.applicability: Change 'assign out = a & b;' to 'assign out = a ^ b;'. Output is wrong for 11 (0 instead of 1) and for 01 and 10 (1 instead of 0).

bug_categories.description: Invert the result so the module behaves as a NAND gate.
bug_categories.applicability: Change 'assign out = a & b;' to 'assign out = ~(a & b);'. Every input combination yields the complement of the expected output.

bug_categories.description: Invert one input before the AND, so the gate responds to the wrong level on that input.
bug_categories.applicability: Change 'assign out = a & b;' to 'assign out = a & ~b;' (or '~a & b'). Output is high only for a=1, b=0, which breaks the expected truth table.

bug_categories.description: Make the output depend on only one input, ignoring the other.
bug_categories.applicability: Change 'assign out = a & b;' to 'assign out = a & a;' or 'assign out = a;'. Output no longer depends on b, so cases with a=1, b=0 wrongly produce 1.

bug_categories.bug_type: Logical vs bitwise operator confusion with constant tie-off
bug_categories.description: Tie the output to a constant, producing a stuck-at fault.
bug_categories.applicability: Change 'assign out = a & b;' to 'assign out = 1'b0;' (stuck-at-0) or 'assign out = 1'b1;' (stuck-at-1). Output ignores both inputs entirely.

bug_categories.description: Replace the AND with another two-input primitive such as NOR or XNOR.
bug_categories.applicability: Change 'assign out = a & b;' to 'assign out = ~(a | b);' (NOR) or 'assign out = ~(a ^ b);' (XNOR). XNOR matches the AND only on 00 where it wrongly gives 1 and on 11 where it correctly gives 1, so 00 is wrong.

bug_categories.bug_type: Extra logic term / unintended third dependency
bug_categories.description: Introduce an additional term into the expression that makes the output depend on a combination not in the spec, such as a hidden constant or a redundant gating mix.
bug_categories.applicability: Change 'assign out = a & b;' to 'assign out = (a & b) | (~a & ~b);' or 'assign out = a & b | ~a;'. The extra term makes the output high for cases like 00 where the original is low.

mutant_rejections.bug_type: Extra logic term / unintended third dependency

bug_categories.description: Replace the addition operator with subtraction (x - y), producing a difference instead of a sum.
bug_categories.applicability: The single assign statement 'sum = x + y' can be changed to 'x - y', giving wrong results for nearly all inputs where y != 0 and generating borrow-wrapped values in the 5-bit output.

bug_categories.description: Replace the arithmetic add with a bitwise operation such as XOR, OR, or AND, which ignores carry propagation between bit positions.
bug_categories.applicability: 'x + y' becomes 'x ^ y' (a carry-less sum), so results match only when no carries occur, and sum[4] (carry out) is always 0.

bug_categories.description: Truncate the result to 4 bits so the MSB carry-out of sum[4] is lost, e.g. assign sum = {1'b0, (x + y)[3:0]} or compute the sum in a 4-bit context.
bug_categories.applicability: Any input pair whose sum exceeds 15 (e.g., 9 + 8 = 17) yields a wrong output since sum[4] is forced to 0 and only the lower 4 bits are kept.

bug_categories.description: Use an operand of incorrect width or sign-extension, such as zero-extending only part of an operand or using a replicated bit instead of zero padding.
bug_categories.applicability: Changing to 'sum = x + {y[3], y}' (sign-extending y) or '{x[3],x} + y' makes results incorrect whenever the MSB of y or x is 1, since the 4-bit unsigned inputs are treated as signed.

bug_categories.description: Reverse or permute the bits of an input or output so that bit significance is mismatched.
bug_categories.applicability: Replace 'x' with '{x[0],x[1],x[2],x[3]}' or assign 'sum = {s[0],s[1],s[2],s[3],s[4]}' from an intermediate, corrupting results for any asymmetric bit pattern.

bug_categories.description: Add or omit a constant term, introducing an erroneous carry-in or offset.
bug_categories.applicability: 'sum = x + y + 1' adds a spurious carry-in, shifting every result by one, and overflowing to 5'd16+ at the max-input case (15 + 15 + 1 = 31).

bug_categories.description: Use the same input for both operands or replace one input with a constant, so the output ignores one input.
bug_categories.applicability: 'sum = x + x' or 'sum = y + y' (doubling a single input), or 'sum = x + 4'b0', causes the output to be independent of one operand and produces wrong sums whenever the inputs differ.

bug_categories.description: Force or invert a specific output bit after the addition, as from a faulty bit-slice or a misrouted assignment.
bug_categories.applicability: Split the assignment into per-bit assigns with an error, e.g., 'assign sum[2] = ~(x[2]^y[2]^c1)' or force sum[4] = 1'b1 / sum[0] = 1'b0, so a specific bit is wrong only in certain input patterns.

bug_categories.description: The ternary condition is inverted so that sel=1 selects input a and sel=0 selects input b, e.g. assign out = (!sel) ? b : a or swapping the two data operands.
bug_categories.applicability: The module is a pure 2:1 mux whose only control is the single-bit sel; swapping the mapping flips every output bit for every input combination and is directly observable.

bug_categories.description: The mux is applied to fewer than 100 bits, for example out[98:0] is driven by the mux while the MSB is tied to 0 or to a only. Equivalent to using a 99-bit slice of a/b.
bug_categories.applicability: Ports a, b and out are 100 bits wide, so an off-by-one in the vector range (e.g. [98:0] instead of [99:0]) silently drops the top bit while remaining valid Verilog.

bug_categories.description: One data input is bit-reversed, e.g. out = sel ? {b[0],b[1],...,b[99]} : a, or the output bits are assigned in reversed order.
bug_categories.applicability: With 100-bit buses, a generate loop or concatenation that reverses indices keeps widths consistent but scrambles bit positions, only detectable with non-symmetric data patterns.

bug_categories.description: A specific output bit (e.g. out[50]) is hard-wired to a constant 0 or 1 or always taken from one input regardless of sel.
bug_categories.applicability: Because the mux is bitwise independent across 100 lanes, a single-lane override is a subtle bug that only shows when the selected input differs from the constant at that bit.

bug_categories.description: The ternary is replaced by a bitwise logic operation such as out = a & b, a | b, or a ^ b (or sel ? b : a replaced by sel ? (a|b) : a).
bug_categories.applicability: For cases where a and b agree the output looks correct, but differing bits produce wrong results, so a mux can be mistaken for a logical combination of the two inputs.

bug_categories.description: The select is applied per-bit incorrectly, e.g. sel is used only for the lower 50 bits while the upper 50 bits are always a (or always b), or select is replaced with a bit of a/b data like a[0].
bug_categories.applicability: The single sel must fan out to all 100 bits; splitting the vector or using the wrong control signal creates half-correct behavior that passes simple tests.

bug_categories.description: Bits are shifted or rotated between lanes, e.g. out = sel ? (b << 1) : a, or out[i] takes a[i+1], causing an off-by-one index error across the vector.
bug_categories.applicability: The wide buses make a shift or rotate on one operand a plausible indexing mistake that stays width-compatible but misaligns data.

bug_categories.description: The assignment is rewritten as an incomplete combinational always block, e.g. always @* if (sel) out = b; (missing else), so out holds its previous value when sel=0 and infers a latch.
bug_categories.applicability: The design is purely combinational with no storage; converting to a procedural block with a missing branch introduces state while still being valid Verilog, breaking the a-path of the mux.

bug_categories.description: The select value is incremented or decremented before indexing, so the output reads a neighboring input bit instead of the selected one.
bug_categories.applicability: Change 'assign out = in[sel];' to 'assign out = in[sel + 1];' or 'in[sel - 1];'. Every select value returns the wrong bit, and sel=255 wraps or goes out of range.

bug_categories.description: Only part of the 8-bit select is used, so the upper bits are ignored and the mux collapses to a smaller one.
bug_categories.applicability: Use 'in[sel[6:0]]' or 'in[{1'b0, sel[6:0]}]'. Selects 128-255 alias to 0-127 and the upper half of the 256-bit input can never be selected.

bug_categories.description: The input vector is indexed from the opposite end, so the bit order is mirrored.
bug_categories.applicability: Use 'in[255 - sel]' or 'in[~sel]'. Each select returns the mirror-image bit, a systematic error that a few directed tests would miss if the test data is symmetric.

bug_categories.description: Two bits of the select signal are swapped or one is inverted before indexing, which scrambles the mapping from sel to input bit.
bug_categories.applicability: Use 'in[{sel[0], sel[7:1]}]' (rotate) or 'in[{sel[7:4], sel[2], sel[3], sel[1:0]}]' or 'in[sel ^ 8'h01]'. Only some select values are mapped wrongly, so the error is partial.

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong operand source or logic inversion on output
bug_categories.description: The selected bit is inverted, or the output is forced by an extra logic term, corrupting the data value rather than the address.
bug_categories.applicability: Use 'assign out = ~in[sel];' or 'assign out = in[sel] & ~(sel == 8'hFF);' or 'in[sel] | in[0]'. Output polarity is wrong for all selects, or wrong only at corner selects.

bug_categories.description: A part-select or shifted vector replaces the single-bit index, so a different bit of the shifted word becomes the output.
bug_categories.applicability: Use '(in >> sel)[0]' variants such as 'out = |(in >> sel)' or 'out = &(in >> sel)', or 'in[sel +: 2]' reduced. The output reflects a group of bits at and above sel rather than a single bit.

bug_categories.description: A special case is added for boundary select values, returning a constant or a wrong bit at the edges of the index range.
bug_categories.applicability: Add 'assign out = (sel == 8'd255) ? in[254] : in[sel];' or 'sel == 0 ? 1'b0 : in[sel]'. The mux is correct except at sel=0 or sel=255, which is hard to catch with random tests.

bug_categories.bug_type: Incorrect index grouping (hierarchical mux decomposition error)
bug_categories.description: The mux is rebuilt as a two-level selection with the high and low select fields swapped, so the row and column of the 16x16 bit array are exchanged.
bug_categories.applicability: Use 'in[{sel[3:0], sel[7:4]}]'. Nibble swap maps sel to index (sel%16)*16 + sel/16, so only selects where the two nibbles are equal return the correct bit.

bug_categories.description: Move the inversion from in2 to in1, changing the expression to ~in1 & in2.
bug_categories.applicability: The design computes in1 & ~in2. Swapping which input is negated makes the output high for in1=0,in2=1 instead of in1=1,in2=0, which is a plausible copy-edit error.

bug_categories.description: Remove the ~ on in2 so the logic becomes in1 & in2 (a plain AND).
bug_categories.applicability: The only inversion in the design is on in2. Dropping it changes the in1=1,in2=0 case to output 0 and the in1=1,in2=1 case to output 1.

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong logical operator (AND replaced by OR)
bug_categories.description: Replace the bitwise AND with OR, giving in1 | ~in2.
bug_categories.applicability: The output would be 1 whenever in2 is 0 or in1 is 1, which differs from the intended result for in1=0,in2=0 and in1=1,in2=1.

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong logical operator (AND replaced by XOR)
bug_categories.description: Replace & with ^, giving in1 ^ ~in2, which is an XNOR of in1 and in2.
bug_categories.applicability: XNOR matches the original on some inputs but outputs 1 for in1=in2=1 and 0 for in1=1,in2=0, so the truth table differs from the intended inhibit function.

bug_categories.bug_type: Extra inversion of the whole result
bug_categories.description: Invert the final output, for example out = ~(in1 & ~in2), producing a NAND-style function.
bug_categories.applicability: With a single assign statement, wrapping the expression in a negation flips the output for every input combination, which is a simple stuck-polarity bug.

bug_categories.description: Invert both operands, giving ~in1 & ~in2 (a NOR).
bug_categories.applicability: Adding an extra ~ to in1 makes the output high only when both inputs are 0, breaking the in1=1,in2=0 case that should assert out.

bug_categories.description: Drop one input from the expression, e.g. out = in1 or out = ~in2, so the output ignores the other input.
bug_categories.applicability: The module has only two inputs, so ignoring either one makes the output depend on a single signal and fails the cases where the ignored input matters.

bug_categories.bug_type: Bitwise vs logical operator misuse / wrong signal reference
bug_categories.description: Change the expression to reference the output or an input incorrectly, such as out = in1 & ~in1 (always 0) or out = in2 & ~in2, or use && and ! in a way that changes behavior.
bug_categories.applicability: Because both inputs are single-bit ports, a typo that reuses the same input on both sides of the AND creates a constant-0 output, a realistic copy-paste bug that is still valid Verilog.

mutants.bug_type: Extra inversion of the whole result

bug_categories.description: Replace the equality operator == with != so the output is asserted when the inputs differ rather than when they match.
bug_categories.applicability: In 'assign z = A[1:0] == B[1:0];' changing '==' to '!=' inverts the comparator's function entirely.

bug_categories.description: Add a logical or bitwise negation to the result so z is the complement of the correct equality result.
bug_categories.applicability: Rewriting as 'assign z = ~(A[1:0] == B[1:0]);' gives z=0 for equal inputs and z=1 for unequal inputs.

bug_categories.description: Compare only a single bit of the 2-bit operands, ignoring the other bit, so inputs that differ in the ignored bit are wrongly reported equal.
bug_categories.applicability: Changing to 'A[0] == B[0]' ignores bit 1, so A=2'b10 and B=2'b00 incorrectly yield z=1.

bug_categories.description: Compare only the upper bit of the operands, dropping the LSB from the comparison.
bug_categories.applicability: Changing to 'A[1] == B[1]' makes A=2'b01 and B=2'b00 incorrectly produce z=1.

bug_categories.description: Compare mismatched bit positions between A and B, such as comparing A's bits to B's bits in reversed order.
bug_categories.applicability: Using '{A[0],A[1]} == B[1:0]' or 'A[1:0] == {B[0],B[1]}' makes A=2'b01, B=2'b10 report equal, while A=2'b11 vs 2'b11 still passes, hiding the bug in some tests.

bug_categories.description: Replace equality with a relational operator such as <=, >= or <, so z is true for a range of input combinations instead of just exact matches.
bug_categories.applicability: Using 'A[1:0] >= B[1:0]' (or '<=') makes z=1 for A=2'b11, B=2'b00, which should not be equal.

bug_categories.bug_type: Bitwise vs logical operator confusion / partial comparison logic
bug_categories.description: Replace the vector equality with a bitwise operation that does not correctly reduce to a full equality check, for example a reduction or OR/AND of per-bit XNORs combined incorrectly.
bug_categories.applicability: Writing 'assign z = (A[1] ~^ B[1]) | (A[0] ~^ B[0]);' asserts z when any one bit matches rather than when both match, so A=2'b01 vs B=2'b00 wrongly gives z=1.

bug_categories.description: Replace == with the case equality operator === (or !==) so the behavior diverges when inputs contain X or Z, while remaining identical for known 0/1 values.
bug_categories.applicability: Changing to 'A[1:0] === B[1:0]' makes z resolve to a definite 0/1 for X/Z inputs, whereas the original '==' yields X, altering behavior under unknown-input stimulus.

mutants.bug_type: Bitwise vs logical operator confusion / partial comparison logic

bug_categories.bug_type: Bit order reversal in output concatenation
bug_categories.description: The output concatenation order is swapped so the selected nibble is bit-reversed, e.g. { in[sel*4+0], in[sel*4+1], in[sel*4+2], in[sel*4+3] }, putting the LSB in the MSB position of out.
bug_categories.applicability: The assign builds out from four individually indexed bits in MSB-to-LSB order. Reordering any of them yields wrong data while remaining valid Verilog.

bug_categories.bug_type: Incorrect index offset in one bit select
bug_categories.description: One of the four bit selects uses the wrong constant offset, e.g. in[sel*4+3] changed to in[sel*4+4] or in[sel*4+2] duplicated, so one output bit comes from the neighboring nibble or is a duplicate of another bit.
bug_categories.applicability: Each output bit uses its own +0/+1/+2/+3 offset, so altering one offset corrupts a single bit and is hard to spot with simple tests.

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong multiplier in index calculation (stride error)
bug_categories.description: Replace sel * 4 with sel * 3, sel * 8, or sel << 1, so the slice stride no longer matches the 4-bit output width and selected groups overlap or skip.
bug_categories.applicability: The design relies on a 4-bit stride (sel*4) to pick one of 256 nibbles from the 1024-bit input. Changing the stride breaks the mapping for every non-zero sel.

bug_categories.description: Cast or truncate the index arithmetic to a narrower width (e.g. a 8-bit intermediate such as sel[5:0]*4 or (sel*4)[7:0]) so large sel values wrap around and select the wrong nibble.
bug_categories.applicability: sel is 8 bits and sel*4+3 reaches 1023, requiring 10 bits. In a context-determined expression this works, but forcing an 8-bit wire for the index makes sel >= 64 alias to lower nibbles.

bug_categories.description: Use only part of sel, such as sel[6:0] or sel[7:1], in the index computation so the highest or lowest select bit is ignored.
bug_categories.applicability: All 8 bits of sel are needed to address 256 nibbles. Dropping a bit halves the reachable range or makes pairs of sel values select the same nibble.

bug_categories.description: Add or subtract one from sel (e.g. (sel+1)*4 or (sel-1)*4) so the selected nibble is shifted by one position; sel=255 may then access out of range, returning X.
bug_categories.applicability: The direct use of sel in the index expression makes an off-by-one easy to inject. It shifts every selection and creates an out-of-range access at the boundary.

bug_categories.description: Drop one bit from the concatenation or replace a bit with a constant, e.g. { 1'b0, in[sel*4+2], in[sel*4+1], in[sel*4+0] }, or tie out[3] to in[sel*4+2].
bug_categories.applicability: The output is a 4-bit concatenation of discrete selects, so replacing, tying off, or duplicating any element is straightforward and silently corrupts one output bit.

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong bit significance in the selection (MSB-first indexing)
bug_categories.description: Index the input from the opposite end, e.g. in[1023 - (sel*4+k)], or use big-endian group ordering so group 0 is taken from the top of in instead of the bottom.
bug_categories.applicability: The input is a 1024-bit vector declared [1023:0] with group 0 at the LSBs. Reversing the indexing direction maps every sel to the mirrored nibble, a plausible endianness bug.

mutants.bug_type: Bit order reversal in output concatenation

bug_categories.description: The ternary condition is inverted so input a is chosen when sel=1 and b when sel=0, e.g. assign out = (!sel) ? b : a;
bug_categories.applicability: The design is a 2:1 mux whose only control is sel. Swapping the polarity causes every input combination with a != b to produce the wrong output.

bug_categories.description: The true and false branches of the ternary are exchanged, e.g. assign out = (sel) ? a : b;
bug_categories.applicability: The mux routes b on sel=1 and a on sel=0. Swapping the operands is syntactically valid and functionally equivalent to inverting the select.

bug_categories.description: The select signal is replaced by a constant or ignored, e.g. assign out = (1'b0) ? b : a; so the output is always a (or always b).
bug_categories.applicability: The design has a single select input. Disconnecting it leaves a pass-through of one data input and breaks selection of the other.

bug_categories.description: The mux is replaced with a boolean expression that matches only some input cases, e.g. assign out = (sel & b) & (~sel & a); or assign out = a & b when sel is 1.
bug_categories.applicability: A mux is equivalent to (sel&b)|(~sel&a). Changing OR to AND or XOR makes the output wrong for many input combinations while still being valid Verilog.

bug_categories.description: The output is inverted, e.g. assign out = ~((sel) ? b : a);
bug_categories.applicability: The output is a single-bit combinational result. Adding an inversion flips the output for every input combination.

bug_categories.bug_type: Data input inversion on one path
bug_categories.description: One of the data inputs is inverted before being selected, e.g. assign out = (sel) ? ~b : a;
bug_categories.applicability: Only the sel=1 path (or the sel=0 path) is corrupted, so the bug is exposed only when that path is chosen, which tests directed coverage of both select values.

bug_categories.bug_type: Select logic combined with a data input
bug_categories.description: The select condition is replaced by an expression involving data, e.g. assign out = (sel & a) ? b : a; or (sel | b) ? b : a;
bug_categories.applicability: Making the select depend on a or b causes incorrect selection only for particular data/select combinations, which is a corner-case bug that random tests may miss.

bug_categories.description: The mux uses the wrong signal for a branch, such as using sel as a data input, e.g. assign out = (sel) ? sel : a; or assign out = (sel) ? b : b;
bug_categories.applicability: With three single-bit inputs of the same width, a wrong signal name compiles without error. The output then ignores one data input or passes the select value, so it fails when the omitted data input differs.

mutants.bug_type: Data input inversion on one path

bug_categories.description: Replace the addition operator with a different operator such as subtraction, so the half adder computes a-b instead of a+b.
bug_categories.applicability: In 'assign { cout, sum } = a + b;', changing '+' to '-' makes sum behave like XOR but cout becomes the borrow (a=0,b=1 gives cout=1), which is incorrect for addition.

bug_categories.description: Swap the arithmetic sum for a bitwise operation that matches the result for some inputs but not all.
bug_categories.applicability: Replacing 'a + b' with 'a | b' makes the 2-bit result {cout,sum} = {0,1} for a=b=1, so cout is never asserted and sum is 1 instead of 0 when both inputs are high.

bug_categories.description: Swap the order of the concatenation on the left-hand side so carry and sum are exchanged.
bug_categories.applicability: Changing '{ cout, sum }' to '{ sum, cout }' makes cout carry the LSB (XOR) and sum carry the MSB (AND), swapping the two output functions.

bug_categories.description: Remove cout from the assignment or tie it to a constant so the carry is never produced.
bug_categories.applicability: Splitting into 'assign sum = a ^ b; assign cout = 1'b0;' loses the carry when a=b=1, giving the wrong result for the 1+1 case.

bug_categories.bug_type: Sum computed with wrong logic function
bug_categories.description: Implement sum using AND/OR/XNOR instead of XOR (the correct function of the LSB of a+b).
bug_categories.applicability: Using 'assign sum = ~(a ^ b);' (XNOR) inverts sum for every input combination while cout from AND stays correct.

bug_categories.bug_type: Carry computed with wrong logic function
bug_categories.description: Implement cout with OR or XOR instead of AND.
bug_categories.applicability: Using 'assign cout = a | b;' asserts carry when only one input is high (a=0,b=1 or a=1,b=0), which is wrong because carry should only occur when a=b=1.

bug_categories.description: Invert one of the outputs, either by adding a negation to the assignment or an inverted copy of the result.
bug_categories.applicability: Writing '{cout, sum} = ~(a + b);' or 'assign sum = ~sum_int' flips both outputs for all input combinations, so cout=1 for 0+0 and sum=1 for 0+0.

bug_categories.bug_type: Input operand corruption / unintended extra operand
bug_categories.description: Introduce an extra or modified operand (e.g., constant carry-in or inverted input) into the addition so the function changes.
bug_categories.applicability: Changing 'a + b' to 'a + b + 1'b1' or 'a + ~b' adds a hidden carry-in or inverts an operand, shifting the truth table (e.g., 0+0 yields sum=1, and 1+1 yields {1,1}).

mutants.bug_type: Sum computed with wrong logic function
Carry computed with wrong logic function

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong reduction operator (XNOR instead of XOR)
bug_categories.description: Replace the XOR reduction '^in' with XNOR reduction '~^in', inverting the parity output for every input.
bug_categories.applicability: The entire design is a single reduction XOR, so switching to XNOR flips parity (even instead of odd) for all 256 input values.

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong reduction operator (AND/OR instead of XOR)
bug_categories.description: Replace '^in' with '&in' or '|in', turning the parity computation into an all-ones or any-one detector.
bug_categories.applicability: The module produces a valid 1-bit output with either operator, but the output is only correct for a few inputs (e.g., 0x00 for OR, 0xFF mismatch for AND).

bug_categories.description: Compute parity over only a subset of the input bits, e.g., '^in[6:0]' or '^in[7:1]', leaving one bit out of the XOR tree.
bug_categories.applicability: The parity output ignores one bit of the 8-bit input, so any input differing only in the omitted bit yields an incorrect parity.

bug_categories.description: Use an incorrect part-select such as '^in[3:0]' or '^in[7:4]', so only a nibble contributes to parity.
bug_categories.applicability: Only half of the 8 input bits are XORed, so the output is wrong whenever the ignored nibble has odd parity.

bug_categories.description: Rewrite the reduction as an explicit XOR expression in which one bit is used twice and another is dropped, e.g., in[0]^in[1]^...^in[6]^in[6].
bug_categories.applicability: The duplicated bit cancels itself in the XOR, effectively removing two bits' contribution and making the output independent of in[6] and in[7].

bug_categories.description: Force the parity output to a constant (1'b0 or 1'b1) or tie it to a single input bit like 'in[0]'.
bug_categories.applicability: The output no longer depends on the full 8-bit input; with a constant, it is correct for only half of the input space.

bug_categories.description: Invert one input bit before reduction, e.g., '^{in[7:1], ~in[0]}', or invert a subset of bits.
bug_categories.applicability: Inverting an odd number of input bits flips the parity for all inputs, while inverting an even number of bits leaves the parity unchanged, producing a subtle fault depending on the count.

bug_categories.bug_type: Incorrect logic composition (OR of partial parities)
bug_categories.description: Split the XOR tree into two halves and combine them with OR or AND instead of XOR, e.g., '(^in[3:0]) | (^in[7:4])'.
bug_categories.applicability: The final stage of the parity tree uses the wrong gate, so the result matches true parity only when the two nibble parities do not both equal 1 (for OR).

mutants.bug_type: Wrong reduction operator (AND/OR instead of XOR)

bug_categories.description: Replace the '+' operators in the addition expression with a bitwise operator such as '^' or '|', e.g. assign {cout, sum} = a ^ b ^ cin or a | b | cin.
bug_categories.applicability: The whole design is a single addition expression. Using XOR/OR yields a correct or near-correct sum in some cases, but cout is always 0 or wrong because the carry is never generated, so the carry-out behavior breaks for input combinations with two or more 1s.

bug_categories.description: Drop cin from the sum expression so it becomes a + b, leaving cin unused.
bug_categories.applicability: When cin=1 the outputs {cout, sum} are off by one compared to the correct result. This affects 4 of the 8 input combinations (cin=1) and breaks use of the module as a chained full adder.

bug_categories.description: Swap the left-hand side bit ordering so it reads assign {sum, cout} = a + b + cin.
bug_categories.applicability: Sum and carry-out are exchanged. Results are wrong whenever the MSB and LSB of the result differ, which is when a+b+cin equals 1 or 2. Inputs where the result is 0 or 3 still look correct, so the bug is only partly masked.

bug_categories.description: Assign the result to only one output bit, e.g. assign sum = a + b + cin and drive cout from a different truncated expression such as a & b, or declare an intermediate wire with a width of 1 bit so the carry is truncated.
bug_categories.applicability: All inputs are 1-bit, so the addition result is 2 bits wide. Truncating to 1 bit discards the carry, forcing cout to be wrong (e.g. missing the cin contribution) in cases where a carry is generated through cin, such as a=1,b=0,cin=1.

bug_categories.description: Replace the carry computation with a wrong boolean expression, such as cout = (a & b) | (a & cin) without the (b & cin) term, or cout = a & b & cin.
bug_categories.applicability: The full adder carry-out is the majority of a, b, and cin. Removing a term or using AND of all three causes cout to be wrong for specific input combos (e.g. b=1,cin=1,a=0), while sum may remain correct, making the bug subtle.

bug_categories.description: Invert one of the inputs or outputs, e.g. use ~cin in the addition, or assign the output as ~sum or ~cout.
bug_categories.applicability: Inverting cin makes the adder behave as if the carry-in has the opposite polarity, changing results for every input combination. Inverting only sum or cout produces a bug that flips one output bit on all vectors while the other output stays correct.

bug_categories.description: Use the wrong input in the expression, e.g. a + a + cin or a + b + b, so that one operand is duplicated and another is ignored.
bug_categories.applicability: The design has three same-width inputs (a, b, cin), so such a substitution is syntactically valid. It makes the output independent of one input and creates wrong results whenever the ignored input differs from the duplicated one.

bug_categories.description: Replace one of the '+' operators with '-', e.g. assign {cout, sum} = a + b - cin or a - b + cin.
bug_categories.applicability: With 1-bit operands the result is evaluated at 2-bit width, so negative values wrap around (e.g. 0+0-1 = 2'b11), producing cout=1,sum=1 in cases that should give 0. This corrupts both outputs for any input where the subtracted operand exceeds the rest of the sum.

bug_categories.description: The enable condition is inverted so the latch becomes transparent when ena is low instead of high (if(!ena) q = d;).
bug_categories.applicability: The single if(ena) condition controls when q follows d; inverting it flips the transparency window and breaks the intended latch behavior.

bug_categories.description: The latch assigns the enable signal or an inverted data value to q instead of d (e.g., q = ena; or q = ~d;).
bug_categories.applicability: The only data path is q = d, so replacing the source or inverting it corrupts the stored/passed value while remaining valid Verilog.

bug_categories.description: Replace always @(*) with a restricted sensitivity list such as always @(ena) or always @(d), so the block does not re-evaluate on changes to both inputs.
bug_categories.applicability: Transparent latch requires q to track d while ena is high; if only ena is in the list, q misses d changes during the transparent phase, and if only d is listed, q misses the ena rising edge.

bug_categories.description: Change the combinational always block to an edge-triggered one, e.g., always @(posedge ena) q = d; or always @(posedge d) if(ena) q = d;.
bug_categories.applicability: The design is a level-sensitive latch; making it edge-sensitive means q only updates at an edge of ena, so d changes during ena=1 are not propagated.

bug_categories.bug_type: Added else branch removing latch behavior
bug_categories.description: Add an else clause that drives q to a constant or to another value (e.g., else q = 1'b0;), turning the latch into combinational AND logic.
bug_categories.applicability: The missing else is what creates memory when ena is low; defining q in all branches removes state retention and changes behavior to q = ena & d.

bug_categories.description: Replace q = d with the non-blocking q <= d inside the combinational always @(*) block.
bug_categories.applicability: Switching assignment type changes scheduling/evaluation order in simulation, potentially causing race conditions or delayed updates of q relative to d and ena changes.

bug_categories.description: Modify the condition to include extra or incorrect terms, such as if(ena & d) q = d; or if(ena | d) q = d;.
bug_categories.applicability: The enable is a single signal; adding d into the condition means the latch only captures when d is high (never capturing a 0) or becomes transparent when d is high even with ena low.

bug_categories.bug_type: Hold value forced by constant assignment
bug_categories.description: Change the assigned value to a constant or stuck-at value, e.g., if(ena) q = 1'b1; or q = 1'b0;, ignoring d.
bug_categories.applicability: The output depends only on d under ena; hardcoding a constant creates a stuck-at fault on q when enabled, which is easy to implement and clearly breaks functionality.

mutants.bug_type: Hold value forced by constant assignment

bug_categories.description: Replace the outer XOR with another logical operator, e.g. `~(in1 ^ in2) | in3` or `~(in1 ^ in2) & in3`.
bug_categories.applicability: The output depends on the final operator combining the XNOR result with in3. Changing it to AND/OR makes out differ for many input combinations, e.g. in3=1 forces out=1 with OR.

bug_categories.description: Remove the bitwise NOT so the expression becomes `(in1 ^ in2) ^ in3`, turning the XNOR into an XOR.
bug_categories.applicability: The `~` flips the output polarity for every input combination. Removing it produces the exact complement of the correct output, a clean functional break that is still valid Verilog.

bug_categories.description: Move the inversion so it applies to a different scope, e.g. `~((in1 ^ in2) ^ in3)` or `(~in1 ^ in2) ^ in3`, or `~(in1 ^ in2 ^ in3)`.
bug_categories.applicability: In a 3-input parity-style function, the placement of `~` changes the result polarity. Some placements are equivalent (`~in1 ^ in2` equals `~(in1 ^ in2)`), others add an extra inversion, so this tests whether the checker detects the subtle inversion.

bug_categories.description: Replace one operand with another input, e.g. `~(in1 ^ in1) ^ in3` or `~(in1 ^ in2) ^ in2`.
bug_categories.applicability: With only three inputs, using in1 or in2 twice makes the result constant or drops the dependence on a signal (e.g. in1^in1=0 so out=~0^in3=1^in3), hiding an input from the output.

bug_categories.description: Remove in3 or in2 from the expression, e.g. `out = ~(in1 ^ in2)` or `out = ~(in1 ^ in3)`.
bug_categories.applicability: The function is a 3-input parity, so every input affects the output on every vector. Dropping one makes the output insensitive to that input, which is easily exposed by toggling it.

bug_categories.description: Tie an input or sub-expression to a constant, e.g. `~(in1 ^ 1'b0) ^ in3` or `out = 1'b0`.
bug_categories.applicability: Forcing an operand to 0 or 1 emulates a stuck-at fault. Since XOR with a constant is either a pass-through or an inversion, the output becomes a function of fewer inputs or is inverted.

bug_categories.description: Replace bitwise operators with logical ones, e.g. `!(in1 ^ in2) ^ in3` or `~(in1 ^ in2) != in3` or use `~^`/`^~` incorrectly with reduction forms.
bug_categories.applicability: On 1-bit signals `~` and `!` behave identically, so some substitutions are benign, but changing to `==`, `!=`, `&&`, or `||` alters the logic. This is a realistic coding slip in a single-bit assign statement.

bug_categories.description: Change the port declaration or intermediate usage, e.g. make `out` or an input a multi-bit vector, or declare `output [1:0] out`, so the assign truncates or extends the 1-bit expression.
bug_categories.applicability: Inputs and output are implicit 1-bit scalars. Widening `out` or inserting a sized constant causes extension where `~` on a wider operand fills upper bits with 1s, which can change the observed value of the LSB or the full output word.

bug_categories.description: Change the sensitivity of the always block from posedge clk to negedge clk, so the flop captures d on the falling edge instead of the rising edge.
bug_categories.applicability: The design is a single D flip-flop triggered by posedge clk, so flipping the edge shifts the sampling time by half a cycle and changes output timing relative to the rest of the system.

bug_categories.description: Invert the captured data so q <= ~d instead of q <= d.
bug_categories.applicability: The only functional logic is the assignment q <= d, so inverting d produces a flop that always outputs the complement of the sampled input.

bug_categories.description: Replace the non-blocking assignment q <= d with a blocking assignment q = d inside the clocked always block.
bug_categories.applicability: Although a single flop may simulate similarly, the blocking assignment changes scheduling semantics and can create race conditions with other logic or testbench sampling q at the clock edge.

bug_categories.description: Change the initial value of q from 1'hx to a defined constant such as 1'b0 or 1'b1.
bug_categories.applicability: The design relies on initial q = 1'hx to model an unknown power-up state; a hard-coded value hides the uninitialized state and alters the behavior observed before the first clock edge.

bug_categories.description: Assign a constant to q in the clocked block (e.g., q <= 1'b0 or q <= 1'b1) so it ignores d.
bug_categories.applicability: The flop's whole function is to sample d, so replacing d with a constant makes the output independent of the input.

bug_categories.bug_type: Added unintended reset or enable logic
bug_categories.description: Introduce a conditional on the capture, e.g., q <= d only when d is 1 or when q is not x, or add a hidden hold condition so q retains its value under some state.
bug_categories.applicability: The module has no reset or enable, so adding a condition such as if (d) q <= d or if (q !== 1'bx) q <= d makes the flop fail to update or never leave the initial x state.

bug_categories.description: Change always @(posedge clk) to always @(clk) or always @(*) so that q follows d as a latch or level-sensitive element rather than a clocked flop.
bug_categories.applicability: The register behavior depends entirely on the edge-triggered sensitivity list; altering it turns the flop into transparent or both-edge sampling logic, changing timing and functionality.

bug_categories.bug_type: Extra pipeline delay / wrong signal sampled
bug_categories.description: Insert an additional internal register stage or sample the previous value of q (e.g., q <= q or a delayed copy of d), adding a cycle of latency or feeding back the output.
bug_categories.applicability: With a single flop, adding a second stage or feeding q back to itself changes latency from one cycle to two cycles or causes q to hold its value instead of tracking d.

mutants.bug_type: Extra pipeline delay / wrong signal sampled

bug_categories.description: Reverse the bit ordering in the concatenation assignment so the outputs are swapped relative to the input vector.
bug_categories.applicability: Change `assign { o2, o1, o0 } = vec;` to `assign { o0, o1, o2 } = vec;` so o2 receives vec[0] and o0 receives vec[2], while outv remains correct.

bug_categories.bug_type: Bit order reversal on vector output
bug_categories.description: Assign outv with its bits reversed using an explicit concatenation, so the vector output no longer matches the input bit positions.
bug_categories.applicability: Replace `assign outv = vec;` with `assign outv = {vec[0], vec[1], vec[2]};` so outv[2] gets vec[0] and outv[0] gets vec[2].

bug_categories.description: Invert one or more bits (or the whole vector) on a path so the output is the complement of the input.
bug_categories.applicability: Change `assign outv = vec;` to `assign outv = ~vec;`, or invert only a single scalar output such as `assign o1 = ~vec[1]` via the concatenation split.

bug_categories.description: Use an incorrect bit index so two outputs are driven by the same input bit and one input bit is dropped.
bug_categories.applicability: Split the concatenation into individual assigns with an error, e.g. `assign o2 = vec[2]; assign o1 = vec[2]; assign o0 = vec[0];`, or `assign outv = {vec[2], vec[2], vec[0]};`.

bug_categories.description: Assign only part of the vector so one or more output bits are left undriven or tied to a constant, creating a width mismatch.
bug_categories.applicability: Change `assign outv = vec;` to `assign outv[1:0] = vec[1:0];` leaving outv[2] undriven (high-Z), or `assign outv = {1'b0, vec[1:0]};` zeroing the MSB.

bug_categories.description: Tie an output bit to a constant 0 or 1 instead of the corresponding input bit.
bug_categories.applicability: Change `assign { o2, o1, o0 } = vec;` to `assign { o2, o1, o0 } = {vec[2], vec[1], 1'b0};` so o0 is stuck at 0 regardless of vec[0].

bug_categories.description: Insert a bitwise or reduction operation that mixes input bits, so outputs depend on more than their corresponding input bit.
bug_categories.applicability: Change `assign outv = vec;` to `assign outv = vec ^ {vec[1:0], 1'b0};` or `assign outv = {vec[2], vec[1] & vec[0], vec[0]};`, making outv differ from the plain pass-through.

bug_categories.description: Rotate or shift the vector by one position so each output bit is driven by a neighboring input bit.
bug_categories.applicability: Change `assign { o2, o1, o0 } = vec;` to `assign { o2, o1, o0 } = {vec[1:0], vec[2]};` (rotate left), or use `vec << 1` / `vec >> 1` on outv so bits are shifted and one is lost.

bug_categories.description: Replace the addition operator in 'assign sum = a + b' with subtraction (a - b) or another operator such as bitwise OR/XOR, so the sum output is functionally wrong.
bug_categories.applicability: The entire datapath depends on the single 'a + b' expression, so changing the operator corrupts s and also the overflow detection, which is derived from s.

bug_categories.description: Remove the inversion of the sign-equality check, e.g. change '!(a[7] ^ b[7])' to '(a[7] ^ b[7])', so overflow is flagged when operands have different signs instead of the same sign.
bug_categories.applicability: The overflow signal requires both operands to have the same sign. Inverting this condition makes overflow fire for mixed-sign additions, which can never overflow, and miss real overflows.

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong bit index in sign comparison
bug_categories.description: Use the wrong bit index in the overflow logic, e.g. compare a[7] with s[6] or b[6] instead of s[7], or use a[6]^b[6] for the sign check.
bug_categories.applicability: The overflow expression indexes the MSBs a[7], b[7] and s[7]. Shifting any index by one selects a magnitude bit and gives wrong overflow results for many input combinations.

bug_categories.description: Change '&&' to '||' in the overflow expression, or replace it with '&' or '|', so the conjunction of the same-sign condition and the result-sign-differs condition is altered.
bug_categories.applicability: Overflow needs both the 'operands share sign' and 'result sign differs' conditions. Using OR makes overflow assert whenever either condition holds, producing many false positives.

bug_categories.description: Change the output slice 's = sum[7:0]' to 'sum[8:1]' or otherwise misalign the bits, so the output is shifted or the carry bit is included in place of the LSB.
bug_categories.applicability: The design uses a 9-bit intermediate sum and truncates to 8 bits. Selecting the wrong slice produces a divided-by-two style result and breaks overflow, which depends on s[7].

bug_categories.bug_type: Bit width mismatch on intermediate sum
bug_categories.description: Shrink the sum wire from [8:0] to [7:0], or otherwise make the width insufficient, so the carry-out bit is lost; or alternatively widen/shorten operands so the addition context changes.
bug_categories.applicability: The sum is declared 9 bits to hold the carry. Changing its width alters the expression-width context and removes the carry bit, which could change behavior if sum[8] is used or if the slice is adjusted.

bug_categories.bug_type: Overflow computed from wrong signal (unsigned carry instead of signed overflow)
bug_categories.description: Replace the signed-overflow expression with the unsigned carry-out, e.g. 'assign overflow = sum[8];', or XOR the carry-in and carry-out of the sign bit incorrectly.
bug_categories.applicability: The module reports two's-complement overflow. Using sum[8] reports unsigned overflow instead, which differs for many cases such as 127+1 (signed overflow, no carry) or 255+1 (carry, no signed overflow).

bug_categories.description: In the overflow expression, replace b[7] with a[7] (e.g. '!(a[7]^a[7])') or in the sum use 'a + a' or 'b + b', so one operand is ignored or duplicated.
bug_categories.applicability: There are two symmetric 8-bit inputs a and b. A copy-paste style error that uses the same operand twice makes the sign check always true and the sum incorrect, while remaining valid Verilog.

mutants.bug_type: Bit width mismatch on intermediate sum
Overflow computed from wrong signal (unsigned carry instead of signed overflow)

bug_categories.description: Replace the non-blocking assignment 'q <= d' with a blocking assignment 'q = d' in the clocked always block.
bug_categories.applicability: Changes simulation scheduling semantics: q updates immediately in the active region, which can cause race conditions with other logic sampling q on the same clock edge. In this single-register design it would show up as a race when the output is sampled by a testbench or downstream logic at the clock edge.

bug_categories.description: Change 'always @(posedge clk)' to 'always @(negedge clk)' so data is captured on the falling edge.
bug_categories.applicability: The register would sample d half a cycle later than expected, so q would reflect values of d at a different time than the specification, breaking cycle-accurate behavior and timing relative to posedge-driven testbenches.

bug_categories.description: Assign only a subset of bits of d to q, e.g. 'q[6:0] <= d[6:0]' leaving the MSB unassigned, or 'q <= {1'b0, d[6:0]}'.
bug_categories.applicability: The 8-bit data path is the core of the design; dropping or forcing the MSB means q[7] never follows d[7], corrupting any data with the top bit set.

bug_categories.description: Reverse or swap bits when assigning, e.g. 'q <= {d[0],d[1],d[2],d[3],d[4],d[5],d[6],d[7]}' or swap nibbles 'q <= {d[3:0], d[7:4]}'.
bug_categories.applicability: Data is still captured every clock but arrives with scrambled bit positions, a subtle bug that passes simple all-zeros/all-ones tests but fails with arbitrary patterns.

bug_categories.description: Change 'initial q = 8'h0' to a nonzero value such as 8'hFF or 8'hA5, or remove the initial statement so q starts as X.
bug_categories.applicability: The design has no explicit reset, so the initial block is the only defined power-up state; altering it makes q's output before the first clock edge wrong (nonzero or unknown).

bug_categories.description: Apply an operation to the data path, such as 'q <= ~d', 'q <= d ^ 8'h01', or 'q <= d + 1'.
bug_categories.applicability: The register is a pure pass-through, so any combinational modification of d changes the functional contract (q should equal previous-cycle d) while remaining valid Verilog.

bug_categories.description: Add a spurious condition to the update, e.g. 'if (d != 8'hFF) q <= d;' or 'if (d[0]) q <= d;', so q holds its old value under certain inputs.
bug_categories.applicability: The register should load every clock cycle; an extra condition makes q retain stale data for specific input values, producing missing updates only on particular data patterns.

bug_categories.bug_type: Extra pipeline delay / stale data sampling
bug_categories.description: Introduce an additional internal register stage, e.g. 'reg [7:0] d_r; always @(posedge clk) begin d_r <= d; q <= d_r; end', so q lags d by two cycles.
bug_categories.applicability: Latency of the single-stage register is the key timing property; adding a stage keeps data values correct but shifts them one cycle late, breaking cycle-accurate comparison against the reference.

bug_categories.description: The wrap-around branch loads q with 0 instead of 1 (q <= 0), or another incorrect constant, so the counter sequence becomes 0..10 (11 states) rather than 1..10.
bug_categories.applicability: The design reloads q to 1 on reset or when q == 10; changing this constant alters the count range and period at every wrap and after every reset.

bug_categories.description: Change the terminal compare from q == 10 to q == 9 or q == 11, so the counter wraps one count early or one count late (11 would show value 11 before wrapping).
bug_categories.applicability: The terminal-count condition (q == 10) defines the counter's upper bound; shifting it changes the count range 1..10 to 1..9 or 1..11.

bug_categories.description: Reset loads a different value than the wrap reload, e.g. reset sets q to 0 while terminal count still reloads 1, by splitting the condition into separate branches with different values.
bug_categories.applicability: Reset and wrap share one branch and one value (1); separating them with inconsistent values creates a different initial state after reset than after wrap.

bug_categories.description: Replace the OR in (reset || (q == 10)) with AND, so the reload only occurs when both reset is high and q == 10; reset alone would no longer reset the counter and the counter would run past 10.
bug_categories.applicability: The single combined condition uses || to merge reset and terminal count; changing the operator breaks both functions.

bug_categories.description: Invert reset to (!reset || q == 10), or drop reset from the condition entirely so only q == 10 triggers the reload.
bug_categories.applicability: Reset is a synchronous, active-high input in the combined condition; inverting or removing it makes the counter reset incorrectly or never respond to reset.

bug_categories.description: Change q <= q + 1 to q <= q + 2 or q <= q - 1, so the counter skips values (and may never hit q == 10 exactly, e.g. starting from 1 with step 2 gives odd values only) or counts down.
bug_categories.applicability: The else branch increments by 1; an incorrect step would cause the counter to miss the terminal value 10 and run to 15 and wrap through 4-bit overflow.

bug_categories.description: Narrow the output q to [2:0] (or otherwise truncate it) so the value 10 cannot be represented, or widen the comparison so it mismatches the register width.
bug_categories.applicability: q is a 4-bit register needed to hold values up to 10; reducing width makes q == 10 unreachable (3 bits compared to 4'd10 never matches) and the counter never wraps correctly.

bug_categories.description: Change the clock edge from posedge clk to negedge clk, or change the nonblocking assignment to blocking, or make the reset asynchronous (posedge clk or posedge reset), altering timing relative to the intended synchronous behavior.
bug_categories.applicability: The always block is a single synchronous process; changing sensitivity to include posedge reset makes the reset asynchronous, and switching to negedge shifts when the counter updates relative to the testbench stimulus.

mutant_rejections.reason: does_not_elaborate (error: ERROR: Multiple edge sensitive events found for this signal!)

bug_categories.description: Remove the inversion on vibrate_mode in the ringer equation so it becomes ring & vibrate_mode, causing the ringer to sound only in vibrate mode.
bug_categories.applicability: The ringer assign uses ~vibrate_mode; dropping the '~' makes ringer and motor identical and breaks mutual exclusivity.

bug_categories.description: Add an inversion to vibrate_mode in the motor equation so it becomes ring & ~vibrate_mode, causing the motor to run in normal ring mode instead of vibrate mode.
bug_categories.applicability: The motor assign uses vibrate_mode directly; inverting it makes both outputs assert together when vibrate_mode=0 and neither when vibrate_mode=1.

bug_categories.description: Replace the AND in the ringer equation with OR, giving ring | ~vibrate_mode, so the ringer is active even when ring is low.
bug_categories.applicability: ringer = ring & ~vibrate_mode becomes asserted whenever vibrate_mode is 0 regardless of ring, causing spurious ringing.

bug_categories.description: Replace the AND in the motor equation with XOR, giving ring ^ vibrate_mode, so the motor activates when vibrate_mode is high without a ring, and deactivates when both are high.
bug_categories.applicability: motor = ring & vibrate_mode becomes ring ^ vibrate_mode, producing wrong output for ring=0,vibrate_mode=1 and ring=1,vibrate_mode=1.

bug_categories.bug_type: Input signal swap / wrong signal reference
bug_categories.description: Swap the control signals so that the ringer uses vibrate_mode in place of ring, e.g., ringer = vibrate_mode & ~ring, ignoring the actual ring input.
bug_categories.applicability: Both assigns depend on exactly two inputs; substituting one for the other yields a valid but functionally wrong expression.

bug_categories.description: Swap the left-hand sides so ringer gets the motor expression and motor gets the ringer expression, exchanging the two outputs' behaviors.
bug_categories.applicability: The two assigns are symmetric in structure, so swapping targets compiles cleanly while routing ring events to the wrong device.

bug_categories.description: Remove the ring term from one output so it depends only on vibrate_mode, e.g., motor = vibrate_mode, causing the motor to run continuously in vibrate mode even without an incoming ring.
bug_categories.applicability: Each output is gated by ring; deleting that term leaves a valid assign but outputs no longer follow the ring request.

bug_categories.description: Replace one output expression with a constant (e.g., assign ringer = 1'b0 or motor = 1'b1), or invert the entire output expression with a leading '~'.
bug_categories.applicability: Pure combinational outputs ringer and motor can be tied to a constant or fully inverted (~(ring & ~vibrate_mode)), producing always-off, always-on, or complemented behavior.

mutants.bug_type: Input signal swap / wrong signal reference

bug_categories.description: Change the reset condition from active-high to active-low (e.g., if(!reset) or if(~reset)), so the counter clears when reset is deasserted and counts while reset is asserted.
bug_categories.applicability: The design has a single synchronous reset input checked in the if(reset) branch; inverting it is a one-token change that remains valid Verilog and completely breaks reset behavior.

bug_categories.description: Reset loads a non-zero constant (e.g., 4'hF or 4'h1) instead of 0, so the counter starts from the wrong value after reset.
bug_categories.applicability: The statement q <= 0 can be changed to q <= 4'd1 or 4'hF, leaving the counter functional but with an incorrect initial sequence after reset.

bug_categories.description: Change the increment from +1 to +2 (or +3, or -1), causing the counter to skip values or count in the wrong direction.
bug_categories.applicability: The else branch q <= q + 1 can become q <= q + 2 or q <= q - 1; the 4-bit counter then skips odd values or counts down, violating the expected sequence.

bug_categories.description: Add a condition that wraps the counter early, e.g., if q == 4'd9 then q <= 0, converting it into a modulo-10 counter instead of a natural modulo-16 counter.
bug_categories.applicability: The 4-bit counter naturally wraps 15->0; inserting an extra comparison against a smaller constant breaks the full 0-15 range.

bug_categories.description: Change the sensitivity list to always @(posedge clk or posedge reset), making reset asynchronous rather than synchronous, which changes timing behavior when reset asserts between clock edges.
bug_categories.applicability: The original reset is synchronous and sampled only at posedge clk; adding posedge reset to the sensitivity list changes when q clears and alters waveform behavior relative to the reference.

bug_categories.description: Reduce the effective counter width, e.g., by only updating the lower 3 bits (q[2:0] <= q[2:0] + 1) or masking the upper bit, so q[3] never toggles properly.
bug_categories.applicability: Output q is declared [3:0]; modifying the assignment to affect only a subset of bits means the counter only cycles through 8 values and the MSB stays stuck.

bug_categories.description: Replace non-blocking assignments (<=) with blocking assignments (=) in the sequential block, altering simulation semantics and potentially causing race conditions with other logic reading q.
bug_categories.applicability: Both q <= 0 and q <= q + 1 can be changed to blocking assignments; for this single-register design the effect is subtle but is a realistic coding-style bug that can cause mismatches in testbench sampling.

bug_categories.description: Introduce faulty gating or priority, such as incrementing only when q[0] is 0, or giving the increment priority so reset is ignored in certain states (e.g., if(q != 4'd15 && reset)), so reset fails to clear the counter in some states.
bug_categories.applicability: The if/else structure gives reset top priority; adding a state-dependent condition to the reset branch means reset is ignored when q is 15, leaving the counter stuck or wrongly continuing.

bug_categories.bug_type: Logic operator error in select condition
bug_categories.description: Replace the AND (&) of sel_b1 and sel_b2 with OR (|) in the mux select condition, so b is chosen when either select is high instead of both.
bug_categories.applicability: Applies to the condition (sel_b1 & sel_b2) in assign out_assign and/or the always @(*) block for out_always. Changing only one path creates a mismatch between the two outputs.

bug_categories.description: Swap the ternary branches so a is selected when both selects are high and b otherwise, or negate the condition with ~ or !.
bug_categories.applicability: Affects the ternary 'sel_b1 & sel_b2 ? b : a' in either output, reversing the data source choice for every input combination.

bug_categories.description: Replace one of the data operands with the wrong signal, e.g. return a in both branches, return b in both branches, or swap a and b.
bug_categories.applicability: Applies to the two data inputs a and b in the ternary expressions; the outputs become independent of the select or of one data input.

bug_categories.description: Drop one select from the condition (use only sel_b1 or only sel_b2) or use a select twice (sel_b1 & sel_b1), so the two-input gating is lost.
bug_categories.applicability: The condition (sel_b1 & sel_b2) in one output; the design then selects b in cases where only one select is asserted.

bug_categories.description: Replace & with ^, ~&, or && variants (or use XOR/NAND), producing different truth tables for the select while still being valid Verilog.
bug_categories.applicability: With 1-bit signals && behaves like &, so use ^ or ~& to get a functional change; applies to the select expression in either output.

bug_categories.bug_type: Inconsistent implementation between assign and always outputs
bug_categories.description: Introduce a discrepancy so out_assign and out_always compute different functions, e.g. an extra term like '| a' or a different select in only one of them.
bug_categories.applicability: The design has two parallel implementations of the same mux; modifying only one violates the intended equivalence out_assign == out_always.

bug_categories.description: Replace always @(*) with an explicit incomplete sensitivity list such as always @(a or sel_b1), or make out_always assigned conditionally without an else, causing stale values or latch behavior.
bug_categories.applicability: Applies to the always @(*) block driving out_always; changes in b or sel_b2 would not update the output in simulation, diverging from out_assign.

bug_categories.bug_type: Blocking/non-blocking or stuck-at output assignment error
bug_categories.description: Force an output to a constant or add a clocked-style non-blocking assignment, e.g. out_always <= 1'b0 or assign out_assign = 1'b0 in a branch, so the output is stuck at a fixed value for some conditions.
bug_categories.applicability: Applies to either branch of the ternary in out_assign or out_always, e.g. replacing b with 1'b0 or a with 1'b1, producing stuck-at behavior when the select condition is met or not met.

mutants.bug_type: Blocking/non-blocking or stuck-at output assignment error

bug_categories.description: Change the wrap comparison from q == 9 to q == 8 or q == 10 so the decade counter wraps early (mod 9) or late (mod 11).
bug_categories.applicability: The terminal value 9 in the (q == 9) condition defines the BCD/mod-10 count range; altering the constant directly changes the counter modulus.

bug_categories.description: Remove the reset term from the condition so that only q == 9 clears the counter, making the reset input ineffective.
bug_categories.applicability: The condition 'reset || (q == 9)' combines synchronous reset with wrap; dropping 'reset' leaves q unknown/X at startup and unresettable.

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong logical operator in reset/wrap condition
bug_categories.description: Replace the OR with AND ('reset && (q == 9)') so the counter only clears when reset is asserted while q is 9, breaking both independent reset and wrap behavior.
bug_categories.applicability: The '||' between reset and (q == 9) is the key combining operator; changing it to && makes wrap and reset non-functional in most states.

bug_categories.description: Change the value loaded on reset/wrap from 0 to 1 (or another nonzero value), so the count sequence becomes 1..9 or starts from a wrong value after reset.
bug_categories.applicability: The assignment q <= 0 serves both reset and wrap; a wrong constant shifts the sequence and changes the modulus to 9.

bug_categories.description: Change q + 1 to q + 2 (or q - 1) so the counter skips values or counts down; with +2 and the q == 9 check, the counter may never hit 9 from an even start and run through 0-15 wrapping naturally.
bug_categories.applicability: The else branch q <= q + 1 defines counting behavior; a different step makes q == 9 unreachable from even values and breaks the decade sequence.

bug_categories.description: Replace q == 9 with q >= 9 or q > 9, or use q != 9, altering when the wrap occurs; q != 9 would constantly reset the counter and q > 9 would let it count to 10 before wrapping.
bug_categories.applicability: The equality test on the 4-bit q is the wrap detector; relational/inequality variants change the wrap timing and the maximum reachable value.

bug_categories.description: Change posedge clk to negedge clk, or make the block asynchronous-reset by adding posedge reset to the sensitivity list, altering timing and reset semantics.
bug_categories.applicability: The always @(posedge clk) block with a reset checked inside makes this a synchronous reset; changing the sensitivity list changes when reset takes effect and the clock phase of the output.

bug_categories.description: Narrow the counter effective width (e.g., declare q as [2:0] or compare only q[2:0] == 1) so the wrap value 9 cannot be represented or detected correctly, causing wrong wrap or overflow at 7/8.
bug_categories.applicability: q is a 4-bit output needed to represent 0-9; reducing width or partially comparing bits (e.g., q[3] & q[0] matching 9, 11, 13, 15 patterns) breaks the decade range.

bug_categories.description: Change the reset condition from active-high to active-low (if(!reset)), so the register clears when reset is deasserted and captures data when reset is asserted.
bug_categories.applicability: The design has a single synchronous reset input controlling q; inverting its sense breaks both normal capture and reset behavior.

bug_categories.description: Change the sensitivity list to always @(posedge clk or posedge reset), turning the synchronous reset into an asynchronous one.
bug_categories.applicability: The original reset only takes effect on a clock edge; making it asynchronous changes timing behavior, causing q to clear immediately when reset rises between clock edges.

bug_categories.description: Reset q to a nonzero constant (e.g., 8'hFF or 8'h01) instead of 0.
bug_categories.applicability: The reset branch assigns q <= 0; altering this constant makes the post-reset output state incorrect.

bug_categories.description: Change the triggering edge from posedge clk to negedge clk, so the register samples on the falling edge.
bug_categories.applicability: Single clocked always block; the edge change shifts capture timing by half a cycle and alters cycle-level behavior relative to the testbench.

bug_categories.description: Reset or load only part of the 8-bit register, e.g., q[3:0] <= 0 on reset or q[6:0] <= d[6:0] on load, leaving bits unchanged.
bug_categories.applicability: q and d are 8 bits wide; partial assignment leaves upper bits holding stale values, producing subtle data corruption.

bug_categories.description: Assign a bit-reversed or swapped version of d to q, e.g., q <= {d[0],d[1],...,d[7]} or swap nibbles {d[3:0],d[7:4]}.
bug_categories.applicability: The data path is a direct 8-bit copy; permuting bits yields valid Verilog but wrong output data.

bug_categories.description: Replace non-blocking assignments (<=) with blocking (=) in the clocked block.
bug_categories.applicability: While functionally similar for this single register in isolation, it introduces simulation race hazards when q is sampled by other logic on the same clock edge, and deviates from proper sequential coding style.

bug_categories.bug_type: Data corruption / logic inversion on load
bug_categories.description: Invert or modify the loaded data, e.g., q <= ~d, q <= d ^ 8'h01, or q <= d + 1.
bug_categories.applicability: The else branch is a plain pass-through of d; any combinational modification changes the registered output value without affecting reset behavior.

bug_categories.description: Replicate a different bit of the input (e.g., in[6] or in[0]) instead of the MSB in[7] as the sign extension bit.
bug_categories.applicability: The replication { 24{ in[7] } } depends on in[7] being the sign bit of the 8-bit input; selecting another bit yields wrong upper bits for many inputs.

bug_categories.description: Change the replication count from 24 to 23 or 25 so the concatenation width no longer equals 32 bits, causing truncation or zero-padding at the output.
bug_categories.applicability: The output is 32 bits made of 24 replicated bits plus 8 input bits; an off-by-one count makes the concatenation 31 or 33 bits wide, so out is implicitly padded or truncated and the MSB or LSB alignment is wrong.

bug_categories.bug_type: Sign extension replaced with zero extension
bug_categories.description: Replace the replicated sign bit with constant zeros (e.g., { 24'b0, in }), so negative values are not sign-extended.
bug_categories.applicability: Inputs with in[7]=1 produce 0x000000XX instead of 0xFFFFFFXX, a classic signed/unsigned confusion bug.

bug_categories.bug_type: Sign extension replaced with one extension
bug_categories.description: Replace the replicated sign bit with constant ones (e.g., { 24'hFFFFFF, in }) or invert the sign bit ({24{~in[7]}}).
bug_categories.applicability: Positive inputs get 0xFFFFFF upper bits (or inverted sign bits), breaking correct extension for in[7]=0 cases.

bug_categories.description: Swap the order of the operands in the concatenation so the input byte occupies the upper bits: { in, {24{in[7]}} }.
bug_categories.applicability: The original places in at out[7:0] and the extension at out[31:8]; swapping puts the data in out[31:24] and the sign bits in out[23:0], corrupting the value.

bug_categories.description: Reverse the bit order of the input in the low byte, e.g., use { in[0], in[1], ..., in[7] } or swap nibbles, instead of passing in directly.
bug_categories.applicability: The low 8 bits of out should equal in; reordering the bits gives incorrect data while keeping the output width at 32.

bug_categories.description: Split the extension so only part of the upper bits use the sign (e.g., { 16{in[7]}, 8'b0, in } or { {23{in[7]}}, 1'b0, in }), leaving some bits not sign-extended.
bug_categories.applicability: The 24 upper bits must all equal in[7]; a hard-coded constant in any slice causes wrong values on out[31:8] for specific bit positions.

bug_categories.bug_type: Data bit corruption in low byte
bug_categories.description: Modify the low byte passthrough, e.g., use { ..., in[7:1], 1'b0 } (dropping in[0]), or replace one bit with in[7] or a constant.
bug_categories.applicability: The low byte out[7:0] should exactly mirror in; altering a single bit produces a subtle error visible only when that bit differs.

original_code:
module dut
(
  input a,
  input b,
  input c,
  input d,
  input e,
  output [24:0] out
);

  assign out = ~{ { 5{ a } }, { 5{ b } }, { 5{ c } }, { 5{ d } }, { 5{ e } } } ^ { 5{ a, b, c, d, e } };

endmodule

bug_categories.description: Remove the bitwise NOT on the replicated-input concatenation so the left operand is no longer inverted before the XOR.
bug_categories.applicability: The expression ~{{5{a}},{5{b}},{5{c}},{5{d}},{5{e}}} ^ {5{a,b,c,d,e}} depends on the inversion; dropping '~' flips every output bit, since out becomes the XOR of the non-inverted pattern.

bug_categories.description: Replace the XOR operator with AND, OR, or XNOR when combining the two 25-bit operands.
bug_categories.applicability: Changing '^' to '&', '|' or '~^' alters every output bit where the two operands differ, yet remains valid 25-bit Verilog.

bug_categories.description: Change one of the replication factors, e.g. {5{c}} to {4{c}} or {6{c}}, in the left concatenation.
bug_categories.applicability: The left operand must be 25 bits (5 groups of 5). Altering a factor changes the width and shifts all lower groups, causing truncation or zero-extension against the 25-bit right operand and misaligning bits.

bug_categories.description: Swap the order of two inputs in the left concatenation, e.g. {5{a}},{5{c}},{5{b}},...
bug_categories.applicability: Groups map to specific out bit ranges (a to [24:20], b to [19:15], etc.). Swapping reorders which input drives which 5-bit slice while the right operand pattern stays the same, producing wrong values in those slices.

bug_categories.description: Replace one input in the left concatenation with another, e.g. {5{d}} becomes {5{e}}, or duplicate an input.
bug_categories.applicability: Each group should use a distinct input; a copy-paste style error makes two slices track the same input and drops dependence on another one.

bug_categories.description: Change the order of the inner concatenation in the repeated pattern {5{a,b,c,d,e}}, e.g. to {5{e,d,c,b,a}}, or a different permutation.
bug_categories.applicability: The right operand repeats the 5-bit pattern abcde five times, so the XOR with each uniform 5-bit group relies on bit position. Reversing or permuting it changes which bit in each group is toggled.

bug_categories.description: Apply the NOT to only part of the concatenation (e.g. invert only some groups like ~{5{a}}) or to the right operand instead of the left, or to the final result.
bug_categories.applicability: Operator scope matters here: moving '~' onto individual replicated terms or the right operand changes bits in only some slices (or, for the right operand, yields the same inversion semantics only coincidentally), creating subtle slice-specific errors.

bug_categories.description: Assign only a portion of the result or insert a bit-select/part-select such as out[23:0] or shift the result by one bit, so the MSB or LSB is lost or constant.
bug_categories.applicability: The output is a 25-bit bus; truncating, shifting, or rotating the result, or tying a bit to a constant, leaves one end of the bus incorrect while the rest looks plausible.
