bug_categories.description: Change out_or_bitwise = a | b to a & b, so each output bit is high only when both inputs are high instead of either.
bug_categories.applicability: Directly alters the 3-bit bitwise OR assignment; outputs differ whenever a and b differ in any bit position (e.g., a=3'b101, b=3'b000).

bug_categories.description: Replace a | b with a ^ b in out_or_bitwise, so the result is wrong only when both inputs have a 1 in the same bit.
bug_categories.applicability: A subtle bug: it passes tests where a and b never overlap in set bits and fails only when a & b != 0 (e.g., a=3'b011, b=3'b001).

bug_categories.description: Change out_or_logical = a || b to a | b (or a bitwise reduction like |(a|b) variant misused), or conversely change out_or_bitwise to use ||, which collapses a 3-bit result into a single bit replicated into bit 0.
bug_categories.applicability: The design intentionally contrasts | and ||; swapping them makes out_or_bitwise become {2'b00, a||b} (zero-extended 1-bit), breaking upper bits, or truncates out_or_logical to bit 0 of a|b, which is wrong for inputs like a=3'b010, b=3'b000.

bug_categories.bug_type: Logical OR changed to logical AND
bug_categories.description: Replace a || b with a && b in out_or_logical so the output is 1 only when both a and b are nonzero.
bug_categories.applicability: Fails whenever exactly one of a or b is nonzero (e.g., a=3'b100, b=3'b000), which the logical-OR output should report as 1.

bug_categories.description: Swap the operands in { ~b, ~a } to { ~a, ~b } so the upper and lower halves of out_not are exchanged.
bug_categories.applicability: out_not[5:3] should hold ~b and out_not[2:0] should hold ~a; swapping them is still valid 6-bit Verilog but is wrong whenever a != b.

bug_categories.description: Remove the bitwise NOT on one operand, e.g., { b, ~a } or { ~b, a }, so one half of out_not passes through uninverted.
bug_categories.applicability: Affects only half of the 6-bit out_not vector, so tests checking only one half could miss it; every input value exposes the error in the affected half.

bug_categories.bug_type: Bitwise NOT replaced with logical NOT
bug_categories.description: Use !b or !a instead of ~b or ~a inside the concatenation, which yields a 1-bit result that is zero-extended/sized to 1 bit within the concatenation, changing the width and layout of out_not.
bug_categories.applicability: { !b, ~a } becomes a 4-bit value zero-padded to 6 bits (with width shifting), so out_not[5:4] become 0 and bit 3 only reflects whether b==0; wrong for most nonzero b values like b=3'b101.

bug_categories.description: Narrow or mis-index an operand, e.g., use a[1:0] | b[1:0] for out_or_bitwise or { ~b[1:0], ~a } for out_not, dropping the MSB or shifting concatenation widths.
bug_categories.applicability: Leaves bit 2 of out_or_bitwise at zero-extended 0 and shrinks out_not's concatenated width to 5 bits, so tests where a[2] or b[2] is 1 (e.g., a=3'b100) expose the bug while low-valued inputs pass.

mutants.bug_type: Logical OR changed to logical AND

bug_categories.description: Change the triggering clock edge from negedge clk to posedge clk, so q updates on the rising edge instead of the falling edge.
bug_categories.applicability: The always block is triggered by @(negedge clk). Switching to posedge shifts the sampling time of d and reset by half a cycle, breaking timing relative to the expected falling-edge behavior.

bug_categories.description: Change the reset constant from 8'h34 to a different value such as 8'h43, 8'h35, or 8'h00.
bug_categories.applicability: The reset branch loads q with 8'h34. Altering this constant makes the post-reset output differ from the specification while remaining valid Verilog.

bug_categories.description: Invert the reset condition so that the reset value is loaded when reset is low (if(!reset)) instead of when it is high.
bug_categories.applicability: The design uses an active-high synchronous reset via if(reset). Inverting it causes q to be stuck at 8'h34 during normal operation (reset=0) and to pass d during reset.

bug_categories.description: Add reset to the sensitivity list (always @(negedge clk or posedge reset)) turning the synchronous reset into an asynchronous one.
bug_categories.applicability: The reset is currently sampled only on the falling clock edge. Making it asynchronous makes q jump to 8'h34 immediately when reset asserts, changing timing behavior.

bug_categories.description: Replace the non-blocking assignments (<=) with blocking assignments (=) in the sequential block.
bug_categories.applicability: q <= 8'h34 and q <= d use non-blocking assignments. Using blocking assignments changes the scheduling semantics and can create race conditions with downstream logic sampling q on the same clock edge.

bug_categories.description: Corrupt the data path by reversing bits, swapping nibbles, or dropping/inverting bits of d when assigned to q (e.g., q <= {d[3:0], d[7:4]} or q <= ~d).
bug_categories.applicability: The else branch assigns q <= d directly across all 8 bits. Any permutation, inversion, or masking of d produces wrong output data while remaining width-correct.

bug_categories.description: Assign only part of the data to q, such as q[6:0] <= d[6:0] or q <= {1'b0, d[6:0]}, leaving the MSB stale or forced to zero.
bug_categories.applicability: q and d are 8 bits wide. Partial-width assignment causes bit 7 to hold its old value or be zeroed, silently corrupting the upper bit of the data.

bug_categories.bug_type: Missing or gated update (enable/priority logic error)
bug_categories.description: Add an incorrect condition on the else branch, such as only updating q when d is nonzero or when q differs from d, or make the reset branch not override by reordering conditions.
bug_categories.applicability: The module has a simple reset-priority-over-data structure. Adding a spurious condition on the data load (or swapping priority so d overrides reset) means q fails to follow d or fails to reset to 8'h34 as expected.

bug_categories.description: Change the reset condition from if(r) to if(!r), so the flop clears when r is low and captures d when r is high.
bug_categories.applicability: The single synchronous reset input r controls the if/else branch in the always block; inverting it flips the entire reset behavior while remaining valid Verilog.

bug_categories.description: Change the reset assignment from q <= 0 to q <= 1, so asserting r sets the output high instead of clearing it.
bug_categories.applicability: The reset branch assigns a constant 0 to q; changing the constant produces a plausible reset-value bug that is only visible when r is asserted.

bug_categories.description: Change the sensitivity list to @(posedge clk or posedge r), making the reset take effect immediately rather than at the next clock edge.
bug_categories.applicability: The design uses a synchronous reset in a posedge clk block; adding posedge r to the sensitivity list changes timing behavior so q clears between clock edges.

bug_categories.description: Change the triggering edge from posedge clk to negedge clk, so the flop samples d and r on the falling edge.
bug_categories.applicability: The always block is triggered by posedge clk; switching to negedge shifts the output timing by half a cycle and changes the sampled values relative to the other synchronous signals.

bug_categories.description: Change the else branch from q <= d to q <= ~d, so the stored value is the complement of the input.
bug_categories.applicability: The non-reset path simply registers d; inverting it yields a valid but functionally wrong flop that outputs the opposite of the expected data.

bug_categories.description: Replace the non-blocking assignments (<=) with blocking assignments (=) in the always block.
bug_categories.applicability: Both branches use non-blocking assignments for sequential logic; blocking assignments can cause race conditions with other logic sampling q on the same clock edge when the module is instantiated in a larger design.

bug_categories.description: Make the reset conditional on both inputs, e.g. if(r & d) or if(r | d), so reset is gated or falsely triggered by the data input.
bug_categories.applicability: The reset condition depends only on r; including d in the condition makes the reset fire incorrectly (when d is high) or fail to fire (when d is low), corrupting both reset and data capture.

bug_categories.bug_type: Stuck-at / missing update (incorrect enable or hold logic)
bug_categories.description: Make q hold its previous value in the else branch (e.g., q <= q) or remove the else path so data is only loaded under a wrong condition, such as q <= d only when d is 1.
bug_categories.applicability: The else branch is the only path that captures d; replacing it with hold behavior or a conditional update leaves q stuck after reset and prevents it from following d correctly.

mutants.bug_type: Stuck-at / missing update (incorrect enable or hold logic)

bug_categories.description: Change the asynchronous reset condition from active-high to active-low, e.g. 'if(!ar)' in the body while the sensitivity list still uses 'posedge ar', or invert the check so the flop is cleared when ar is deasserted.
bug_categories.applicability: The ar signal is the sole asynchronous reset. Inverting its polarity in the if-condition makes the flop load d during reset and clear to 0 during normal operation, breaking basic functionality.

bug_categories.description: Change the reset assignment from 'q <= 0' to 'q <= 1', so the asynchronous reset sets the output instead of clearing it.
bug_categories.applicability: The design is a single-bit D flip-flop with async reset to 0. Resetting to 1 is a valid-Verilog change that violates the specified reset state.

bug_categories.bug_type: Sensitivity list error (async reset to sync)
bug_categories.description: Remove 'or posedge ar' from the sensitivity list so the reset becomes synchronous: 'always @(posedge clk)'.
bug_categories.applicability: The module's defining feature is the asynchronous reset. With a synchronous reset, q does not clear until the next clock edge, and a reset pulse between clock edges is missed entirely.

bug_categories.description: Change 'posedge clk' to 'negedge clk' in the sensitivity list so data is captured on the falling edge.
bug_categories.applicability: Shifts the sampling point by half a cycle, so q captures d at a different time and the output timing relative to the clock changes, breaking cycle-accurate behavior.

bug_categories.description: Change 'posedge ar' to 'negedge ar' in the sensitivity list while keeping 'if(ar)' in the body.
bug_categories.applicability: The reset would trigger on deassertion of ar rather than assertion, so the flop is not cleared when ar rises. Reset is only evaluated on a clock edge or on ar falling, where the if(ar) check fails and q loads d.

bug_categories.description: Replace one or both non-blocking assignments '<=' with blocking '=' in the sequential always block.
bug_categories.applicability: For a single flop the simulated behavior is mostly unchanged, but it introduces a race condition with downstream logic sampling q on the same clock edge, and is a realistic coding-style bug that can alter behavior in a larger testbench or composed design.

bug_categories.description: Assign the inverted data 'q <= ~d' or tie the data to a constant or to ar in the non-reset branch.
bug_categories.applicability: The only data path is q <= d. Inverting or replacing it makes the output wrong on every clock edge while leaving the reset behavior intact, so the bug is only visible in normal operation.

bug_categories.description: Gate the reset with the clock-data condition, e.g. 'if(ar && d) q <= 0;' or swap the branches so that d takes priority over ar: 'if(d) q <= 1; else if(ar) q <= 0; else q <= d;'.
bug_categories.applicability: Reset must have absolute priority over data. Altering the priority or adding extra conditions means ar fails to clear q when d is high, leaving the flop in an incorrect state during reset.

bug_categories.description: Replace one or both OR operators in the reduction with AND, e.g. out = a & b & c, so the output only asserts when all inputs are high.
bug_categories.applicability: The entire design is a single 3-input OR expression, so swapping the operator fundamentally changes the function and is trivially detectable by any vector where only one input is high.

bug_categories.description: Replace OR with XOR, e.g. out = a ^ b ^ c, making the output a parity function that deasserts when two inputs are high.
bug_categories.applicability: Matches OR on vectors with 0 or 1 high inputs but differs when exactly two inputs are high (output 0 instead of 1), a subtle bug requiring multi-input-high vectors to detect.

bug_categories.description: Drop one operand from the expression, e.g. out = a | b, so input c is ignored.
bug_categories.applicability: Simulates an incomplete connection or forgotten input; output is wrong only when c is the sole asserted input, requiring directed tests on c alone.

bug_categories.description: Introduce an incorrect operator mix such as out = a | b & c, where AND binds tighter than OR, so b and c are ANDed before being ORed with a.
bug_categories.applicability: With three operands in a flat expression, a mistaken mixed operator yields wrong output when b or c is high alone, a classic precedence mistake.

bug_categories.description: Invert one input in the expression, e.g. out = a | ~b | c, so b behaves as active-low.
bug_categories.applicability: Output becomes 1 whenever b is 0, so the output is stuck high for most vectors and only deasserts with a=0, b=1, c=0.

bug_categories.description: Negate the full result, e.g. out = ~(a | b | c), producing a NOR function.
bug_categories.applicability: Output is the complement of the correct value for every input combination, mimicking a polarity or inversion error on the output stage.

bug_categories.bug_type: Bitwise vs logical operator mismatch / wrong operator class
bug_categories.description: Use a reduction or logical operator that changes semantics, such as out = a || b && c or out = (a | b) & c, introducing a gating term.
bug_categories.applicability: Since all signals are 1-bit, logical and bitwise forms mostly coincide, but mixing in && or gating with c makes the output depend on c being high, breaking cases where only a or b is asserted.

bug_categories.description: Replace one operand with a constant, e.g. out = a | b | 1'b0 (dropping c) or out = a | b | 1'b1 (stuck high), or tie the output to a constant.
bug_categories.applicability: Models a stuck-at fault on an input net; a stuck-at-1 forces out high regardless of inputs, while stuck-at-0 on one input masks that input's contribution.

bug_categories.description: Replace the reduction AND on 'in' with a reduction OR (or NAND/XOR), e.g. 'assign out_and = |in;' so out_and no longer requires all bits to be 1.
bug_categories.applicability: out_and uses ∈ swapping to another reduction operator is syntactically valid and changes behavior for every input except 0000 and 1111 (for OR) or flips the result entirely (for NAND).

bug_categories.description: Add a logical or bitwise negation to one output, e.g. 'assign out_or = ~|in;' (NOR) or 'assign out_xor = ~^in;' (XNOR), inverting the polarity of that output.
bug_categories.applicability: All three outputs are single-bit reduction results, so inverting any of them is a trivial yet functionally significant error that fails on every input vector.

bug_categories.description: Apply the reduction to a subset of the input, e.g. 'assign out_xor = ^in[2:0];' or 'assign out_and = &in[3:1];', omitting a bit.
bug_categories.applicability: The 4-bit input 'in' feeds all reductions; dropping the MSB or LSB makes the output ignore one input bit, producing wrong results whenever that bit matters.

bug_categories.description: Replace the reduction with an explicit bit expression that uses a wrong or duplicated index, e.g. 'assign out_xor = in[0]^in[1]^in[2]^in[2];' or 'in[0]&in[1]&in[2]&in[2]'.
bug_categories.applicability: Expanding the reductions into explicit per-bit expressions invites index typos; a duplicated index cancels in XOR (ignoring in[3] and in[2]) and silently drops a bit in AND/OR.

bug_categories.description: Use a logical operator instead of a reduction operator, e.g. 'assign out_or = in || 1'b0;' or 'assign out_and = in && 4'hF;', or apply a bitwise operator that truncates to one bit.
bug_categories.applicability: Logical operators treat 'in' as a boolean (non-zero = true), so out_and written as '!!in' behaves like OR, and a bitwise op with a wider constant is truncated to the single-bit output, creating subtle mismatches.

bug_categories.description: Swap the expressions driven onto two outputs, e.g. 'assign out_and = |in; assign out_or = ∈' or swap out_or and out_xor.
bug_categories.applicability: The three outputs have identical widths and types, so exchanging their drivers compiles cleanly with no warnings but gives wrong functionality on most input vectors.

bug_categories.description: Tie an output to a constant or to a single input bit, e.g. 'assign out_or = 1'b0;' or 'assign out_xor = in[0];', producing a stuck-at fault.
bug_categories.applicability: Purely combinational design with no state; hard-wiring an output to a constant or a lone bit is simple to insert and is only exposed when the vectors exercise the differing input combinations.

bug_categories.description: Replace a reduction with a counting or comparison condition that is almost correct, e.g. 'assign out_and = (in >= 4'hE);' or 'assign out_or = (in > 4'd1);' or 'assign out_xor = ~(^in) & |in;'.
bug_categories.applicability: Reductions can be re-expressed as comparisons or compound conditions; boundary errors only fail on specific vectors (e.g. 1110 or 0001), making these corner-case bugs hard to catch with sparse testing.

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong reduction operator on AND output
bug_categories.description: Replace the reduction AND (&in) with reduction OR, NAND, or XOR so out_and no longer indicates that all bits are 1.
bug_categories.applicability: out_and = &in is a single-line assignment; changing it to |in or ~&in is valid Verilog and makes out_and wrong whenever in is not all zeros or all ones.

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong reduction operator on OR output
bug_categories.description: Replace the reduction OR (|in) with reduction AND, NOR, or XNOR so out_or fails to flag any set bit.
bug_categories.applicability: out_or = |in becoming &in or ^in would only match the correct result for all-zero or all-one inputs, so most random vectors expose it.

bug_categories.description: Change ^in to ~^in (XNOR reduction) so out_xor reports even parity instead of odd parity.
bug_categories.applicability: With 100 inputs, out_xor is the odd-parity of in; inverting it flips the result for every input vector, a subtle bug that is easy to miss.

bug_categories.bug_type: Bit width truncation of input range
bug_categories.description: Apply the reductions to a partial slice such as in[98:0] or in[99:1], so one bit (MSB or LSB) is ignored.
bug_categories.applicability: The 100-bit in bus makes an off-by-one slice plausible; e.g. out_and = &in[98:0] gives wrong results when only bit 99 is 0, and out_xor wrong when only bit 99 toggles.

bug_categories.description: Use inconsistent ranges among outputs, e.g. out_and over in[99:0], out_or over in[98:0], out_xor over in[99:1].
bug_categories.applicability: Three parallel reductions on the same bus can silently diverge in bit coverage, so each output is wrong only for stimulus on a specific bit position.

bug_categories.description: Swap the expressions driving two outputs, e.g. out_and = |in and out_or = &in, or out_or = ^in and out_xor = |in.
bug_categories.applicability: All three outputs are single-bit wires with identical type, so swapping their drivers compiles cleanly while giving functionally wrong outputs.

bug_categories.bug_type: Bit-reversal or partial bit-permutation of input
bug_categories.description: Feed reductions with a reordered or concatenated version of in, such as {in[49:0], in[99:50]} or a bit-reversed vector, or mix halves for one output.
bug_categories.applicability: AND, OR, and XOR reductions are permutation-invariant, so full permutation is harmless, but replacing part of the vector with duplicated bits, e.g. {in[99:50], in[99:50]}, changes coverage and breaks the outputs, particularly the XOR parity, where duplicates cancel.

bug_categories.bug_type: Hard-coded constant or masked input bits
bug_categories.description: Mask the input with a constant before reduction, e.g. &(in | 100'h1) or ^(in & ~100'h1), or tie a bit to 0 or 1.
bug_categories.applicability: A stuck-at mask on a single bit makes out_and ignore that bit, out_or always 1 or ignore it, and out_xor parity shift, emulating a stuck-at fault on the 100-bit input bus.

mutants.bug_type: Wrong reduction operator on AND output
Wrong reduction operator on OR output

bug_categories.description: Replace the XOR in 'out <= in ^ out' with OR, AND, XNOR, or NAND so the toggle behavior changes.
bug_categories.applicability: The design is a T-flip-flop-style toggle: out flips when in=1 and holds when in=0. With OR the output latches high; with AND it can only fall to 0 or stay 0; with XNOR it toggles on in=0 instead of in=1.

bug_categories.description: Invert the input in the expression, e.g. 'out <= ~in ^ out', so toggling happens when in=0 rather than in=1.
bug_categories.applicability: The single input in directly controls the toggle enable. Inverting it reverses the active level, and the output toggles every cycle while in is idle.

bug_categories.description: Change 'initial out = 0' to 'initial out = 1' or remove the initialization so out starts at 1 or X.
bug_categories.applicability: There is no reset signal, so the initial block alone defines the starting state. A different start value inverts the whole output sequence, and no initialization leaves X permanently because X ^ in remains X.

bug_categories.description: Change 'always @(posedge clk)' to 'negedge clk' or to both edges.
bug_categories.applicability: The toggle is sampled on the rising edge. Using the falling edge shifts timing by half a cycle, and using both edges makes the output toggle twice as often per clock period.

bug_categories.description: Replace the non-blocking '<=' with the blocking '=' in the sequential always block.
bug_categories.applicability: With a single register and no other readers in the block, simulation behavior may appear the same, but races can appear with other logic sampling out on the same clock edge, which makes the change a subtle bug.

bug_categories.description: Drop the feedback so the register no longer uses its own value, e.g. 'out <= in'.
bug_categories.applicability: The design's function depends on out feeding back into the XOR. Removing it turns the toggle flop into a simple D flop that passes in delayed by one cycle.

bug_categories.bug_type: Feedback from wrong or stale signal
bug_categories.description: Replace the feedback with a delayed or wrong value, such as an extra register holding the previous in value, or XOR with a constant: 'out <= in ^ 1'.
bug_categories.applicability: The toggle relies on XOR with the current out. Using a constant or a stale input value makes the output a plain inverse of in or an incorrect toggle pattern.

bug_categories.description: Change the sensitivity list from 'posedge clk' to a level-sensitive or combinational form such as 'always @(*)' or 'always @(in)'.
bug_categories.applicability: The design requires clocked state. A combinational or input-sensitive block creates a feedback loop out = in ^ out, or updates only on changes of in, so toggling is no longer synchronized to the clock.

bug_categories.description: Replace the AND between j and ~Q with OR, giving Q <= j | ~Q | ~k & Q (or similar), which changes set/toggle behavior.
bug_categories.applicability: The term 'j & ~Q' implements the set/toggle path of the JK flip-flop; changing & to | makes Q set to 1 whenever j is high or Q is low, breaking hold and reset behavior.

bug_categories.description: Remove the inversion on k in the hold term, so it becomes k & Q instead of ~k & Q.
bug_categories.applicability: With k=0 the flop no longer holds and clears instead; with k=1 it holds instead of resetting. This inverts the semantics of the K input.

bug_categories.description: Change ~Q in the set term to Q (j & Q), removing the inversion of the feedback.
bug_categories.applicability: j=1,k=0 no longer sets/toggles Q correctly; Q can never go from 0 to 1 through j, so the flop gets stuck at 0 after initialization.

bug_categories.description: Swap j and k in the expression: Q <= k & ~Q | ~j & Q.
bug_categories.applicability: Both inputs are single-bit signals of the same type, so the swap is valid Verilog but exchanges set and reset roles, making the J=1,K=0 and J=0,K=1 behaviors wrong.

bug_categories.description: Change posedge clk to negedge clk in the sensitivity list.
bug_categories.applicability: The design is a single synchronous process; using the opposite edge shifts when Q updates by half a cycle relative to the inputs, causing timing/sampling mismatches with the expected behavior.

bug_categories.description: Replace the non-blocking assignment <= with blocking = in the always block.
bug_categories.applicability: Q feeds back into its own next-state expression; blocking assignment changes race behavior with other logic reading Q at the same clock edge in simulation, potentially causing ordering-dependent results.

bug_categories.description: Add parentheses that change the evaluation order, e.g. Q <= j & (~Q | ~k) & Q, or (j & ~Q | ~k) & Q.
bug_categories.applicability: The expression relies on & binding tighter than |; regrouping alters the logic so toggle (j=k=1) and set/hold behaviors differ from the JK truth table.

bug_categories.description: Modify the expression so the j=k=1 case holds or sets rather than toggles, e.g. Q <= j & ~Q | ~k & Q | j & k & Q, or replace ~k & Q with ~(k & ~j) & Q.
bug_categories.applicability: The toggle condition is the defining feature of a JK flop; altering the Q-feedback terms makes j=k=1 produce a constant or held value instead of inverting Q each clock.

bug_categories.description: Remove or add an inversion on one literal in the first product term, e.g. change ~c & ~b to c & ~b or ~c & b.
bug_categories.applicability: The term ~c & ~b covers the minterms where both b and c are low. Flipping either literal makes the output wrong for those input combinations, so a functional mismatch is guaranteed.

bug_categories.description: Replace an AND with OR inside a product term, e.g. ~d & ~a becomes ~d | ~a, or replace one of the OR operators between terms with AND.
bug_categories.applicability: The sum-of-products expression relies on AND within terms and OR between them. Swapping any operator changes the covered minterms substantially, and the result is still valid Verilog.

bug_categories.description: Delete one of the four product terms, for example drop b & c & d.
bug_categories.applicability: Each term covers unique minterms. Removing b & c & d leaves minterm 1110 (b=1,c=1,d=1,a=0) uncovered, so out goes low when it should be high.

bug_categories.description: Replace one input with another in a term, e.g. a & c & d becomes a & b & d, or ~d & ~a becomes ~d & ~b.
bug_categories.applicability: The four 1-bit inputs a, b, c, d are used symmetrically in similar-looking terms, so a copy-paste style swap is plausible and it changes the truth table.

bug_categories.description: Add parentheses that regroup the expression, e.g. ~c & (~b | ~d) & ~a | ... or (a | b) & c & d changed into a | (b & c & d).
bug_categories.applicability: The expression mixes & and | and depends on & binding tighter than |. Inserting or moving parentheses alters the grouping and thus the logic function.

bug_categories.bug_type: Inversion scope error (bitwise vs. grouped negation)
bug_categories.description: Change ~c & ~b into ~(c & b) or ~(c | b) variants, or replace ~d & ~a with ~(d & a).
bug_categories.applicability: Applying negation over a group is not equivalent to negating each literal (De Morgan). ~c & ~b equals ~(c | b), but ~(c & b) differs, so the output changes while the form still looks natural.

bug_categories.bug_type: Redundant/extra literal added to a term
bug_categories.description: Add an additional literal to a term, e.g. a & c & d becomes a & c & d & b, or remove one literal such as a & c & d becoming a & c.
bug_categories.applicability: The three-literal terms a & c & d and b & c & d each cover 2 minterms. Adding a literal shrinks the covered set, and removing one expands it to cover the minterm where d=0, causing false-high outputs.

bug_categories.description: Force the output or a term to a constant, e.g. assign out = (expr) | 1'b0 replaced with out = (expr) & ~(a & b & c & d), or replace one term with 1'b1/1'b0.
bug_categories.applicability: The design is a purely combinational single-output function, so forcing a term or the output to a constant, or masking the all-ones input case, creates a stuck-at style fault that is easy to inject and detect only on specific input vectors.

mutant_rejections.bug_type: Redundant/extra literal added to a term

original_code:
module dut
(
  input a,
  input b,
  input c,
  output w,
  output x,
  output y,
  output z
);

  assign { w, x, y, z } = { a, b, b, c };

endmodule

bug_categories.description: Swap the order of elements in the right-hand-side concatenation, e.g. { a, b, b, c } becomes { b, a, b, c } or { c, b, b, a }, so outputs are routed from the wrong inputs.
bug_categories.applicability: The design is a pure concatenation-based routing of a, b, b, c to w, x, y, z. Reordering the elements directly misroutes w and x (or w and z) while remaining syntactically valid.

bug_categories.description: Replace one element in the concatenation with a different input, e.g. { a, b, b, c } becomes { a, b, a, c } or { a, b, b, b }, so one output is driven by the wrong input.
bug_categories.applicability: Since b is fanned out to both x and y, a copy-paste style error can easily make y come from a or c, or z come from b, breaking the intended one-to-one mapping.

bug_categories.description: Add a bitwise inversion to one of the concatenated elements, e.g. { a, b, ~b, c }, so one output is the logical complement of its intended value.
bug_categories.applicability: x and y are intended to be identical copies of b. Inverting only y makes them always differ, which is easy to detect and a realistic polarity error.

bug_categories.description: Replace one input in the concatenation with a constant 1'b0 or 1'b1, e.g. { a, b, b, 1'b0 }, so an output is stuck regardless of input.
bug_categories.applicability: Any of the four outputs w, x, y, z is a direct wire from an input, so substituting a constant simulates a stuck-at fault or tie-off error on that output.

bug_categories.bug_type: Bit width mismatch / truncation in concatenation
bug_categories.description: Change an element to a sized literal or multi-bit expression, or drop one element so the concatenation width differs from 4 bits, e.g. { a, b, c } or { a, b, b, c, 1'b0 }, causing truncation or zero-padding when assigned.
bug_categories.applicability: The LHS is a 4-bit concatenation {w,x,y,z}; a mismatched RHS width causes MSB/LSB truncation or padding that shifts all assignments and silently corrupts outputs.

bug_categories.description: Replace a direct wire with a logic expression combining inputs, e.g. { a, b, b ^ c, c } or { a & b, b, b, c }, altering the pure pass-through behavior.
bug_categories.applicability: The design is purely combinational pass-through, so inserting AND/OR/XOR between inputs creates plausible functional errors that only manifest for certain input combinations.

bug_categories.description: Split the single assign into separate assigns and leave one output undriven or drive it from a wrong source, e.g. assign w = a; assign x = b; assign y = b; with z omitted (floating/high-Z or default).
bug_categories.applicability: With four outputs derived from three inputs, decomposing the concatenation makes it easy to omit or misconnect one output, such as leaving z undriven so it becomes 'z/x' in simulation.

bug_categories.description: Reverse the entire RHS ordering so the mapping becomes { c, b, b, a }, mimicking an MSB/LSB ordering mistake between the concatenation and output list.
bug_categories.applicability: The output vector {w,x,y,z} maps MSB-first to {a,b,b,c}; reversing it swaps w<->z so w gets c and z gets a, while x and y remain unchanged since both come from b, making the bug subtle.

endmodule

(
  input a,

  input c,
  output w,
  output x,
  output y,
  output z
);

  assign { w, x, y, z } = { a, b, b ^ c, c };

endmodule

bug_categories.description: Swap the priority of L and E so that the enable branch is evaluated first: 'if(E) Q <= w; else if(L) Q <= R;'.
bug_categories.applicability: When both L and E are asserted, Q captures w instead of R, breaking the load-over-enable priority specified by the if/else-if chain.

bug_categories.description: Swap the data inputs so the load path uses w and the enable path uses R: 'if(L) Q <= w; else if(E) Q <= R;'.
bug_categories.applicability: Load and enable both update Q but with the wrong input data, a subtle functional error that still looks like a valid register mux.

bug_categories.description: Invert the polarity of the enable condition, e.g. 'else if(!E) Q <= w;' or invert L in the first condition.
bug_categories.applicability: Q updates when E is deasserted and holds when asserted, reversing the enable semantics of this flop.

bug_categories.description: Replace the non-blocking assignments '<=' with blocking '=' in the clocked always block.
bug_categories.applicability: Q is an output reg sampled by downstream logic in the same clock edge; blocking assignment can introduce race conditions and simulation ordering differences versus the intended sequential behavior.

bug_categories.description: Change 'posedge clk' to 'negedge clk' in the sensitivity list.
bug_categories.applicability: The register updates on the falling edge, shifting timing by half a cycle and causing mismatches with testbenches and surrounding logic that assume rising-edge capture.

bug_categories.description: Add a final 'else Q <= 1'b0;' (or Q <= ~Q) so that when neither L nor E is asserted, Q is cleared or toggled instead of holding its value.
bug_categories.applicability: The design relies on the implicit hold when L=0 and E=0; adding a default branch turns the enable flop into one that loses or flips its state.

bug_categories.bug_type: Incorrect logic combining of load and data
bug_categories.description: Replace the loaded value with a logic expression, e.g. 'Q <= R & w' or 'Q <= ~R' in the load branch.
bug_categories.applicability: The load path no longer faithfully captures R, corrupting stored value when L is asserted while the structure remains valid Verilog.

bug_categories.description: Remove the E gating or merge conditions, e.g. change 'else if(E)' to plain 'else' or change 'if(L)' to 'if(L & E)'.
bug_categories.applicability: With plain 'else', Q always loads w whenever L is low, ignoring E; with 'L & E', load only occurs when both asserted, so enable is no longer respected and load is incorrectly restricted.

mutants.bug_type: Incorrect logic combining of load and data

bug_categories.description: The ternary condition is inverted so that a is chosen when sel is 0 and b when sel is 1, e.g. out = (!sel) ? a : b or (~sel) ? a : b.
bug_categories.applicability: The design is a single 2:1 mux driven by sel, so swapping the polarity of sel flips every output and is functionally wrong for every input combination where a != b.

bug_categories.description: The two data operands in the ternary expression are exchanged, e.g. out = (sel) ? b : a, so the selected source is the opposite of what the specification requires.
bug_categories.applicability: Both a and b are 8-bit inputs of equal width, so the swap is syntactically and type valid and passes compilation while silently reversing the mux behavior.

bug_categories.description: Only part of the bus is muxed, e.g. out = (sel) ? {b[7:4], a[3:0]} : b, or out[7] is tied to a fixed value, so some bits take the wrong source.
bug_categories.applicability: The 8-bit data path allows individual bits or nibbles to be wired from the wrong input, producing errors only for specific bit positions that a shallow test might miss.

bug_categories.description: The selected data is bit-reversed or byte-nibble-swapped, e.g. out = (sel) ? {a[0],a[1],a[2],a[3],a[4],a[5],a[6],a[7]} : b, or the nibbles of a are swapped.
bug_categories.applicability: Because a and b are 8-bit vectors, concatenation-based reordering is legal Verilog and corrupts data only when sel selects the affected input, with palindromic values hiding the bug.

bug_categories.description: The mux is replaced with a bitwise or logical operation, e.g. out = (sel) ? a : b is changed to out = a & b, a | b, a ^ b, or sel ? a : a ^ b.
bug_categories.applicability: The one-line combinational assign can be swapped for a different expression of a, b, and sel that matches the mux for some inputs but diverges for others.

bug_categories.description: The selector is replaced by an expression that uses data bits, e.g. out = (sel | a[0]) ? a : b or out = (sel & b[7]) ? a : b, so selection depends on data values.
bug_categories.applicability: sel is a single-bit control, and mixing in bits of a or b creates a data-dependent select that behaves correctly only for some data patterns, making it a subtle corner-case bug.

bug_categories.description: The output is forced to a constant or one branch is replaced by a literal, e.g. out = (sel) ? a : 8'h00 or out = (sel) ? 8'hFF : b.
bug_categories.applicability: Replacing one branch with a constant still compiles, and the output ignores one data input entirely, so tests need to exercise both sel values with varied data to catch it.

bug_categories.description: The assign is changed to an incomplete conditional in a combinational always block, e.g. always @(*) if (sel) out = a; so out holds its previous value when sel is 0, inferring a latch.
bug_categories.applicability: The output is declared as output reg, so converting the continuous assignment to a procedural block with a missing else branch is directly feasible and creates unintended state.

bug_categories.description: Swap the priority of shift_ena and count_ena so that count_ena is checked first in the if/else-if chain, causing decrement to override shift when both are asserted.
bug_categories.applicability: The design relies on shift_ena having priority in 'if(shift_ena) ... else if(count_ena)'. Reordering the conditions changes behavior whenever both enables are high simultaneously.

bug_categories.description: Change the decrement q - 1'b1 into an increment q + 1'b1, making the counter count up instead of down.
bug_categories.applicability: The count_ena branch performs q <= q - 1'b1. Replacing the operator yields a valid but functionally incorrect up-counter.

bug_categories.description: Change the shift concatenation from {q[2:0], data} to {data, q[3:1]}, converting a left shift (data enters at LSB) into a right shift (data enters at MSB).
bug_categories.applicability: The shift_ena branch implements a left shift register with serial input at bit 0. Reversing the concatenation order changes the bit ordering of loaded data.

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong bit slice in shift concatenation
bug_categories.description: Use q[3:1] or q[3:0] slices incorrectly, e.g. { q[3:1], data } or a shifted slice that duplicates/drops a bit, so the shift does not move bits correctly.
bug_categories.applicability: The expression { q[2:0], data } must discard the MSB and insert data at LSB; an off-by-one slice yields a legal 4-bit value but corrupts the shift pattern.

bug_categories.description: Invert the serial input (~data) or tie the inserted bit to a constant (1'b0), so the shifted-in bit no longer matches the input.
bug_categories.applicability: The LSB of the shift result comes directly from the 'data' port; inverting or replacing it corrupts every shifted-in bit.

bug_categories.description: Change the decrement constant from 1'b1 to 2'd2 (or another value), so the counter decrements by the wrong amount per count_ena cycle.
bug_categories.applicability: The counter uses q - 1'b1; altering the literal keeps the code valid but skips counts and breaks expected count sequences.

bug_categories.description: Alter enable conditions, e.g. gate count_ena with !shift_ena redundantly changed to require both enables (shift_ena & count_ena), or invert count_ena, so the operations trigger at wrong times.
bug_categories.applicability: Both branches are controlled solely by shift_ena and count_ena; inverting or combining them changes when shifting or counting occurs and can leave q holding when it should update.

bug_categories.description: Change the always block to trigger on negedge clk, or replace nonblocking assignments with blocking assignments, altering timing relative to other logic.
bug_categories.applicability: The module uses 'always @(posedge clk)' with nonblocking assignments to q; switching to negedge clk shifts update timing by half a cycle relative to the testbench sampling and inputs.

original_code:
module dut
(
  input [4:0] a,
  input [4:0] b,
  input [4:0] c,
  input [4:0] d,
  input [4:0] e,
  input [4:0] f,
  output [7:0] w,
  output [7:0] x,
  output [7:0] y,
  output [7:0] z
);

  assign { w, x, y, z } = { a, b, c, d, e, f, 2'b11 };

endmodule

bug_categories.description: Swap two adjacent inputs in the concatenation, e.g. {b, a, c, d, e, f, 2'b11}, so the bit fields that land in w, x, y, z are exchanged.
bug_categories.applicability: The design is a pure bit-repacking of six 5-bit inputs (30 bits) plus 2 constant bits into four 8-bit outputs. Any reordering of a-f moves data into the wrong output bytes and bit positions.

bug_categories.description: Change the trailing constant from 2'b11 to 2'b00, 2'b01 or 2'b10, so the two least significant bits of z are wrong.
bug_categories.applicability: The two LSBs of z (z[1:0]) come solely from the 2'b11 literal. Altering it changes only those bits, a subtle bug that is easy to miss in tests.

bug_categories.description: Change the literal to a different width, e.g. 1'b1 or 3'b111, so the total concatenation width is 31 or 33 bits instead of 32. All fields then shift relative to the 32-bit output vector.
bug_categories.applicability: The LHS {w,x,y,z} is 32 bits and the RHS must be 30 + 2 = 32 bits. A wrong-width literal shifts every field by one bit, or truncates or extends it, moving data across the w/x/y/z boundaries.

bug_categories.description: Replace a full input with a partial or wrongly indexed slice, e.g. use a[3:0] with a zero pad, or b[4:1], instead of the full 5-bit vector.
bug_categories.applicability: Each input is 5 bits and spans byte boundaries in the output (e.g. b straddles w and x). Dropping or shifting one bit corrupts the boundary bits between adjacent outputs.

bug_categories.description: Reverse the bit order of one or more inputs, e.g. use {a[0],a[1],a[2],a[3],a[4]} instead of a, or reverse the whole concatenation.
bug_categories.applicability: The design maps inputs directly to output bit positions, so reversing the bit order within an input produces valid-width but functionally wrong data in w, x, y or z.

bug_categories.description: Swap the output order on the LHS, e.g. assign {x, w, y, z} or {z, y, x, w}, so the bytes are routed to the wrong ports.
bug_categories.applicability: Four 8-bit outputs receive consecutive bytes of the packed 32-bit value. Reordering the LHS makes each port carry another port's byte while all widths remain valid.

bug_categories.description: Replace one input with another, e.g. use a twice and omit f, or use {a,b,c,d,e,e,2'b11}.
bug_categories.applicability: All six inputs a-f are needed to fill the 30 data bits. Duplicating one input and dropping another keeps the width correct but makes one input have no effect and another appear twice in the output.

bug_categories.description: Apply a bitwise inversion or other operator to one input in the concatenation, e.g. ~c or (d ^ e) in place of d.
bug_categories.applicability: Because the module is only wiring, adding an inversion or logic operator to one field gives the correct width but wrong values in the specific output bits that field maps to (e.g. c affects y and parts of x).

bug_categories.description: Replace the reduction AND in the p1y gate with reduction OR, turning the 4-input NAND into a 4-input NOR (~|{p1a,p1b,p1c,p1d}).
bug_categories.applicability: p1y = ~&{p1a,p1b,p1c,p1d} becomes ~|{...}; output differs from NAND whenever inputs are mixed (e.g., 4'b0001 gives 0 instead of 1).

bug_categories.description: Remove the inversion operator so the gate becomes a plain 4-input AND, inverting the output polarity for every input combination.
bug_categories.applicability: p2y = &{p2a,p2b,p2c,p2d} instead of ~&{...}; output is the exact complement of the correct value for all 16 input patterns.

bug_categories.description: Remove one of the four inputs from the concatenation so the gate effectively becomes a 3-input NAND and ignores one input.
bug_categories.applicability: p1y = ~&{p1a,p1b,p1c} omits p1d; with p1a=p1b=p1c=1, p1d toggling no longer changes p1y (should go 1 to 0).

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong signal substituted (copy-paste / cross-channel wiring error)
bug_categories.description: Use an input from the other gate in the concatenation, creating unintended coupling between the two independent NAND gates.
bug_categories.applicability: p2y = ~&{p2a,p2b,p2c,p1d} (or p1y uses p2a) so p1d affects p2y, breaking independence between the channels.

bug_categories.description: Repeat one input in place of another so one input is ignored and another counted twice, a typo-style bug that still compiles.
bug_categories.applicability: p1y = ~&{p1a,p1b,p1c,p1c}; p1d has no effect on p1y while p1c is redundant.

bug_categories.description: Swap the logic driving the two outputs so each output reflects the other channel's inputs.
bug_categories.applicability: assign p1y = ~&{p2a,p2b,p2c,p2d}; assign p2y = ~&{p1a,p1b,p1c,p1d}; the module still compiles but port functionality is crossed.

bug_categories.description: Replace the reduction AND with reduction XOR, converting the NAND into a parity (XNOR) function.
bug_categories.applicability: p2y = ~^{p2a,p2b,p2c,p2d} yields an even-parity detector; outputs differ from NAND for many inputs, e.g., 4'b0000 gives 1 (same) but 4'b0001 gives 0 (should be 1).

bug_categories.description: Tie one of the gate inputs to a constant, or replace the expression with a constant, causing a stuck-at fault condition.
bug_categories.applicability: p1y = ~&{p1a,p1b,p1c,1'b0} forces p1y permanently to 1; or p2y = ~&{p2a,p2b,p2c,1'b1} makes p2d ignored and reduces to a 3-input NAND.

bug_categories.description: Change the rollover comparison from q == 9 to q == 10 (or q == 8), so the decade counter wraps at the wrong value, producing counts 0-10 or 0-8 instead of 0-9.
bug_categories.applicability: The `if(q == 9) q <= 0;` condition defines the modulo-10 behavior. Altering the constant directly breaks the BCD count range and is easily detected by checking the rollover point.

bug_categories.description: On reaching terminal count, load a nonzero value (e.g., q <= 1) instead of 0, or fail to reset and simply let q continue to 10 and beyond.
bug_categories.applicability: The `q <= 0` assignment in the q == 9 branch sets the post-rollover state. Changing it to 1 makes the count sequence skip 0 after the first cycle.

bug_categories.description: Change the sensitivity list to `always @(posedge clk or posedge reset)` so reset becomes asynchronous, or invert reset polarity so the counter clears when reset is low.
bug_categories.applicability: The design uses a synchronous active-high reset `if(reset) q <= 0;`. Making it async or active-low changes reset timing/behavior and breaks testbenches that assert reset synchronous to clk.

bug_categories.description: Reset q to a nonzero value such as 4'd1 or 4'd9 rather than 0.
bug_categories.applicability: The reset branch `q <= 0` establishes the initial count. A wrong reset value makes the sequence start from the wrong digit after reset.

bug_categories.bug_type: Priority inversion between reset and slowena
bug_categories.description: Reorder the conditions so slowena is checked before reset (e.g., if(slowena) ... else if(reset) ...), so reset only takes effect when slowena is high.
bug_categories.applicability: The if/else-if chain gives reset priority over the enable. Swapping them means reset asserted while slowena=0 is ignored, which is a subtle bug visible only in specific stimulus.

bug_categories.description: Invert or remove the enable qualification, e.g., use `if(!slowena)` or drop the slowena check so the counter increments every clock cycle.
bug_categories.applicability: slowena gates counting. Inverting it makes the counter run when it should hold, and removing it ignores the slow-enable throttling entirely.

bug_categories.description: Change the increment from q + 1 to q + 2 (or q - 1 for a down-count), altering the counting sequence.
bug_categories.applicability: The `q <= q + 1;` statement defines the step. With +2 the counter skips values and may never hit q == 9 exactly (odd values skipped), so the wrap never occurs and it rolls over at 16.

bug_categories.description: Narrow or alter the comparison/assignment width, e.g., compare only lower bits (q[2:0] == 3'd1 style partial match) or reduce the counter to 3 bits, so the terminal count detection fires incorrectly or the counter cannot reach 9.
bug_categories.applicability: q is a 4-bit reg needed to represent 0-9. Using a partial-bit comparison like `q[2:0] == 1` triggers at both 1 and 9, causing early wrap, while truncating q to 3 bits makes 9 unreachable.

bug_categories.description: Remove or add an inversion on x3 in the first product term (~x3 & x2 & ~x1), e.g. change it to x3 & x2 & ~x1, so the minterm 010 is replaced by 110.
bug_categories.applicability: The function is a sum of four minterms (010, 011, 101, 111). Each literal's polarity determines which minterm is selected, so flipping a single inversion silently moves a minterm to a wrong input combination.

bug_categories.description: Replace an AND operator inside a product term with OR, e.g. ~x3 & x2 | ~x1, which changes the term's logic and, through operator precedence, the entire expression.
bug_categories.applicability: The expression mixes & and | with no parentheses, so replacing one & with | changes the grouping and produces a function that is true for many extra input combinations.

bug_categories.description: Change one of the top-level OR operators combining the product terms into AND or XOR, e.g. the OR between the x3&~x2&x1 term and the x3&x2&x1 term becomes XOR.
bug_categories.applicability: With XOR, minterms that overlap or are combined would cancel or differ, and with AND the combined terms would nearly always evaluate to 0. Either way, the output differs from the original truth table.

bug_categories.description: Delete one of the four product terms, for example the x3 & x2 & x1 term (minterm 111), so the function only covers three of the original four on-set minterms.
bug_categories.applicability: The design is a canonical sum of minterms, so each term maps to exactly one input combination. Dropping a term forces f to 0 for that input row.

bug_categories.description: Add an additional product term such as x3 & ~x2 & ~x1 (minterm 100) to the OR expression, so f becomes 1 for an input that should produce 0.
bug_categories.applicability: Four of the eight input combinations are in the on-set. Adding one of the off-set minterms (000, 001, 100, 110) is a realistic mistake that corrupts the truth table.

bug_categories.description: Swap two input signals in one term, e.g. use x1 in place of x3 in x3 & ~x2 & x1, producing x1 & ~x2 & x1 which reduces to ~x2 & x1.
bug_categories.applicability: All three inputs share the same 1-bit type, so swapping or duplicating a signal is still valid Verilog but changes the covered minterm and can collapse the term to fewer literals.

bug_categories.description: Remove one literal from a product term, e.g. turn ~x3 & x2 & ~x1 into ~x3 & x2, which widens the term to cover minterms 010 and 011 and makes the function incorrect when combined with the other terms.
bug_categories.applicability: Each term has three literals specifying one minterm. Dropping a literal mimics an incomplete-minimization error and enlarges the on-set, which here introduces overlapping coverage and may add or retain wrong outputs.

bug_categories.description: Invert the whole right-hand side, e.g. assign f = ~(expression), or invert only the final OR term so the output polarity is wrong for some or all inputs.
bug_categories.applicability: The output f is a single combinational assign, so a stray negation or wrong grouping with a leading ~ flips the truth table for all eight input combinations, or for the specific term inverted.

bug_categories.description: Remove or add an inversion on a or b in the term ~a & ~b & c, e.g. change it to ~a & b & c or a & ~b & c.
bug_categories.applicability: out_sop's second product term depends on the exact polarity of a and b. Changing one literal changes which input combinations (a,b = 0,0) activate the output when d=0, so out_sop no longer matches the intended function.

bug_categories.description: Replace the OR joining the two product terms in out_sop with AND, or replace an AND inside a term with OR (e.g. c & d | ~a & ~b & c becomes c & d & ~a & ~b & c).
bug_categories.applicability: out_sop is a two-term sum of products. Swapping the | operator collapses the function to a much narrower or wider set of minterms, producing clearly wrong output for most input patterns.

bug_categories.description: Delete the common factor c from one product term or from one of the POS sum terms, e.g. out_sop = c & d | ~a & ~b, or pos0 = (~b | d) & (~a | b).
bug_categories.applicability: Every term in both forms is gated by c. Dropping c makes the output assert when c=0 (for a=0,b=0 in SOP), violating the design where c=0 forces the output low.

bug_categories.bug_type: Incorrect sum term in POS expression
bug_categories.description: Change a clause in pos0 or pos1, such as (~b | d) to (b | d), or (~a | b) in pos0 to (~a | ~b).
bug_categories.applicability: pos0 and pos1 are meant to be equivalent factorizations. Altering a clause in only one of them breaks the equivalence, so the pos0 == pos1 check fails for some inputs and out_pos becomes x instead of a valid value.

bug_categories.bug_type: Inconsistent redundant-term mismatch between pos0 and pos1
bug_categories.description: Make pos1 use a different third clause than pos0, e.g. change (~a | d) in pos1 to (a | d), or change (~a | b) in pos0 to (~a | d).
bug_categories.applicability: The consensus structure relies on pos0 and pos1 being logically equal for all 16 input combinations. A subtle difference in only the third clause leads to disagreement on a subset of inputs, which drives out_pos to 1'bx on those cases.

bug_categories.description: Change (pos0 == pos1) to (pos0 != pos1), or use case equality (===), or swap the select branches so pos0 is returned on mismatch and x on match.
bug_categories.applicability: out_pos is gated by a ternary on pos0 == pos1. Inverting the comparison makes the output x whenever the two POS forms agree (always), so out_pos becomes unknown for all inputs, or yields wrong values when they differ.

bug_categories.description: Replace 1'bx in the false branch with 1'b0 or 1'b1, or replace the true branch pos0 with pos1 or a constant.
bug_categories.applicability: The 1'bx fallback is used as a consistency flag. Changing it to a defined value masks any mismatch between pos0 and pos1, hiding the bug in simulation, while changing the true branch alters the output function directly.

bug_categories.description: Cross-connect the outputs, e.g. assign out_pos from the SOP expression and out_sop from pos0, or drive out_sop from pos1 through the ternary and out_pos from the SOP expression.
bug_categories.applicability: The module has two functionally equivalent outputs built from different forms. Swapping their drivers changes where x-propagation appears (out_sop could become x) and breaks the expected interface, since out_sop should never be x.

bug_categories.description: Change the reset condition from active-low (!resetn) to active-high (resetn), so the register clears when resetn is deasserted high and operates normally while resetn is low.
bug_categories.applicability: The design uses an active-low synchronous reset on resetn; inverting the check makes q reset during normal operation and load data during reset.

bug_categories.description: Invert the condition on one byte enable (e.g., if(!byteena[0])) so the lower byte is written when the enable is low and held when high.
bug_categories.applicability: byteena[0] gates q[7:0] and byteena[1] gates q[15:8]; inverting either enable flips which writes occur, which is easily missed if tests only use byteena=2'b11 or 2'b00.

bug_categories.description: Swap the byteena bits so byteena[1] controls the lower byte q[7:0] and byteena[0] controls the upper byte q[15:8].
bug_categories.applicability: The two enables map to separate halves of q; swapping indices keeps the code valid but mis-routes writes for asymmetric enable patterns such as 2'b01 and 2'b10.

bug_categories.description: Assign the wrong slice of d to a byte lane, e.g., q[15:8] <= d[7:0] or q[7:0] <= d[15:8], causing data duplication or byte swapping.
bug_categories.applicability: Each byte lane of q is loaded from the corresponding byte of d; using a mismatched slice produces valid-width assignments but corrupts data.

bug_categories.description: Alter part-select ranges so they overlap or leave gaps, e.g., q[8:0] <= d[8:0] for the lower byte, or q[14:8] <= d[14:8] for the upper byte.
bug_categories.applicability: The two 8-bit lanes split the 16-bit bus; an off-by-one range lets the lower lane overwrite bit 8 or leaves bit 15 never updated, so byte-enable isolation is broken.

bug_categories.description: Change the reset value from 0 to a nonzero constant (e.g., 16'hFFFF or 16'h0001) or reset only part of the register (e.g., q[7:0] <= 0).
bug_categories.applicability: q <= 0 clears all 16 bits on reset; resetting a partial range or a different constant leaves stale or wrong initial state that appears after reset.

bug_categories.description: Change the sensitivity list to always @(posedge clk or posedge resetn) or negedge resetn with mismatched polarity, making the reset asynchronous or triggering on the wrong edge.
bug_categories.applicability: The design uses a purely synchronous reset sampled on posedge clk; adding an async edge changes timing behavior so q clears immediately instead of at the next clock edge, or triggers incorrectly.

bug_categories.description: Restructure the logic so byte-enable writes take priority over reset (e.g., remove the else, so enabled bytes load d even when resetn is low), or make the byte writes conditional on an additional term.
bug_categories.applicability: Reset is the highest-priority branch with byte enables in the else clause; removing that priority means asserted byteena bits override reset for those lanes, leaving partial reset behavior.

bug_categories.description: Swap the order of the three next-state terms in the concatenation so that bits are assigned to the wrong state register positions (e.g., { ~s[0] | x, ~s[1] & x, s[2] ^ x }).
bug_categories.applicability: The next-state vector s <= { s[2] ^ x, ~s[1] & x, ~s[0] | x } maps each term to a specific bit; reordering changes the state transition function and the z output sequence.

bug_categories.description: Replace one of the bitwise operators in the next-state logic with a different one, e.g., change s[2] ^ x to s[2] | x, ~s[1] & x to ~s[1] | x, or ~s[0] | x to ~s[0] & x.
bug_categories.applicability: Each of the three next-state bits uses a different operator (XOR, AND, OR); altering any of them produces different state evolution while remaining valid Verilog.

bug_categories.description: Remove or add a bitwise inversion on a state bit in the next-state expressions, e.g., use s[1] & x instead of ~s[1] & x, or ~s[2] ^ x instead of s[2] ^ x.
bug_categories.applicability: The terms ~s[1] and ~s[0] rely on inversion; dropping or adding it flips toggle behavior of bits 1 and 0 and changes when z asserts.

bug_categories.description: Use an incorrect bit index of s in one of the next-state terms, e.g., s[1] ^ x instead of s[2] ^ x, or ~s[2] & x instead of ~s[1] & x.
bug_categories.applicability: Each next-state bit depends on a specific s bit (s[2], s[1], s[0]); using a different index creates incorrect inter-bit dependencies in the 3-bit FSM.

bug_categories.description: Change the output reduction from NOR to another reduction, e.g., z = ~&s, z = |s, z = ^s, or ~^s.
bug_categories.applicability: z = ~|s asserts only when state is 000; replacing the reduction operator changes which states produce z=1 and breaks the output behavior.

bug_categories.description: Invert the output polarity (z = |s) or decode only a subset of state bits (e.g., z = ~|s[1:0] or ~|s[2:1]).
bug_categories.applicability: z depends on all three bits of s; ignoring a bit or inverting the sense makes z assert in wrong states.

bug_categories.bug_type: Bit width mismatch on state register
bug_categories.description: Reduce or alter the width of the state register or its assignments, e.g., declare reg [1:0] s so the MSB term is truncated, or assign a narrower concatenation.
bug_categories.applicability: s is 3 bits and the concatenation supplies exactly 3 terms; shrinking s or dropping a term truncates the FSM and changes both next-state and z (~|s) behavior.

bug_categories.description: Change the initial value assigned to s from 0 to a non-zero value (e.g., 3'b001 or 3'b111), or alter how it is initialized.
bug_categories.applicability: The design has no explicit reset and relies on s = 0 for initial state; a different initial value shifts the whole state trajectory and z at startup (z initially 1 with s=0).

bug_categories.description: Change the clock edge from posedge to negedge, or change the nonblocking assignment to a blocking assignment in the sequential block.
bug_categories.applicability: The always @(posedge clk) block updates s with <=; switching to negedge shifts timing relative to input x sampling, altering the observed z sequence.
