bug_categories.description: The asynchronous reset loads the wrong initial state (e.g., 0 or 2 instead of 1), so the 2-bit saturating counter starts in the wrong prediction state.
bug_categories.applicability: Change `state <= 1` in the areset branch to `state <= 0`, `state <= 2`, or `state <= 3`. Reset behavior and the first predictions after reset will differ from the weakly not-taken specification.

bug_categories.description: The reset is made synchronous or active-low, so it no longer behaves as an asynchronous active-high reset.
bug_categories.applicability: Change the sensitivity list to `always @(posedge clk)` or `negedge areset` while keeping `if(areset)`. Reset would then wait for a clock edge, or trigger on the wrong edge or level.

bug_categories.description: The upper saturation limit comparison is off by one, causing the counter to wrap or overflow at the top of its range.
bug_categories.applicability: Change `state < 3` to `state <= 3` (state 3 increments and wraps to 0) or `state < 2` (the counter cannot reach 3). This breaks strongly-taken saturation.

bug_categories.description: The lower saturation limit comparison is off by one, causing underflow or preventing the counter from reaching 0.
bug_categories.applicability: Change `state > 0` to `state >= 0` (state 0 decrements and wraps to 3) or `state > 1` (the counter cannot reach 0). This breaks strongly-not-taken saturation.

bug_categories.description: The polarity of `train_taken` is inverted in one or both branches, so the counter moves in the wrong direction or in the same direction for both outcomes.
bug_categories.applicability: Change `&& train_taken` to `&& !train_taken` in the increment branch, or `!train_taken` to `train_taken` in the decrement branch. The counter then trains opposite to the actual branch outcome.

bug_categories.description: The `train_valid` qualifier is removed, inverted, or bypassed, so the counter updates when no training is requested or fails to update when it is.
bug_categories.applicability: Change `else if(train_valid)` to `else if(!train_valid)` or remove the check entirely. The state would change on every clock or only on invalid cycles.

bug_categories.description: The increment or decrement magnitude or operation is wrong, so the counter skips states or moves incorrectly.
bug_categories.applicability: Change `state + 1` to `state + 2` or `state - 1` to `state - 2`, or swap the + and - operations. The state sequence 0-1-2-3 is no longer followed one step at a time.

bug_categories.description: The nested if/else-if structure is altered so that branches overlap or are mis-prioritized, changing which update wins in boundary conditions.
bug_categories.applicability: Replace `else if((state > 0) && !train_taken)` with a plain `else`, or make the two branches independent `if` statements. For example, with state==3 and train_taken==1, the plain `else` would wrongly decrement instead of holding at 3.

bug_categories.description: Two of the case branches select the wrong data input, e.g. 3'h2 assigned data3 and 3'h3 assigned data2, so those select values return swapped data.
bug_categories.applicability: The mux has six case items mapping sel 0..5 to data0..data5. Swapping any two (or duplicating one, such as 3'h4: out = data3) is syntactically valid and only affects specific sel values.

bug_categories.description: The default branch drives a non-zero value (e.g. 4'hF) or one of the data inputs instead of 4'b0 for the unused select codes 6 and 7.
bug_categories.applicability: sel is 3 bits but only 6 values are used, so sel=6 and sel=7 fall to default. Changing 4'b0 to 4'hF or data0 alters output only for these two codes.

bug_categories.description: One case item (e.g. 3'h5: out = data5) is removed so that sel=5 falls into default and outputs zero.
bug_categories.applicability: Removing the last valid branch still compiles and the default silently masks it, making the bug visible only when sel=5 is tested.

bug_categories.description: A data input is assigned with a partial or shifted slice, e.g. out = {1'b0, data3[2:0]} or out = data4 >> 1, losing or misplacing bits.
bug_categories.applicability: All data inputs and out are 4 bits wide. Truncating or shifting one branch corrupts the MSB or LSB for a single sel value.

bug_categories.description: A case label is changed to the wrong value, such as 3'h5 becoming 3'h6, or two labels become identical so the later one is unreachable.
bug_categories.applicability: With duplicate labels (e.g. two 3'h3 items) the first match wins, so data4 or data5 becomes unreachable, or data5 is selected on sel=6 instead of 5.

bug_categories.bug_type: Bit inversion / wrong operator on data
bug_categories.description: One branch applies a bitwise operator, e.g. out = ~data2 or out = data1 & data2, instead of passing the data straight through.
bug_categories.applicability: Each case branch is a plain assignment, so inserting an inversion or logic operation on one input produces wrong data only for that select value.

bug_categories.description: Replace always @(*) with an explicit incomplete sensitivity list (e.g. always @(sel or data0 or data1)) or drop the default branch so the output holds its previous value.
bug_categories.applicability: The combinational block depends on sel and six data inputs. Omitting some inputs causes stale outputs when data2..data5 change; removing default infers a latch for sel=6,7.

bug_categories.description: The case selector is altered to use a subset or reordering of sel bits, e.g. case(sel[1:0]) or case({sel[0],sel[1],sel[2]}), changing which data input is chosen.
bug_categories.applicability: sel is a 3-bit vector. Using only two bits makes data4/data5 unreachable and aliases sel values, while bit reordering permutes the mapping of select codes to inputs.

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong logical operator (AND to OR) in first term
bug_categories.description: Change assign w1 = a & b to w1 = a | b, so the first product term fires when either a or b is high instead of both.
bug_categories.applicability: w1 is a direct 2-input AND term feeding the output OR. Any input vector with exactly one of a/b high and c&d low produces an incorrect out and out_n.

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong logical operator (AND to XOR) in second term
bug_categories.description: Change assign w2 = c & d to w2 = c ^ d, so w2 is high when c and d differ and low when both are high.
bug_categories.applicability: This breaks the c=d=1 case (w2 becomes 0) and wrongly asserts w2 for c!=d, which is visible at out whenever a&b is 0.

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong output combine operator (OR to AND)
bug_categories.description: Change assign out = w1 | w2 to out = w1 & w2, so out is high only when both product terms are true, turning the sum-of-products into a 4-input AND.
bug_categories.applicability: The output stage is the only OR in the design. Vectors where only one of (a&b) or (c&d) is true now give the wrong out.

bug_categories.description: Change assign out_n = ~out to out_n = out, so out_n no longer complements out.
bug_categories.applicability: out_n is intended as the inverse of out. Removing the inversion makes both outputs identical and fails on every input vector.

bug_categories.description: Invert one input or term, e.g. w1 = a & ~b or w2 = ~(c & d), so one product term has the wrong polarity.
bug_categories.applicability: Affects the 2-input AND terms. Only specific input combinations (such as a=1,b=1 or c=1,d=1) behave differently, which makes it a subtler bug to detect.

bug_categories.description: Use the wrong input in a term, e.g. w2 = c & b or w1 = a & d, so the pairing of inputs in the AND-OR structure is incorrect.
bug_categories.applicability: With four symmetric-looking inputs and two paired terms, swapping an operand yields a valid but functionally different SOP and is only exposed by vectors that distinguish the pairings.

bug_categories.description: Have out use the same intermediate twice or bypass one, e.g. out = w1 | w1 or out = w1 | (c & b), or have out_n derive from w1 instead of out (out_n = ~w1).
bug_categories.applicability: The design has two named intermediates (w1, w2) and a derived output. Dropping w2 from out or deriving out_n from a partial term makes the circuit ignore c/d or produce an inconsistent out_n.

bug_categories.description: Tie a term or input to a constant, e.g. w2 = c & 1'b0, w1 = a & 1'b1, or out_n = 1'b0, creating a stuck-at fault.
bug_categories.applicability: Constants applied to one input of the AND gates, or to an output, effectively remove an input's influence or freeze an output, which is detectable only with vectors that exercise the affected term.

mutants.bug_type: Wrong logical operator (AND to OR) in first term

bug_categories.description: Change the posedge clock edge on the qp capture block to negedge (or the negedge on qn to posedge), so both registers sample on the same edge.
bug_categories.applicability: The design relies on qp capturing d on posedge and qn capturing d on negedge to implement a dual-edge (DDR-style) flop. Making both use the same edge removes the dual-edge sampling and q no longer updates on both edges.

bug_categories.description: Invert the select condition in the output mux, changing (clk)? qp : qn to (!clk)? qp : qn or swapping the qp/qn operands.
bug_categories.applicability: The mux must output qp while clk is high (qp was just captured at the rising edge) and qn while clk is low. Inverting the select makes q show the stale value from the opposite phase, giving a half-cycle latency error.

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong signal sampled in capture register
bug_categories.description: Make one of the capture registers sample a wrong signal, e.g. qn <= qp or qp <= q instead of d.
bug_categories.applicability: qn <= d on negedge is the sole input path for the falling-edge half. Sampling qp (or q) creates a chained or feedback path, delaying data and breaking the independent dual-edge capture.

bug_categories.description: Change the non-blocking assignments in the clocked blocks to blocking (qp = d; qn = d;) or change the combinational q <= assignment to blocking =.
bug_categories.applicability: The always @(*) block uses non-blocking q <= ..., which already introduces a delta-cycle delay; switching assignment types in the edge-triggered blocks or the mux alters race behavior between clk edges and the mux evaluation, causing glitches or different simulated timing at clock edges.

bug_categories.description: Replace always @(*) with a restricted sensitivity list such as always @(clk) or always @(qp), so the mux does not re-evaluate on all input changes.
bug_categories.applicability: q depends on clk, qp and qn. If the sensitivity list omits qp or qn, q will not update when a register changes while clk is stable (e.g. qp changes just after posedge), leaving q stale or out of sync.

bug_categories.bug_type: Missing or added logic on data path
bug_categories.description: Insert an inversion or constant on the data path, e.g. qp <= ~d, or qn <= 1'b0, or qp <= d & qn.
bug_categories.applicability: Each half of the design is a single-bit register with no logic. Inverting or gating d for only one edge makes the output differ between high and low clock phases, producing a wrong, asymmetric output pattern.

bug_categories.description: Replace the mux with a constant selection such as q <= qp or q <= qn, or tie the select to a constant (1'b1 / 1'b0).
bug_categories.applicability: The mux is what combines the two edge-captured registers into a dual-edge output. Removing the clk-based selection makes q behave as a single-edge flop (updating only on one edge's data), silently dropping half of the data samples.

bug_categories.description: Change the mux to a conditional assignment that lacks an else branch, e.g. always @(*) if (clk) q <= qp; so q holds its value when clk is low.
bug_categories.applicability: The always @(*) block drives q with a full ternary covering both clk levels. Removing the qn branch infers a latch, so during clk low q holds the previous qp value instead of following qn, breaking falling-edge data propagation.

mutant_rejections.bug_type: Wrong signal sampled in capture register

bug_categories.description: Invert the polarity of the 'in' qualifier in one next_state term, e.g. change next_state[A] from '& ~in' to '& in'.
bug_categories.applicability: next_state[A] and next_state[C] use ~in while next_state[B] and next_state[D] use in. Flipping any one of them breaks the one-hot transition pattern for that state.

bug_categories.description: Replace the OR in a state-combining term with AND, e.g. next_state[A] = (state[A] & state[C]) & ~in.
bug_categories.applicability: next_state[A], [B] and [C] each OR multiple source states. Replacing | with & means the state is entered only when multiple one-hot bits are set, which never occurs, so the state becomes unreachable.

bug_categories.description: Swap or substitute a source state index in a transition term, e.g. next_state[C] = (state[A] | state[D]) & ~in instead of (state[B] | state[D]).
bug_categories.applicability: Each next_state bit depends on specific state[] bits. Changing one index (B to A in next_state[C], or C to B in next_state[D]) reroutes the FSM to the wrong transition.

bug_categories.description: Drop one of the OR'd source states from a transition term, e.g. remove state[D] from next_state[B] so it becomes (state[A] | state[B]) & in.
bug_categories.applicability: next_state[B] has three sources (A, B, D) and next_state[A] and [C] have two. Omitting one eliminates a transition arc such as D->B or C->A.

bug_categories.bug_type: Moore output tied to wrong state bit
bug_categories.description: Change the output assignment to reference a different state bit or to a combination, e.g. assign out = state[C] or state[C] | state[D].
bug_categories.applicability: out = state[D] is a Moore-style output. Using another state bit asserts the output in the wrong state, or in two states.

bug_categories.description: Change a parameter value so that two state names map to the same bit index or to a wrong bit, e.g. parameter C = 3 or D = 2.
bug_categories.applicability: A, B, C, D are used as bit indices into next_state and state. Changing one aliases two states (multiple drivers on one bit, leaving another bit undriven) or permutes the state encoding.

bug_categories.description: Assign a next_state expression to the wrong destination bit, e.g. swap the left-hand sides of next_state[B] and next_state[C].
bug_categories.applicability: Four separate bit-wise assigns drive next_state[A..D]. Swapping or misindexing the LHS yields valid Verilog but the states exchange transitions, producing wrong next-state encoding.

bug_categories.description: Remove the in or ~in qualifier from one term so the transition becomes unconditional, e.g. next_state[D] = state[C] instead of state[C] & in.
bug_categories.applicability: Every next_state bit is gated by in or ~in. Removing the gate in next_state[D] or next_state[A] makes the state entered regardless of input, causing multiple bits to go high at once (loss of one-hot property).

mutants.bug_type: Moore output tied to wrong state bit

bug_categories.description: Change the terminal count condition from count_value == 0 to count_value == 1 (or the decrement guard to != 1), so tc asserts one cycle early or the counter stops at the wrong value.
bug_categories.applicability: The assign tc = count_value == 0 and the guard count_value != 0 both define the end-of-count; altering the constant shifts when tc asserts and where the counter halts.

bug_categories.description: Replace the decrement count_value - 1 with an increment count_value + 1 or a decrement by 2, so the counter counts in the wrong direction or at the wrong rate.
bug_categories.applicability: The down-counter relies on count_value - 1 in the else-if branch; changing it breaks the countdown timing and the guard against reaching zero would no longer terminate properly.

bug_categories.description: Change count_value != 0 to count_value == 0 (or remove the guard), so the counter decrements only when already zero, or wraps around from 0 to 1023 instead of holding at zero.
bug_categories.applicability: The hold-at-zero behavior depends on the != 0 guard; removing it causes underflow wrap-around and tc to deassert after reaching zero.

bug_categories.description: Invert the load condition (if(!load)) or reorder so decrement takes priority over load, so loading data fails or behaves incorrectly.
bug_categories.applicability: The if(load) / else if structure establishes that load overrides counting; inverting or reordering it changes when data is captured.

bug_categories.bug_type: Bit width mismatch / truncation of data
bug_categories.description: Truncate the loaded value, e.g., load only data[8:0] or zero-extend/shift data (data >> 1), or declare count_value narrower than 10 bits so the upper bit is lost.
bug_categories.applicability: The 10-bit data input is loaded into count_value; narrowing the register or slicing the data drops the MSB and shortens the count for values >= 512.

bug_categories.description: Invert the terminal count output (assign tc = count_value != 0) or use a reduction operator mismatch, so tc is asserted while counting and deasserted at zero.
bug_categories.applicability: tc is a combinational decode of count_value == 0; flipping the comparison inverts the flag's meaning for all downstream consumers.

bug_categories.description: Change the always block to trigger on negedge clk, or convert the counter update to blocking assignment or a different sensitivity, shifting timing relative to the rest of the system and the load input.
bug_categories.applicability: The counter is updated in always @(posedge clk) with nonblocking assignments; using negedge changes the sampling of load/data and the cycle in which tc reflects the load.

bug_categories.bug_type: Load value modification / corrupted data path
bug_categories.description: Load data plus or minus one (count_value <= data + 1 or data - 1), or load a constant or bitwise-inverted data, causing the count length to be off.
bug_categories.applicability: The load branch assigns count_value <= data directly; any modification changes the number of cycles before tc asserts, e.g., data=0 would load 1 and tc would not assert immediately.

mutants.bug_type: Bit width mismatch / truncation of data

original_code:
module dut
(
  input p1a,
  input p1b,
  input p1c,
  input p1d,
  input p1e,
  input p1f,
  output p1y,
  input p2a,
  input p2b,
  input p2c,
  input p2d,
  output p2y
);

  assign p1y = &{ p1a, p1b, p1c } | &{ p1d, p1e, p1f };
  assign p2y = &{ p2a, p2b } | &{ p2c, p2d };

endmodule

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong logical operator (AND to OR in reduction)
bug_categories.description: Change the reduction-AND of the first product term in p1y to a reduction-OR, e.g. p1y = |{p1a, p1b, p1c} | &{p1d, p1e, p1f}.
bug_categories.applicability: p1y relies on &{p1a,p1b,p1c}; making it an OR makes the output true when any single one of p1a/p1b/p1c is high, breaking the 3-input AND-OR function.

bug_categories.description: Replace the final '|' that combines the two product terms with '&', e.g. p2y = &{p2a,p2b} & &{p2c,p2d}.
bug_categories.applicability: Both p1y and p2y are sum-of-products; using AND instead of OR means the output requires all inputs high rather than either group, drastically reducing when the output asserts.

bug_categories.description: Remove one input from a concatenation, e.g. p1y = &{p1a, p1b} | &{p1d, p1e, p1f} (p1c dropped) or p2y = &{p2a} | &{p2c, p2d}.
bug_categories.applicability: The AND groups have 3 and 2 inputs. Dropping p1c, p1f, p2b or p2d leaves an input unused and makes the output assert with fewer conditions.

bug_categories.bug_type: Input signal swap / cross-wiring between groups
bug_categories.description: Substitute an input from one product term into the other, e.g. p1y = &{p1a, p1b, p1d} | &{p1c, p1e, p1f}.
bug_categories.applicability: Six symmetric-looking inputs in two groups make it easy to mis-assign one signal; the result is valid Verilog but yields a different logic function for specific input patterns.

bug_categories.description: Use an input from the p2 port group in the p1y expression or vice versa, e.g. p1y = &{p1a, p1b, p2a} | &{p1d, p1e, p1f}.
bug_categories.applicability: The module has two independent logic cones with similarly named ports (p1x/p2x); mixing them creates unintended coupling between the two otherwise independent outputs.

bug_categories.description: Invert the output of one assign, e.g. assign p2y = ~(&{p2a,p2b} | &{p2c,p2d}) (AND-OR-INVERT) or apply negation to a single term.
bug_categories.applicability: Both outputs are plain combinational functions; adding a '~' converts the AND-OR into AOI, flipping the output for every input combination.

bug_categories.description: Invert a single input within a group, e.g. &{p1a, ~p1b, p1c} or &{p2a, p2b} | &{~p2c, p2d}.
bug_categories.applicability: Each product term is a pure AND of true-polarity inputs; negating one input changes the minterm that activates the output, a subtle bug only caught by exhaustive stimulus.

bug_categories.description: Replace one reduction AND with reduction XOR or NAND, e.g. p2y = ^{p2a,p2b} | &{p2c,p2d} or p1y = &{p1a,p1b,p1c} | ~&{p1d,p1e,p1f}.
bug_categories.applicability: The unary reduction operators (&) on the concatenations can be swapped for ^ or ~& while remaining legal Verilog, turning the AND term into parity or a NAND and altering the truth table for many input combinations.

mutants.bug_type: Wrong logical operator (AND to OR in reduction)

bug_categories.description: Change the shift register update from { q[6:0], S } to { S, q[7:1] }, shifting right instead of left so new data enters at the MSB and ages toward the LSB.
bug_categories.applicability: The shift register q uses a left shift with S entering at q[0]; reversing direction changes which bit index corresponds to which sample age, so the mux output Z returns wrong historical bits.

bug_categories.description: Reorder the concatenation in the mux select from { A, B, C } to { C, B, A } (or { B, A, C }), so the index is bit-reversed or permuted.
bug_categories.applicability: Z = q[{A,B,C}] relies on A being the MSB of the index; permuting the select bits maps input combinations to the wrong q bits for most codes.

bug_categories.description: Invert the enable condition to if(!enable), so the register shifts only when enable is low and holds when enable is high.
bug_categories.applicability: The shift is gated by enable inside the clocked always block; inverting it flips when data is captured while remaining valid Verilog.

bug_categories.description: Replace the shifted-in serial data S with another signal such as A, or with a constant (1'b0), e.g. q <= { q[6:0], A }.
bug_categories.applicability: The only data entering the shift register is S at q[0]; substituting another input or constant corrupts stored history without changing widths.

bug_categories.bug_type: Shift slice off-by-one / bit width mismatch
bug_categories.description: Change the shifted slice from q[6:0] to q[7:1] or q[5:0] (with padded bit), e.g. { q[7:1], S }, or drop one bit so the register loses a stage or duplicates a bit.
bug_categories.applicability: The 8-bit register is updated by concatenating a 7-bit slice and S; altering slice bounds makes the vector a different effective length or breaks the shift chain while still being legal Verilog with width truncation.

bug_categories.description: Replace q <= {q[6:0], S} with a blocking assignment q = {q[6:0], S} in the clocked block.
bug_categories.applicability: The shift register is sequential logic; blocking assignment makes q update immediately, which can create simulation race conditions with the combinational read of q in the assign for Z and deviates from intended timing behavior.

bug_categories.bug_type: Select index truncation / reduced mux range
bug_categories.description: Narrow the select to two bits, e.g. Z = q[{A, B}] or q[{1'b0, B, C}], so the upper half of q is unreachable or index C is ignored.
bug_categories.applicability: Z uses a 3-bit index to choose among 8 bits of q; removing or fixing one select bit makes some stages of the shift register unobservable and changes output for many A/B/C combinations.

bug_categories.description: Change the always block trigger from posedge clk to negedge clk, or make the shift unconditional by removing the enable gating.
bug_categories.applicability: The shifting happens on posedge clk with enable gating; switching the edge shifts data timing by half a cycle relative to the inputs, and removing enable makes q shift every cycle, both altering the observed output sequence.

mutants.bug_type: Shift slice off-by-one / bit width mismatch

bug_categories.description: Remove 'posedge areset' from the sensitivity list so the always block becomes @(posedge clk), making reset take effect only on a clock edge instead of immediately.
bug_categories.applicability: The module is specified with an asynchronous active-high reset (posedge clk or posedge areset). Making it synchronous changes timing: q does not clear until the next clock edge, breaking asynchronous-reset behavior.

bug_categories.description: Change the reset condition from 'if(areset)' to 'if(!areset)' (or change the edge to negedge areset) so the register is reset when areset is low and operates normally only while reset is asserted.
bug_categories.applicability: The reset is active-high; inverting the polarity makes q stuck at 0 during normal operation (areset=0) and the load/shift logic only works when areset=1.

bug_categories.description: Change the reset assignment from 'q <= 0' to a non-zero constant such as 4'hF or 4'b1000 so the register resets to the wrong value.
bug_categories.applicability: The 4-bit output q is reset to 0; a different reset constant causes incorrect initial state after areset.

bug_categories.bug_type: Priority inversion between load and ena
bug_categories.description: Swap the order of the 'else if(load)' and 'else if(ena)' branches so that ena takes precedence over load when both are asserted.
bug_categories.applicability: The design gives load priority over shift enable. Reordering means when load=1 and ena=1 simultaneously, q shifts instead of loading data, a subtle behavioral difference only visible when both are asserted.

bug_categories.description: Change the shift expression to shift left instead of right, e.g., 'q <= {q[2:0], 1'b0}' in place of the right-shift behavior.
bug_categories.applicability: The ena branch performs a right-shift/arithmetic-style operation on q; reversing the direction produces a different shift sequence while remaining valid 4-bit Verilog.

bug_categories.bug_type: Shift fill bit / sign extension error
bug_categories.description: Change the ena branch so the MSB is filled incorrectly, e.g., 'q <= {1'b1, q[3:1]}' or 'q <= {q[0], q[3:1]}' (rotate) instead of the intended arithmetic shift that preserves q[3] as {q[3], q[3:1]}.
bug_categories.applicability: The existing expression 'q[3:1]' is only 3 bits wide and is zero-extended to 4 bits (logical right shift with 0 in the MSB). Changing the fill bit to 1, to q[0] (rotate), or to q[3] (arithmetic shift) alters the shifted-in value and changes the output sequence.

bug_categories.description: Alter the part-select range in the shift, e.g., 'q <= q[2:0]' or 'q <= q[3:2]' or 'q <= q[2:1]', so a wrong subset of bits is shifted and the result is zero-extended into a different alignment.
bug_categories.applicability: The ena branch relies on the slice q[3:1] being zero-extended to 4 bits. Off-by-one slicing shifts by a wrong amount or drops/duplicates bits, producing incorrect values in q.

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong data load path / bit reordering
bug_categories.description: Change the load assignment from 'q <= data' to a modified version such as 'q <= data[3:1]' (truncated, zero-extended), 'q <= {data[0], data[3:1]}', 'q <= ~data', or bit-reversed data '{data[0],data[1],data[2],data[3]}'.
bug_categories.applicability: The load branch copies the 4-bit data input directly into q. Corrupting this path (truncation, inversion, or bit reversal) yields incorrect loaded values while remaining syntactically valid.

mutants.bug_type: Wrong data load path / bit reordering
Priority inversion between load and ena

bug_categories.description: Replace the AND operator in out_and with OR (a | b), or replace the OR operator in out_or with AND (a & b), making the output identical to another gate's output.
bug_categories.applicability: out_and = a & b and out_or = a | b are single-operator assigns, so swapping the operator is trivial and valid Verilog while producing wrong truth tables at (a=0,b=1) and (a=1,b=0).

bug_categories.description: Remove the bitwise NOT from an inverted-output gate so that it behaves like its non-inverted counterpart.
bug_categories.applicability: out_nand = ~(a & b) becomes a & b, or out_nor = ~(a | b) becomes a | b. The outputs would then duplicate out_and and out_or respectively, failing for every input combination.

bug_categories.description: Move the inversion so it applies to the wrong sub-expression, changing the function because of how ~ binds relative to & and |.
bug_categories.applicability: out_nand = ~a & b (or ~a & ~b) instead of ~(a & b), and out_nor = ~a | ~b instead of ~(a | b). The latter silently turns NOR into NAND, which is a subtle De Morgan error.

bug_categories.bug_type: Inverted operand swapped to the wrong input
bug_categories.description: Apply the inversion to the wrong operand in an asymmetric function.
bug_categories.applicability: out_anotb = a & ~b becomes ~a & b (computing b AND NOT a). The result differs at (a=1,b=0) and (a=0,b=1), and the function is not symmetric so the bug is easily missed.

bug_categories.description: Alter the XNOR expression so that it becomes XOR, or alter XOR so that it becomes XNOR.
bug_categories.applicability: out_xnor = a ^ ~b can be changed to a ^ b (making it identical to out_xor), or out_xor = a ^ b changed to ~(a ^ b). Every input combination yields the wrong value for the affected output.

bug_categories.description: Replace a bitwise operator with a logical one or vice versa, which is valid Verilog and gives the same results on 1-bit signals in most cases but changes behavior when the inversion is used.
bug_categories.applicability: out_anotb = a && !b is equivalent, but out_nand = !(a & b) vs ~(a & b) are equivalent too; a meaningful bug is out_xnor = a ^ !b mixed with other changes, or out_nor = !a | !b, which changes the function. Useful for testing that checkers catch operator-class substitutions on 1-bit signals.

bug_categories.description: Swap the right-hand-side expressions between two output ports so that each output carries another gate's function.
bug_categories.applicability: Exchange the expressions of out_and and out_nand, out_or and out_nor, or out_xor and out_xnor. The seven outputs are independent continuous assigns, so swapping is simple and produces inverted-polarity outputs on all input combinations.

bug_categories.description: Replace an output's expression with a constant 0 or 1, or with a single input, simulating a stuck-at fault or a lost logic function.
bug_categories.applicability: For example assign out_xor = 1'b0, out_or = a (dropping b), or out_nor = 1'b1. Each output is a pure combinational function of a and b, so a tied or dropped-operand version is valid Verilog and fails on at least one input combination.

mutants.bug_type: Inverted operand swapped to the wrong input

bug_categories.description: Change the sensitivity list from 'posedge clk or posedge areset' to only 'posedge clk', making the reset synchronous instead of asynchronous.
bug_categories.applicability: The state register is reset by areset asynchronously; making it synchronous delays reset until the next clock edge, so state and output z stay wrong between areset assertion and the clock edge.

bug_categories.description: Reset the state register to B instead of A (state <= B in the areset branch).
bug_categories.applicability: After reset the FSM starts in the absorbing state B, so it never leaves B and z becomes ~x permanently, rather than starting in A where z = x.

bug_categories.description: Change the reset condition or sensitivity to negedge areset / treat areset as active-low (if(!areset)).
bug_categories.applicability: The design uses active-high areset; inverting it would hold the FSM in reset during normal operation or fail to reset when areset is asserted, so the state never advances to B.

bug_categories.description: Invert the condition in state A's transition so it goes to B when x is 0: A: state <= (x) ? A : B.
bug_categories.applicability: The FSM should move from A to B on the first x=1; the inverted condition shifts the transition to the first x=0, changing the timing of when the output behaviour switches.

bug_categories.description: Change B's transition to return to A or depend on x, e.g., B: state <= (x) ? B : A.
bug_categories.applicability: State B is meant to be a terminal latch state; allowing it to exit makes the FSM oscillate and alters the z output sequence after the first x=1.

bug_categories.description: Replace the OR in the z assignment with AND (or XOR/other operator), e.g., z = (state==A && x==1) & (state==B && x==0).
bug_categories.applicability: The two product terms are mutually exclusive, so ANDing them makes z constantly 0, whereas the intended OR makes z equal x in A and ~x in B.

bug_categories.bug_type: Output condition inversion / wrong state or input comparison
bug_categories.description: Swap a comparison in the z expression, such as (state == A) && (x == 0), or (state == B) && (x == 1).
bug_categories.applicability: The output equation depends on both state and x comparisons; flipping one produces incorrect z in half the state/input combinations, e.g., z = ~x in A or z = x in B.

bug_categories.description: Swap or alter the parameter values (e.g., A = 1, B = 0, or both set to the same value) while leaving the reset and logic unchanged.
bug_categories.applicability: With a 1-bit state, changing parameter values flips the encoding; setting A and B equal collapses the two states so the case statement and z logic misbehave, and the FSM can never distinguish the states.

bug_categories.description: Change the asynchronous reset value of the state register from A to a different state (e.g., B or C), or invert the reset polarity so the FSM resets when areset is low.
bug_categories.applicability: The reset branch 'if(areset) state <= A;' determines the initial state. Resetting to C would make z assert immediately after reset, and negating areset would break initialization entirely.

bug_categories.bug_type: Sensitivity list error (async vs sync reset)
bug_categories.description: Remove 'or posedge areset' from the always block sensitivity list, turning the asynchronous reset into a synchronous one, or change posedge areset to negedge areset.
bug_categories.applicability: The always block is '@(posedge clk or posedge areset)'. A synchronous reset would delay state clearing until the next clock edge, and negedge would trigger on the wrong event, causing a mismatch with expected asynchronous reset behavior.

bug_categories.description: Alter the next-state value in one of the case arms, e.g., in state A change 'x ? C : A' to 'x ? B : A', so the FSM goes to the wrong state on input x.
bug_categories.applicability: State A transitions to C when x=1. Redirecting to B changes the output sequence since z is only high in C, and subsequent behavior diverges from the reference FSM.

bug_categories.description: Swap the ternary branches or negate the condition in a transition, such as changing state B from '(x)? B : C' to '(x)? C : B', or state C from '(x)? B : C' to '(x)? C : B'.
bug_categories.applicability: States B and C both depend on x to choose between B and C. Inverting x in one of them alters the hold/transition behavior and produces a different z waveform.

bug_categories.description: Change the output assignment from 'state == C' to 'state != C', 'state == B', or 'state == A', altering which state asserts z.
bug_categories.applicability: z = (state == C) is a Moore output. Modifying the compared state constant or inverting the comparison flips or relocates the output assertion while the state machine itself looks correct.

bug_categories.description: Change parameter values so encodings collide or use an unused code, e.g., set C = 1 (same as B) or C = 3, or set A = 1.
bug_categories.applicability: Parameters A=0, B=1, C=2 are used in the case items and output comparison. Making B and C equal creates duplicate case labels (first match wins, making one arm unreachable), and C=3 together with a mismatch elsewhere breaks decoding. Reset to A with a changed value also shifts the initial state.

bug_categories.bug_type: Missing case / default handling (incomplete case, latch/stuck state)
bug_categories.description: Remove one case arm (e.g., the B or C branch) or leave the 2-bit state value 3 unhandled with no default, so the FSM holds its value in some states.
bug_categories.applicability: The 2-bit state register has 4 possible values but only 3 are handled, with no default. Deleting the B arm makes the FSM stuck in B forever, and state 3 (if reached) has no recovery path to A.

bug_categories.bug_type: Blocking vs non-blocking assignment / state width mismatch
bug_categories.description: Change 'state <= ...' to blocking '=' in the sequential block, or reduce the state register width from [1:0] to a single bit so that C (2) is truncated.
bug_categories.applicability: The state register is declared as reg [1:0] and assigned with non-blocking assignments. Narrowing it to 1 bit truncates C=2 to 0 (aliasing with A), causing z to never assert and the FSM to behave incorrectly; blocking assignments can introduce simulation race ordering differences relative to the clock.

mutants.bug_type: Missing case / default handling (incomplete case, latch/stuck state)

bug_categories.description: Replace the bitwise AND with a bitwise OR so q = a | b, producing 1 whenever either input is high.
bug_categories.applicability: The design's only function is q = a & b; swapping to OR changes the output for input patterns 01 and 10 while remaining valid Verilog.

bug_categories.description: Replace the AND with XOR so q = a ^ b, which is high when inputs differ and low when both are 1.
bug_categories.applicability: Output differs from the correct AND for 01, 10 and 11, making the bug easy to detect with an exhaustive truth-table test.

bug_categories.description: Invert the result so q = ~(a & b), flipping the output for every input combination.
bug_categories.applicability: A single misplaced negation on the assign expression makes the gate a NAND, which is functionally wrong on all four input patterns.

bug_categories.description: Invert one input operand so q = a & ~b (or ~a & b), creating an active-low polarity error on one input.
bug_categories.applicability: Only one input polarity is wrong, so the output is incorrect only for 01/11 (or 10/11) combinations, a subtler bug than full inversion.

bug_categories.description: Remove one operand so q = a (or q = b), ignoring the other input entirely.
bug_categories.applicability: The output becomes independent of one input, and is wrong whenever the omitted input is 0 while the other is 1.

bug_categories.description: Replace & with && or a reduction-style variant, or use a different operator such as &~ or ~&, that behaves differently from the intended function.
bug_categories.applicability: For single-bit inputs && is equivalent, so this is a benign mutation; but substituting related operators like ~& or &~ in the assign yields a real functional change in this 1-bit design.

bug_categories.description: Tie the output to a constant, e.g. q = 1'b0 or q = 1'b1, or AND with a constant such as a & 1'b1.
bug_categories.applicability: Stuck-at-0 or stuck-at-1 on q makes the output ignore the inputs; a & 1'b1 reduces the gate to a buffer of a, mimicking a stuck-at fault on input b.

bug_categories.description: Reference the same signal twice or an incorrect signal, such as q = a & a or q = b & b, instead of a & b.
bug_categories.applicability: The module has only two inputs, so a copy-paste style error using one input twice makes the output ignore the other input and break the AND function.

bug_categories.description: Change the AND in Y1 to OR so Y1 = y[0] | w instead of y[0] & w.
bug_categories.applicability: Y1 would be asserted whenever either y[0] or w is high, not only when both are, which breaks the state-and-input qualified output. It is a simple one-token change that remains valid Verilog.

bug_categories.description: Remove the inversion on w in Y3 so Y3 = (y[1] | y[2] | y[4] | y[5]) & w, or add an inversion to w in Y1.
bug_categories.applicability: Y1 and Y3 are meant to be mutually exclusive via w and ~w. Removing the inversion lets both outputs assert together when w=1, and makes Y3 respond to the wrong input polarity.

bug_categories.description: Change an index in the Y3 OR term, for example y[4] to y[3], or change y[0] in Y1 to y[1].
bug_categories.applicability: The design looks like a one-hot FSM next-state/output decode where y[3] is deliberately excluded from Y3. Using y[3] changes which states drive Y3, and using the wrong bit for Y1 ties it to the wrong state.

bug_categories.description: Drop one of the four terms (y[1], y[2], y[4], y[5]) from the Y3 OR expression.
bug_categories.applicability: Y3 would fail to assert when only the dropped state bit is set. The error shows only for that specific one-hot input, so it is a subtle corner-case bug.

bug_categories.bug_type: Extra term added to OR reduction
bug_categories.description: Add y[3] or y[0] to the OR list in Y3, giving (y[0] | y[1] | y[2] | y[4] | y[5]) & ~w.
bug_categories.applicability: Y3 would assert for states that should not drive it. It is a plausible copy-paste error and is only visible when the extra bit is set with w=0.

bug_categories.description: Remove or move the parentheses in Y3 so it becomes y[1] | y[2] | y[4] | (y[5] & ~w).
bug_categories.applicability: Because & binds tighter than |, ~w would qualify only y[5], and Y3 would assert for y[1], y[2] or y[4] even when w=1. The code stays syntactically valid and is only wrong for w=1 with those bits set.

bug_categories.description: Replace the OR chain with a different operator, such as using XOR (y[1] ^ y[2] ^ y[4] ^ y[5]) or AND between the y bits, in Y3.
bug_categories.applicability: With XOR, Y3 would deassert when an even number of those bits are set. With AND, it would require all of them. For one-hot inputs XOR behaves like OR, so the bug only appears on multi-hot input patterns.

bug_categories.description: Swap the expressions assigned to Y1 and Y3, or have Y1 use the Y3 condition on w (Y1 = y[0] & ~w).
bug_categories.applicability: The two outputs have different input dependencies, so swapping them or flipping w polarity on only one of them changes the functional mapping on every input combination. It is easy to introduce when editing the two adjacent assign statements.

bug_categories.description: Replace the bitwise AND in out_both with OR (in[98:0] | in[99:1]), so the output asserts when either neighbor is set instead of both.
bug_categories.applicability: out_both relies on a single & between adjacent bits; swapping the operator is a valid one-token change that makes out_both identical to out_any in its lower 99 bits.

bug_categories.description: Change the XOR in out_different to XNOR (~^) or OR, inverting or corrupting the 'neighbors differ' detection.
bug_categories.applicability: out_different = in ^ rotated(in); XNOR makes every output bit report equality instead of difference, and OR makes it report any-set.

bug_categories.description: Change the constant 1'b0 in the MSB of out_both or the LSB of out_any to 1'b1, producing a constant-1 on the boundary bit.
bug_categories.applicability: out_both uses {1'b0, ...} and out_any uses {..., 1'b0}; flipping either constant yields a stuck-at-1 boundary bit that still has correct width.

bug_categories.description: Move the 1'b0 padding to the opposite end of the concatenation, e.g. out_both = {in[98:0] & in[99:1], 1'b0}, misaligning outputs by one bit.
bug_categories.applicability: out_both and out_any use opposite padding positions (MSB vs LSB); swapping them shifts the whole result vector relative to the intended bit alignment.

bug_categories.description: Alter slice ranges, e.g. in[99:1] changed to in[99:0] truncated/in[98:0] paired with in[98:0], or in[98:0] & in[98:0], so neighbor pairing is wrong (compared bit with itself or wrong neighbor).
bug_categories.applicability: The design pairs in[i] with in[i+1] via offset slices [98:0] and [99:1]; shifting either index by one changes which neighbor is compared and may alter effective width.

bug_categories.description: In out_different, change the rotated operand from {in[0], in[99:1]} to {in[98:0], in[99]} (opposite direction) or to a non-wrapping shift {1'b0, in[99:1]}.
bug_categories.applicability: out_different uses a circular right rotation so bit 99 compares against in[0]; reversing direction compares each bit to the other neighbor, and removing wrap changes bit 99's result.

bug_categories.description: Replace in[0] in the rotation concatenation with in[99] or in[1] (or constant 0), breaking only the wrap-around comparison at the MSB.
bug_categories.applicability: Only out_different[99] depends on the concatenated in[0]; this subtle bug leaves 99 bits correct and corrupts a single boundary bit, a hard-to-detect corner case.

bug_categories.description: Add a spurious bitwise NOT to one operand or whole expression, e.g. out_any = {~(in[98:0] | in[99:1]), 1'b0} or in[98:0] & ~in[99:1] in out_both.
bug_categories.applicability: All three outputs are simple combinational bitwise expressions where a stray ~ remains valid Verilog and turns 'any' into NOR, 'both' into an asymmetric 'and-not', or inverts the difference result.

bug_categories.description: Replace the OR operator in mux_in[0] with AND or XOR, e.g. assign mux_in[0] = c & d; or c ^ d;
bug_categories.applicability: mux_in[0] = c | d is a simple two-input gate; changing the operator yields a valid but functionally different truth table (e.g., output differs for c=1,d=0 and c=0,d=1).

bug_categories.description: Replace the AND operator in mux_in[3] with OR or XOR, e.g. assign mux_in[3] = c | d; or c ^ d;
bug_categories.applicability: mux_in[3] = c & d is only high when both inputs are high; switching operators changes the output for the mixed input cases (01, 10) and breaks the expected mux data input.

bug_categories.description: Change the constant tie-off of mux_in[1] from 0 to 1 (assign mux_in[1] = 1;).
bug_categories.applicability: mux_in[1] is hard-wired to 0. Flipping it to 1 is valid Verilog and makes this mux input incorrectly high for all input combinations.

bug_categories.description: Remove the inversion on d in mux_in[2], giving assign mux_in[2] = d;, or invert it incorrectly elsewhere.
bug_categories.applicability: mux_in[2] = ~d relies on a single bitwise NOT; dropping it inverts the logical behavior of that bit for every input value.

bug_categories.description: Add an inversion to an output that should be non-inverted, e.g. assign mux_in[0] = ~(c | d); (NOR) or mux_in[3] = ~(c & d); (NAND).
bug_categories.applicability: Bits 0 and 3 are non-inverted gate outputs; adding a NOT flips their polarity while the design remains syntactically valid.

bug_categories.description: Use the wrong input signal in an expression, e.g. assign mux_in[2] = ~c; instead of ~d.
bug_categories.applicability: Only two inputs (c, d) exist and bit 2 depends solely on d; substituting c creates a plausible copy-paste style error that changes behavior.

bug_categories.description: Swap the bit indices of two assignments, e.g. assign mux_in[0] = c & d; and assign mux_in[3] = c | d; or swap mux_in[1] and mux_in[2] assignments.
bug_categories.applicability: The four output bits are driven by distinct expressions on a 4-bit bus; permuting which index receives which expression routes the wrong data to the mux input positions.

bug_categories.bug_type: Bit width / bus partial assignment error
bug_categories.description: Drop or merge assignments so a bit is left undriven or driven by a reduced expression, e.g. remove the assign for mux_in[1] (leaving it floating 'z') or declare output as [2:0] mux_in and shift assignments.
bug_categories.applicability: The output is a 4-bit vector with each bit assigned individually; omitting an assignment or changing the vector width leaves bits undriven or misaligned, breaking the interface to the downstream mux.

bug_categories.description: Remove the bitwise NOT so the register captures a directly (q <= a), turning the inverter into a plain D flip-flop.
bug_categories.applicability: The only logic is q <= ~a; dropping '~' changes the function from inverting to non-inverting on every clock edge.

bug_categories.description: Replace bitwise NOT '~' with logical NOT '!' or an equivalent construct. For a 1-bit signal this is functionally the same, so it is a benign or equivalent mutation, and in a widened design it would give different results.
bug_categories.applicability: Applied to q <= ~a, it checks whether the testbench distinguishes equivalent forms. It becomes a real bug if the port is widened, since '!' reduces the whole vector to one bit.

bug_categories.description: Change the sensitivity from posedge clk to negedge clk, so the output updates on the falling edge and shifts timing by half a cycle.
bug_categories.applicability: The always block is @(posedge clk); switching to negedge changes when q is sampled and updated, breaking cycle-accurate behavior.

bug_categories.description: Replace the non-blocking '<=' with blocking '=' in the clocked block. For a single register this may be simulation-equivalent but can introduce race conditions with other logic sampling q on the same clock edge.
bug_categories.applicability: q <= ~a becomes q = ~a; downstream logic or the testbench reading q at posedge clk may see the new value instead of the old one, causing a race.

bug_categories.description: Change the clocked always block to a combinational one (always @(*) q = ~a), removing the register so q follows ~a immediately without a clock-edge delay.
bug_categories.applicability: The output has no one-cycle latency anymore, so q changes asynchronously with a rather than being sampled at posedge clk.

bug_categories.bug_type: Asynchronous reset or enable insertion error
bug_categories.description: Add an unintended control such as an async reset to a constant or a gating condition so q is forced to a fixed value or holds its value in certain cases.
bug_categories.applicability: For example, always @(posedge clk or posedge a) if (a) q <= 1'b0; else q <= ~a; makes q react asynchronously to a and diverges from the clocked-only specification.

bug_categories.bug_type: Stale or delayed data (extra pipeline stage)
bug_categories.description: Insert an intermediate register so q reflects ~a from two cycles ago instead of one, adding an extra cycle of latency.
bug_categories.applicability: Introduce a reg a_d sampled at posedge clk and assign q <= ~a_d. The output is correct logically but delayed by an additional clock cycle relative to the original.

bug_categories.description: Drive q from the wrong source, such as from clk or from q itself (q <= ~q), or tie it to a constant, so the output no longer depends on the input a.
bug_categories.applicability: With q <= ~q the output toggles every clock regardless of a; with q <= ~clk or a constant, the dependence on a is lost, which is easy to detect with any input pattern change.

mutants.bug_type: Stale or delayed data (extra pipeline stage)
Asynchronous reset or enable insertion error

bug_categories.description: Replace the AND in Y1 with OR, so Y1 = y[0] | ~w instead of y[0] & ~w.
bug_categories.applicability: Y1 is a single AND of y[0] and ~w. Changing it to OR makes Y1 high whenever w is 0 or y[0] is 1, which diverges from the intended behavior on most input combinations.

bug_categories.description: Remove the inversion on w in Y1 (y[0] & w), or add one to w in Y3 (... & ~w).
bug_categories.applicability: Y1 depends on ~w and Y3 on w. Flipping either polarity makes the outputs active in the wrong w state and can make Y1 and Y3 active simultaneously instead of mutually exclusive.

bug_categories.description: Change one of the y indices in Y1 or Y3, e.g. use y[3] instead of y[2] in Y3, or y[1] instead of y[0] in Y1.
bug_categories.applicability: The design selects specific bits of the 6-bit y input. Bit 3 is unused in Y3, so swapping an index to 3 or duplicating one index silently changes which states trigger the outputs.

bug_categories.description: Remove one of the four terms in Y3's OR, e.g. (y[1] | y[2] | y[4]) & w with y[5] omitted.
bug_categories.applicability: Y3 is a four-input OR over y[1], y[2], y[4], y[5]. Dropping any term means that single-bit input no longer asserts Y3, a corner-case failure only visible when that bit alone is set.

bug_categories.bug_type: Extra term added to OR reduction
bug_categories.description: Add y[3] or y[0] into the OR group of Y3: (y[1] | y[2] | y[3] | y[4] | y[5]) & w.
bug_categories.applicability: y[3] is intentionally excluded from the outputs and y[0] is handled by Y1. Including either causes Y3 to assert for input states that should not trigger it.

bug_categories.description: Remove the parentheses in Y3 so it becomes y[1] | y[2] | y[4] | y[5] & w.
bug_categories.applicability: Without parentheses, & binds tighter than |, so w only gates y[5]. Y3 then goes high whenever y[1], y[2], or y[4] is set regardless of w, which is valid Verilog but wrong.

bug_categories.bug_type: Bitwise vs logical operator confusion / wrong reduction operator
bug_categories.description: Change the OR in Y3 to AND among the y bits, e.g. (y[1] & y[2] & y[4] & y[5]) & w, or replace the outer & with |.
bug_categories.applicability: Y3 relies on an OR of the y bits gated by w. Using AND requires all four bits set, and using | for the outer operator ungates the output from w, either of which drastically changes the truth table.

bug_categories.description: Swap the expressions driving Y1 and Y3, or make Y1 depend on the Y3 logic partially (e.g. Y1 = y[0] & ~w | y[1]).
bug_categories.applicability: Both outputs are simple continuous assigns with distinct expressions. Swapping them or mixing a term from one into the other produces valid code with wrong output-to-condition mapping, and the 1-bit port widths hide any type mismatch.

mutants.bug_type: Extra term added to OR reduction

bug_categories.description: Replace the bitwise OR in 'assign q = c | b;' with AND, so q is high only when both b and c are high.
bug_categories.applicability: The entire design is a single OR expression; changing the operator to AND alters the truth table for the (b=1,c=0) and (b=0,c=1) cases.

bug_categories.description: Replace '|' with '^' so q goes low when both b and c are 1.
bug_categories.applicability: Output differs from the correct design only when b=1 and c=1, a subtle corner-case bug that simple tests may miss.

bug_categories.description: Replace input c with unused input a (q = a | b) or replace b with d (q = c | d).
bug_categories.applicability: Inputs a and d are currently unused, so substituting them is syntactically valid and changes functionality by making q depend on the wrong inputs.

bug_categories.description: Drop one operand so q = b or q = c, ignoring the other input entirely.
bug_categories.applicability: The output depends on only two inputs; removing either makes q ignore a required input, failing when only the dropped input is high.

bug_categories.description: Invert the result, e.g. q = ~(c | b) (NOR), or invert only one operand such as q = c | ~b.
bug_categories.applicability: A single-bit combinational output makes inversion a simple change that flips the truth table in several or all input combinations.

bug_categories.description: Add an additional term involving unused inputs, e.g. q = c | b | (a & d), or q = (c | b) & a.
bug_categories.applicability: Inputs a and d are available but unused; adding them makes q depend on extra inputs and produces wrong output whenever the added term is active.

bug_categories.bug_type: Bitwise vs logical operator confusion / precedence error
bug_categories.description: Introduce a precedence or grouping mistake such as q = c | b & a or q = c || (b & d), changing how operands combine.
bug_categories.applicability: With four inputs available, regrouping operands with mixed AND/OR creates valid Verilog whose output differs from c|b when a or d take certain values.

bug_categories.description: Force one operand or the output to a constant, e.g. q = c | 1'b0, q = c | 1'b1, or q = 1'b0.
bug_categories.applicability: A stuck-at constant simulates a tie-off mistake: q becomes insensitive to b or always fixed, making the output independent of the intended inputs.

bug_categories.description: Replace the OR in the first group with AND, so the first term becomes (a & b) instead of (a | b).
bug_categories.applicability: q = (a & b) & (c | d). The output now requires both a and b high, so cases where only one of a or b is high incorrectly yield 0.

bug_categories.description: Replace the top-level AND that combines the two OR groups with OR.
bug_categories.applicability: q = (a | b) | (c | d). The output becomes 1 whenever any input is high, which removes the product-of-sums requirement that one input from each pair must be high.

bug_categories.description: Replace the OR in the second group with XOR, so the term becomes (c ^ d).
bug_categories.applicability: q = (a | b) & (c ^ d). When c and d are both 1, the output wrongly goes to 0, although the original gives 1 when a or b is high.

bug_categories.description: Invert one operand or one group, such as negating input a or the whole second group.
bug_categories.applicability: q = (~a | b) & (c | d), or q = (a | b) & ~(c | d). The truth table changes for every vector where the inverted signal matters.

bug_categories.description: Replace one input in an expression with another input, a copy-paste style error that leaves some inputs unused or duplicated.
bug_categories.applicability: q = (a | b) & (c | c), or q = (a | a) & (c | d). Input d or b no longer affects the output, and the design becomes insensitive to it.

bug_categories.description: Remove or move the parentheses so the operator precedence changes the logic. In Verilog & binds tighter than |.
bug_categories.applicability: q = a | b & c | d is parsed as a | (b & c) | d. This gives 1 whenever a or d is high regardless of the other pair, which breaks the intended product-of-sums.

bug_categories.description: Invert the final output, or apply a reduction or negation operator to the whole expression, for example by switching to a NAND-style structure.
bug_categories.applicability: q = ~((a | b) & (c | d)). Every output value in the truth table is complemented, so the function becomes the exact opposite of the intended one.

bug_categories.description: Regroup the four inputs across the two OR terms so that the pairs differ from the intended (a,b) and (c,d).
bug_categories.applicability: q = (a | c) & (b | d). The truth table differs for vectors such as a=1, b=0, c=1, d=0, where the original gives 1 and this gives 0, and for a=1, b=1, c=0, d=0, where the original gives 0 and this also gives 0 but with different intermediate terms.

bug_categories.description: Replace one of the XOR operators in the parity chain with a different bitwise operator such as OR or AND, e.g. q = ~a ^ b | c ^ d, or q = ~a ^ b ^ c & d.
bug_categories.applicability: The expression is a pure chain of XOR operations, so swapping any single operator with | or & changes the truth table for many input combinations while remaining valid Verilog.

bug_categories.description: Remove the unary inversion on input a so the output becomes a ^ b ^ c ^ d, flipping the output polarity for every input combination.
bug_categories.applicability: The design relies on a single bitwise NOT on 'a' to produce XNOR-style (inverted parity) behavior. Dropping it yields plain even/odd parity with the opposite output on every input.

bug_categories.description: Move the inversion from a to a different input, or invert two inputs, e.g. q = a ^ ~b ^ c ^ d or q = ~a ^ ~b ^ c ^ d.
bug_categories.applicability: Inverting a different single input gives the same function (functionally equivalent), but inverting two inputs cancels the inversion and yields plain parity. This tests whether the verifier detects polarity parity errors.

bug_categories.description: Apply the inversion to the whole expression or to a sub-expression rather than just 'a', e.g. q = ~(a ^ b) ^ c ^ d is equivalent, but q = ~(a ^ b ^ c ^ d) or q = ~a ^ (b | c) ^ d changes grouping and behavior.
bug_categories.applicability: Bitwise ~ binds tighter than ^, so adding or moving parentheses subtly changes which terms are inverted or combined. Wrongly grouped sub-expressions with other operators change the logic.

bug_categories.description: Omit one of the inputs from the XOR chain, e.g. q = ~a ^ b ^ c, so output ignores d.
bug_categories.applicability: The output depends on all four inputs. Dropping any one makes the output independent of that input, which breaks the parity function in half of the cases.

bug_categories.description: Replace one operand with another input, e.g. q = ~a ^ b ^ c ^ c or q = ~a ^ b ^ b ^ d, causing two operands to cancel out.
bug_categories.applicability: With only four single-bit inputs combined by XOR, duplicating an input cancels itself and removes its contribution, quietly degrading the parity function to depend on only two inputs.

bug_categories.description: Force one operand or the result to a constant, e.g. q = ~a ^ b ^ c ^ 1'b0 with d tied low, or q = 1'b1 on some term.
bug_categories.applicability: Tying an input to a constant 0 or 1 emulates a stuck-at fault. Constant 1 flips output polarity; constant 0 removes the input's influence. Both are valid Verilog and change the function.

bug_categories.description: Replace the chain with a reduction or mixed-width expression, e.g. q = ~^{a,b,c} (omitting d) or q = ^{a,b,c,d} (no inversion), or use logical operators like ! and || instead of bitwise ones.
bug_categories.applicability: The design can be rewritten with reduction XOR over a concatenation, where an incorrect concatenation, a reduction XNOR (~^) instead of XOR, or a logical-NOT (!a) can alter polarity or drop terms. Since all signals are 1-bit, logical and bitwise operators often behave similarly, making errors subtle.

bug_categories.description: Invert the polarity of the select condition so that Q <= (L) ? q_in : r_in or Q <= (!L) ? r_in : q_in, swapping which input is loaded when L is asserted.
bug_categories.applicability: The design is a single 2:1 mux on L feeding a flop. Swapping the mux inputs or inverting L directly changes the selected data source for every cycle.

bug_categories.description: Replace one of the mux data inputs with the wrong signal, e.g. Q <= (L) ? r_in : r_in or Q <= (L) ? q_in : q_in, or substitute L itself as a data input.
bug_categories.applicability: Only two data inputs (q_in, r_in) exist. Duplicating one makes the select irrelevant, and the design still compiles with unused-input warnings only.

bug_categories.description: Change the non-blocking assignment Q <= ... to a blocking assignment Q = ... in the clocked always block.
bug_categories.applicability: Although a single flop usually still simulates the same, this introduces race conditions with other logic sampling Q in the same timestep and violates synchronous design style.

bug_categories.description: Change always @(posedge clk) to always @(negedge clk), or to a level-sensitive/combined edge list such as @(posedge clk or negedge clk).
bug_categories.applicability: Q would update on the wrong edge, shifting the output timing by half a cycle, or update on both edges, producing double-rate sampling of L, q_in, r_in.

bug_categories.description: Change initial Q = 0 to initial Q = 1 (or remove the initial block so Q starts as X).
bug_categories.applicability: The design has no reset; the initial block is the only defined power-up state. Altering it changes the output before the first clock edge and the early-cycle behavior.

bug_categories.bug_type: Asynchronous behavior introduced into sequential logic
bug_categories.description: Make the logic combinational or partially asynchronous, e.g. always @(posedge clk or posedge L) or always @(*) Q <= ..., so Q responds to L without waiting for the clock.
bug_categories.applicability: L is a control input to the mux; adding it to the sensitivity list makes Q change immediately on L rising, breaking synchronous load semantics.

bug_categories.description: Add an extra condition that suppresses or alters the update, e.g. Q <= (L & q_in) ? r_in : q_in, or only update when q_in != r_in, so Q holds its old value or takes the wrong value in some cases.
bug_categories.applicability: The select expression is a simple single-bit signal; compounding it with data inputs creates data-dependent selection errors that only manifest for specific input combinations.

bug_categories.description: Invert the stored value or apply a wrong bitwise operator, e.g. Q <= ~((L) ? r_in : q_in) or Q <= (L) ? (r_in ^ q_in) : q_in.
bug_categories.applicability: Q is a 1-bit register driven by a single expression; an added inversion or XOR on the data path corrupts the value on every clock while still being valid Verilog.

bug_categories.description: Swap the rotate-right and rotate-left operations so ena==2'h1 performs a left rotate and ena==2'h2 performs a right rotate.
bug_categories.applicability: The two branches use { q[0], q[99:1] } and { q[98:0], q[99] }. Exchanging the enable conditions or the concatenations silently reverses the direction of rotation while remaining valid Verilog.

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong bit index in rotate concatenation
bug_categories.description: Use an incorrect wrap-around bit in a rotate, e.g. { q[99], q[99:1] } (arithmetic-shift-like sign replicate) or { q[98:0], q[0] }, so the wrapped bit is not the one shifted out.
bug_categories.applicability: The rotate-right wraps q[0] into bit 99 and the rotate-left wraps q[99] into bit 0. Replacing the wrap bit changes the rotation into a duplicating shift and corrupts the data pattern.

bug_categories.bug_type: Off-by-one slice width / bit width mismatch
bug_categories.description: Change a part-select bound so the concatenation has 99 or 101 bits, e.g. { q[0], q[98:1] } or { q[0], q[99:0] }, causing truncation or padding on assignment to the 100-bit q.
bug_categories.applicability: The concatenations must total exactly 100 bits: 1 + q[99:1] (99) and q[98:0] (99) + 1. Altering a bound produces an implicit width mismatch and misaligned or dropped bits.

bug_categories.description: Modify the ena comparison constants, e.g. ena==2'h3 for one rotate, or both branches using the same value, so one rotate becomes unreachable or the wrong encoding triggers it.
bug_categories.applicability: ena is 2 bits with 01 = right rotate and 10 = left rotate, 00/11 = hold. Changing a constant makes 2'b11 trigger a rotate or makes a rotate mode dead.

bug_categories.bug_type: Priority inversion between load and enable
bug_categories.description: Reorder the if/else chain so the rotate conditions take priority over load, or make load only apply when ena==0.
bug_categories.applicability: load is currently highest priority. If rotation is checked first, asserting load together with ena=1 or 2 rotates q instead of loading data, violating the spec.

bug_categories.description: Replace one or more non-blocking assignments (<=) with blocking (=) in the clocked always block.
bug_categories.applicability: q is assigned in a sequential always @(posedge clk). Using = alters simulation semantics and can cause race conditions with other logic sampling q in the same time step, though in this single-register module the effect is mainly on downstream simulation ordering.

bug_categories.description: Add a final else branch that clears q or loads data, or make ena==2'h0/2'h3 modify q, breaking the required hold behavior.
bug_categories.applicability: Currently when load=0 and ena is 0 or 3, q retains its value via the implicit latch-free hold in the clocked block. An added else q <= 0 or q <= data causes unintended state loss.

bug_categories.description: Change the sensitivity from posedge clk to negedge clk, or make the block level-sensitive or include load in the sensitivity list asynchronously.
bug_categories.applicability: The register updates on posedge clk. Switching to negedge shifts timing by half a cycle relative to inputs, and adding posedge load makes loading asynchronous, changing synchronous behavior.

bug_categories.description: Change one of the hex scancode match constants, e.g. 16'he06b to 16'he06d, or 16'he075 to 16'he057, so the key no longer matches the correct PS/2 arrow code.
bug_categories.applicability: Each of the four case items (e06b, e072, e074, e075) uses a literal constant, so a single-digit change silently breaks one direction while the design remains valid Verilog.

bug_categories.bug_type: Output signal swap / wrong assignment target
bug_categories.description: Swap the output assigned in two case branches, e.g. 16'he06b drives right instead of left, or e072 drives up instead of down.
bug_categories.applicability: Four one-hot outputs (up, left, down, right) are assigned in separate branches, so exchanging targets produces plausible but wrong direction mapping.

bug_categories.description: Remove or alter the default clearing statement '{ up, left, down, right } = 0;' so outputs are not cleared for non-matching scancodes, causing latches or stale outputs.
bug_categories.applicability: The combinational block relies on the default zeroing for outputs to deassert; without it, outputs hold previous values and incomplete assignment infers latches.

bug_categories.bug_type: Concatenation order error in default clear
bug_categories.description: Change the default clear to set one output to 1 (e.g. '{ up, left, down, right } = 4'b0001' or '= 4'b1000') so a direction is asserted when no key matches.
bug_categories.applicability: The default clear uses a concatenation of all four outputs with a literal 0; replacing it with a non-zero sized value makes an output stuck high by default.

bug_categories.bug_type: Bit width mismatch in case constants
bug_categories.description: Reduce the width or change the base of the case constants, e.g. use 8'h6b instead of 16'he06b, or compare against only the lower byte, so the extended prefix e0 is ignored and aliasing occurs.
bug_categories.applicability: The scancode input is 16 bits with an E0 extended prefix; matching only the low byte causes non-extended codes (e.g. 16'h006b, keypad) to falsely trigger outputs.

bug_categories.description: Replace 'case' with 'casez' or 'casex' and introduce wildcard bits (e.g. 16'he0?b or x bits) in a pattern so multiple scancodes match a single direction.
bug_categories.applicability: The exact-match 16-bit case is sensitive to every bit; wildcarding allows incorrect scancodes to assert outputs and can create overlapping matches.

bug_categories.description: Make two case items use the same scancode (e.g. both e072 and e074 constants set to e074) so the first match wins and one direction can never be asserted.
bug_categories.applicability: Case items are evaluated in order with first-match semantics, so duplicating a constant makes a direction unreachable while the code stays syntactically valid.

bug_categories.bug_type: Multiple outputs asserted in a branch (one-hot violation)
bug_categories.description: Make a branch assert additional outputs, e.g. 'left = 1; up = 1;' or assign down and right in the same item, violating mutual exclusivity of direction outputs.
bug_categories.applicability: The design assumes at most one of up/left/down/right is high at a time; adding extra assignments in a branch produces illegal simultaneous direction outputs.

module dut
(
  input clk,
  input load,
  input [511:0] data,
  output reg [511:0] q
);


  always @(posedge clk) begin
    if(load) q <= data; 
    else begin
      q <= q[$bits(q)-1:1] ^ { q[$bits(q)-2:0], 1'b0 };
    end
  end


endmodule

bug_categories.description: Replace the XOR between the right-shifted and left-shifted copies of q with a different operator such as AND, OR, or XNOR.
bug_categories.applicability: The next-state update q <= q[$bits(q)-1:1] ^ {q[$bits(q)-2:0],1'b0} is the core of this design (a Rule-90-style cellular automaton). Changing ^ to | or & changes the evolution rule entirely and produces wrong state sequences after the first non-load cycle.

bug_categories.description: Swap the shift directions so that the neighbor taken is the wrong one, e.g. use { 1'b0, q[$bits(q)-1:1] } for the left operand or shift both operands the same way.
bug_categories.applicability: The design XORs each bit's two neighbors. If both operands come from the same direction, or the zero fill goes on the wrong side, the neighbor relation (q[i+1] ^ q[i-1]) is broken and boundary bits get wrong values.

bug_categories.description: Alter the part-select bounds, e.g. use q[$bits(q)-1:0] or q[$bits(q)-2:1] so the operand widths differ from the 512-bit target and are implicitly zero-extended or truncated.
bug_categories.applicability: The first operand q[511:1] is 511 bits and is zero-extended to 512 at the MSB, while the second operand is the 511-bit slice concatenated with 1'b0. Changing a slice bound shifts bits incorrectly or drops/duplicates a position in the 512-bit vector.

bug_categories.description: Change the boundary fill value, e.g. replace the 1'b0 appended on the LSB side with 1'b1 or with q[$bits(q)-1] (wrap-around/circular boundary).
bug_categories.applicability: Rule 90 here assumes zero boundaries. The LSB gets q[1]^0 and the MSB gets 0^q[510]. Using 1'b1 or a wrap-around alters the edge cells and propagates errors inward over subsequent cycles.

bug_categories.description: Invert the load condition (if(!load)) or remove the else so that the update overrides the load, or make load take effect only when another condition holds.
bug_categories.applicability: The load input selects between loading data and stepping the automaton. Inverting it makes q evolve while load is asserted and load data when it is not, breaking initialization of the 512-bit state.

bug_categories.description: Replace one of the non-blocking assignments (<=) with a blocking assignment (=) in the sequential block.
bug_categories.applicability: q is an output reg updated in a clocked always block. Using = for q can cause race conditions in simulation with downstream logic sampling q on the same clock edge, producing mismatched cycle-level behavior.

bug_categories.description: Load a modified value from data, such as a bit-reversed, byte-swapped, inverted, or partially masked/truncated version of data, or only load a subset of bits.
bug_categories.applicability: On load, q <= data takes the full 512-bit input. Loading ~data, reversing bit order, or only loading the lower 256 bits (leaving upper bits at old values or zero) yields a wrong initial state and thus a wrong sequence thereafter.

bug_categories.description: Change the triggering edge from posedge clk to negedge clk, or alter the sensitivity list so the update is not purely synchronous.
bug_categories.applicability: The module is a single-clock synchronous design. Triggering on negedge shifts the timing of loads and updates by half a cycle relative to the testbench, causing cycle-misaligned outputs of q versus the expected reference.

bug_categories.description: Change one of the scan-code match constants to a wrong hex value, e.g. 8'h1e changed to 8'h1d, or two constants swapped so that digits 2 and 3 map to each other's codes.
bug_categories.applicability: The design is a PS/2 scan code to digit decoder built from a case table of 10 hardcoded 8-bit constants. Altering any constant makes the correct key decode as invalid or maps another key to the wrong digit.

bug_categories.description: Assign the wrong digit to a valid scan code, e.g. 8'h3d: out = 6 instead of 7, or 8'h46: out = 8 instead of 9.
bug_categories.applicability: Each case arm drives out with a 4-bit decimal value. Off-by-one or duplicated values produce incorrect decoding while valid stays 1, which is hard to spot without a full sweep of inputs.

bug_categories.description: Change the default branch so valid is set to 1 instead of 0, or invert the initial default: valid = 0 at the top and valid = 1 only in the default arm.
bug_categories.applicability: valid is initialized to 1 and cleared only in the default arm. Inverting this logic makes all unknown codes appear valid, or all known codes appear invalid.

bug_categories.description: Remove one case arm (e.g. 8'h25 for digit 4) so that code falls through to default and is flagged invalid.
bug_categories.applicability: With 10 individual arms and no overlap, deleting any arm silently makes that digit undecodable, with valid=0 for a legitimate key code.

bug_categories.description: Change one case constant to equal another existing constant (e.g. 8'h26 changed to 8'h25) so the first matching arm wins and one digit becomes unreachable.
bug_categories.applicability: Verilog case takes the first match, so a duplicated scan code shadows the later arm. Digit 3 or 4 would become unreachable while the design still compiles.

bug_categories.description: Change the initial assignment out = 0 to a nonzero value (e.g. out = 4'hF), or remove it so out is not assigned in the default path.
bug_categories.applicability: out is defaulted to 0 before the case. Changing it alters the out value for invalid codes; removing it would infer a latch on out, since the default arm only assigns valid.

bug_categories.bug_type: Bit width / truncation mismatch in case label
bug_categories.description: Use a case label with a mismatched width or base, e.g. 4'h5 or 8'd45 (decimal) instead of 8'h45, so the matched value differs from the intended scan code.
bug_categories.applicability: The case labels are 8-bit hex constants compared against the 8-bit code input. Switching base to decimal (8'd45 = 0x2D) or shortening the width zero-extends the label and changes which code matches.

bug_categories.description: Replace always @(*) with a restricted sensitivity list such as always @(code[3:0]), or convert one output assignment to be conditional so it is not driven on all paths (valid not assigned in some arm).
bug_categories.applicability: Both outputs are driven from a combinational always block. A partial sensitivity list makes out and valid fail to update when upper code bits change, e.g. 8'h16 vs 8'h26, causing stale outputs in simulation.
