bug_categories.bug_type: Arithmetic right shift sign bit error
bug_categories.description: In the amount==2'b10 case (arithmetic right shift by 1), replace the replicated sign bit q[63] with 1'b0 so it becomes a logical right shift: { 1'b0, q[63:1] }.
bug_categories.applicability: Negative values lose their sign on right shift, corrupting signed arithmetic behavior of the 1-bit arithmetic right shift.

bug_categories.description: In the amount==2'b01 case (left shift by 8), change the slice to q[56:0] with 7 zeros or q[54:0] with 9 zeros, or use q[55:0] with only 7 padded zeros, so the shift distance is not 8 bits.
bug_categories.applicability: Left shift by 8 produces a wrong shift distance (and possibly width mismatch/truncation), breaking byte-wise shifting.

bug_categories.description: In the amount==2'b11 case (arithmetic right shift by 8), change the replication { 8{q[63]} } to { 7{q[63]} } or { 9{q[63]} } with matching slice width changes, or replicate q[62] instead of q[63].
bug_categories.applicability: Upper byte after the 8-bit arithmetic right shift is filled incorrectly, so sign extension is wrong for negative numbers.

bug_categories.description: Swap the direction of two shift cases, e.g. make amount==2'b00 shift right ({1'b0, q[63:1]}) or make amount==2'b01 shift right by 8, while keeping the case labels unchanged.
bug_categories.applicability: Left/right shifts are mapped to the wrong amount encodings, so the amount-to-operation decoding is wrong.

bug_categories.bug_type: Priority inversion between load and enable
bug_categories.description: Reorder the control logic so that ena is checked before load (if(ena) ... else if(load) q <= data), so shifting takes priority when both are asserted.
bug_categories.applicability: When load and ena are both high, the register shifts instead of loading data, violating load-over-shift priority.

bug_categories.description: Swap the case labels for two operations, e.g. exchange 2'b10 and 2'b11 so the 1-bit arithmetic right shift is selected by 2'b11 and the 8-bit one by 2'b10.
bug_categories.applicability: Specific amount values trigger the wrong shift operation, which only shows up for those input encodings.

bug_categories.description: Change the shift guard from else if(ena) to else if(!ena) or remove the ena condition so shifting happens unconditionally when load is low.
bug_categories.applicability: The register shifts when it should hold its value (or holds when it should shift), breaking the enable/hold behavior.

bug_categories.description: Corrupt the load path, e.g. load a bit-reversed or partially truncated/zero-extended data (q <= {32'b0, data[31:0]}) or use a non-blocking/blocking mix, or make load happen on a different condition such as load & ena.
bug_categories.applicability: Loaded value in q does not match the 64-bit data input, so subsequent shifts operate on incorrect values.

bug_categories.description: Change the constant loaded into q when input a is asserted from 4 to a different value (e.g., 0, 3, 5, or 7).
bug_categories.applicability: The synchronous load `if(a) q <= 4;` defines the restart state of the counter. Altering the constant shifts the sequence start point and the number of cycles before wraparound, which is directly observable at q.

bug_categories.description: Change the terminal-count comparison from q == 6 to another value (e.g., 5 or 7), or to a different relational operator such as q >= 6 or q != 6.
bug_categories.applicability: The counter is meant to cycle 0..6 and skip 7. Using 7 makes it count through all 8 states; using 5 shortens the period to 6; using q >= 6 or != changes the wrap behavior and the handling of state 7 after a load or reset.

bug_categories.description: Change the value assigned on wrap from 0 to another value (e.g., 1 or 4), or leave q unchanged.
bug_categories.applicability: `else if(q == 6) q <= 0;` sets the cycle start. A different target changes the sequence period and the values appearing on q after state 6.

bug_categories.description: Swap the priority of the load and wrap branches, so the q == 6 check is evaluated before the `a` check.
bug_categories.applicability: Currently `a` overrides everything. If q==6 is checked first, asserting a while q==6 produces 0 instead of 4, a corner-case mismatch that only appears when a coincides with the terminal count.

bug_categories.description: Change the increment from q + 1'b1 to q + 2, q + 0, or q - 1 (decrement).
bug_categories.applicability: The default branch counts up by one. Using a different step skips states, freezes the counter, or reverses direction, and may prevent q from ever hitting 6 so the wrap logic is never exercised.

bug_categories.description: Invert the sense of the input a (e.g., `if(!a)` or `if(~a)`), so the load occurs when a is low.
bug_categories.applicability: The control input a is a single-bit synchronous load. Inverting it makes the counter continuously reload 4 in normal operation and count only when a is asserted.

bug_categories.description: Replace one or more non-blocking assignments (<=) with blocking assignments (=) in the clocked always block.
bug_categories.applicability: The design uses `<=` for q in a clocked block. Mixing in `=` changes scheduling semantics; while single-register behavior may seem similar, it can cause simulation race conditions with downstream logic reading q and alters synthesis/simulation consistency.

bug_categories.description: Change the clock edge from posedge clk to negedge clk, or make the sensitivity list include a (e.g., `@(posedge clk or posedge a)`) turning the load into an asynchronous one.
bug_categories.applicability: The module has a single clock and a synchronous load. Using negedge shifts timing relative to testbench stimulus; adding posedge a makes the load asynchronous, so q jumps to 4 immediately on a rising edge rather than at the next clock edge, and the else branches would behave differently.

module dut
(
  input clk,
  input areset,
  input predict_valid,
  input predict_taken,
  output [31:0] predict_history,
  input train_mispredicted,
  input train_taken,
  input [31:0] train_history
);


  always @(posedge clk or posedge areset) if(areset) begin
    predict_history = 0;
  end else begin
    if(train_mispredicted) predict_history <= { train_history, train_taken }; 
    else if(predict_valid) predict_history <= { predict_history, predict_taken }; 
  end


endmodule

bug_categories.bug_type: Priority inversion between training and prediction
bug_categories.description: Swap the order of the if/else-if so that predict_valid is checked before train_mispredicted, causing normal prediction shifts to override misprediction recovery.
bug_categories.applicability: The history register update uses a priority chain 'if(train_mispredicted) ... else if(predict_valid)'. Reversing it means when both are asserted simultaneously the history is shifted with predict_taken instead of being restored from train_history, breaking misprediction recovery.

bug_categories.description: Reverse the order of concatenated elements so the new taken bit is placed at the MSB side or the history is shifted the wrong direction.
bug_categories.applicability: Change { train_history, train_taken } to { train_taken, train_history } or { predict_history, predict_taken } to { predict_taken, predict_history }. This changes which bit position holds the newest outcome and corrupts the history semantics.

bug_categories.description: Use the wrong input in the concatenation, such as predict_taken in the training path or train_taken in the prediction path.
bug_categories.applicability: Replace train_taken with predict_taken in the misprediction recovery branch, or replace predict_taken with train_taken in the prediction shift branch, so the wrong outcome bit is inserted into the history.

bug_categories.description: Change the asynchronous reset value of predict_history to a nonzero constant such as all ones or 32'h1, instead of all zeros.
bug_categories.applicability: The reset branch assigns predict_history = 0. Changing it to 32'hFFFFFFFF or 32'h1 makes the history start in an incorrect state after areset, causing mispredictions in the first lookups after reset.

bug_categories.description: Invert the reset condition or change the sensitivity list so reset is active-low or only synchronous.
bug_categories.applicability: Change 'if(areset)' to 'if(!areset)', or change 'posedge areset' to 'negedge areset' in the sensitivity list. The register would then be held in reset during normal operation or never reset correctly.

bug_categories.description: Alter assignment types within the sequential block, e.g. use blocking '=' in the clocked branches or non-blocking in the reset branch, creating simulation race or ordering differences.
bug_categories.applicability: The reset branch already uses blocking '=' while other branches use '<='. Changing the update branches to blocking or modifying the reset assignment style alters scheduling semantics of predict_history relative to other logic reading it.

bug_categories.description: Remove or weaken the predict_valid gating, or add an extra condition so the history shifts when it should hold, or fails to shift when it should.
bug_categories.applicability: Dropping 'else if(predict_valid)' to an unconditional else makes the history shift every cycle; alternatively gating the train_mispredicted branch with predict_valid or train_taken prevents recovery when no prediction is valid.

bug_categories.bug_type: Bit width / truncation or slice error
bug_categories.description: Use a partial slice of the history in the concatenation so the shift amount or retained bits are wrong.
bug_categories.applicability: Replace { predict_history, predict_taken } with { predict_history[30:0], predict_taken } vs [31:1], or use train_history[30:0] in the recovery path. This shifts the wrong bits, drops the wrong MSB/LSB, or changes effective history length, so the 33-bit concatenation truncates incorrectly into the 32-bit register.

bug_categories.applicability: For example, change 4'h5: out = 0 to out = 1, or 4'hf: out = 0 to out = 1. Only one of the 16 minterms is wrong, so the bug is hard to detect without exhaustive testing.

bug_categories.description: Swap the input patterns of two case items so their outputs are exchanged.
bug_categories.applicability: The design is a 16-entry lookup. Swapping labels such as 4'h6 and 4'h7, or 4'hc and 4'hd, changes the output for two input combinations. These pairs differ only in d, which is the pattern the function depends on.

bug_categories.description: Reorder the bits in the case selector, e.g. {a,b,c,d} becomes {d,c,b,a} or {b,a,c,d}, so every case label maps to a different input combination.
bug_categories.applicability: The case statement uses {a,b,c,d}. Permuting the bits remaps many entries at once and gives a different Boolean function while remaining valid Verilog.

bug_categories.bug_type: Missing case item causing latch inference
bug_categories.description: Delete one case item and add no default branch, so a combinational always block holds its previous value for that input.
bug_categories.applicability: There is no default and all 16 values are enumerated. Removing an entry like 4'hb or 4'h3 makes out a latch, which is functionally wrong and produces non-combinational behavior.

bug_categories.description: Change one case label to duplicate another, so the first match wins and the intended entry is never reached.
bug_categories.applicability: For example, change 4'h9 to 4'h8 (value 1). Then 4'h9 is unhandled, which creates a latch, and the duplicate label is shadowed by the earlier match, so out for 4'h9 is wrong.

bug_categories.description: Drop one input from the case selector, e.g. use {a,b,c} or {a,b,c,1'b0}, so that the case expression is a different width from the 4-bit labels.
bug_categories.applicability: The labels are 4'hX literals. A 3-bit or zero-extended selector means the labels are compared with zero-padding or constant bits and the function ignores one input, so many entries become unreachable.

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong radix or literal value in case label
bug_categories.description: Change a label's literal so it names a different input combination, e.g. 4'he becomes 4'h8 or the base is changed so 4'hc is read as a different value.
bug_categories.applicability: Entries such as 4'hc, 4'hd, 4'he, 4'hf are hex-coded. Mistyping one, e.g. 4'hc to 4'h0, makes entries collide with others and leaves the intended minterm unassigned.

bug_categories.description: Replace the @(*) sensitivity list with an incomplete list such as @(a or b or c), or change out = to out <= in some branches.
bug_categories.applicability: The always block depends on all four inputs. Omitting d from the sensitivity list means out does not update when only d changes, giving stale output in simulation even though the case logic looks correct.

mutants.bug_type: Missing case item causing latch inference

bug_categories.description: Replace the addition operator in the do_sub=0 branch with subtraction (out = a - b), or replace the subtraction in the do_sub=1 branch with addition (out = a + b).
bug_categories.applicability: The design's core function is selecting between a+b and a-b; swapping either operator makes the add/subtract operation wrong for one or both modes.

bug_categories.description: Swap the case item selectors so do_sub=0 performs subtraction and do_sub=1 performs addition (e.g., 0: out = a - b; 1: out = a + b).
bug_categories.applicability: The single control input do_sub decides the operation; inverting its meaning makes every operation the opposite of what is intended while the code remains valid Verilog.

bug_categories.description: Reverse the operands in the subtraction branch so it computes b - a instead of a - b.
bug_categories.applicability: Subtraction is non-commutative, so out = b - a yields the negated result for do_sub=1 whenever a != b, while addition remains unaffected and the bug is subtle.

bug_categories.description: Change the zero detection from 'out == 0' to 'out != 0', or compare against a non-zero constant such as 'out == 1' or 'out == 8'hFF'.
bug_categories.applicability: result_is_zero is derived directly from out; altering the comparison inverts or corrupts the flag so it is asserted for the wrong results.

bug_categories.bug_type: Zero flag derived from wrong signal
bug_categories.description: Compute result_is_zero from an input or partial expression instead of the final out, e.g., 'a == 0', '(a - b) == 0' regardless of do_sub, or 'out[6:0] == 0' ignoring the MSB.
bug_categories.applicability: The flag should reflect the computed result for both modes; using a or a fixed subtraction, or truncating the bit range, makes it wrong during addition or when only bit 7 is set (e.g., 0x80).

bug_categories.description: Restrict operand or result widths, e.g., use a[6:0] + b[6:0] or a[7:1] - b[7:1], or compare only a nibble of out in the zero check (out[3:0] == 0).
bug_categories.applicability: The datapath is 8 bits wide; slicing operands or the zero-detect comparison drops the upper bits, causing incorrect results or false zero flags for values that differ only in high bits.

bug_categories.description: Remove one case branch (e.g., delete the do_sub=1 item) or change a case label so that one value of do_sub leaves out unassigned in the combinational block.
bug_categories.applicability: The always @(*) block has no default and relies on both case items assigning out; omitting one infers a latch holding the previous out value, and result_is_zero then reflects stale data.

bug_categories.bug_type: Stale value / ordering error in combinational logic
bug_categories.description: Move the 'result_is_zero = out == 0;' assignment before the case statement, or use a non-blocking assignment for out (out <= a + b), so the flag evaluates the previous out value rather than the newly computed one.
bug_categories.applicability: result_is_zero depends on out computed in the same always block with blocking assignments; reordering or switching to non-blocking makes the flag lag one evaluation behind the actual result.

original_code:
module dut
(
  input clk,
  input load,
  input [511:0] data,
  output reg [511:0] q
);


  always @(posedge clk) begin
    if(load) q <= data; 
    else begin
      q <= ~(q[$bits(q)-1:1] & q[$bits(q)-1:0] & { q[$bits(q)-2:0], 1'b0 } | ~q[$bits(q)-1:1] & ~q[$bits(q)-1:0] & ~{ q[$bits(q)-2:0], 1'b0 } | q[$bits(q)-1:1] & ~q[$bits(q)-1:0] & ~{ q[$bits(q)-2:0], 1'b0 });
    end
  end


endmodule

bug_categories.description: Invert the polarity of the load condition (e.g., `if(!load)`) or swap the load and update branches so that data is loaded when load is low and the rule is applied when load is high.
bug_categories.applicability: The design has a single `if(load) q <= data; else ...` structure, so inverting the condition completely reverses when the register is loaded versus when the cellular-automaton update runs.

bug_categories.bug_type: Bit width / slice mismatch in neighbor selection
bug_categories.description: Change the slice bounds of one of the operands, for example using q[$bits(q)-1:1] where q[$bits(q)-1:0] was intended, or shrinking/extending a slice, causing implicit zero-extension or truncation and misaligned bits.
bug_categories.applicability: The expression mixes 511-bit slices (q[511:1]), 512-bit slices (q[511:0]), and a 512-bit concatenation ({q[510:0],1'b0}). Altering any slice bound changes width and extension behavior and silently alters the boundary bits.

bug_categories.description: Change the left-shifted neighbor `{q[$bits(q)-2:0], 1'b0}` to a right-shifted form such as `{1'b0, q[$bits(q)-1:1]}`, or use `q[$bits(q)-2:0]` offset by the wrong amount, so the wrong neighbor is used in the rule.
bug_categories.applicability: The update depends on each bit's left and right neighbors. Fetching the wrong neighbor changes the rule's neighborhood and the pattern evolution across all 512 bits.

bug_categories.description: Change the fill bit in the shifted vector from 1'b0 to 1'b1 (or to a wrap-around bit such as q[511]), altering the boundary behavior at the LSB edge.
bug_categories.applicability: The concatenation `{q[$bits(q)-2:0], 1'b0}` supplies a constant 0 at the edge. Changing it modifies the edge cell's next state, and wrap-around vs. zero boundary is a realistic design variant.

bug_categories.description: Replace one of the AND operators with OR or XOR within a product term (e.g., `a & b & c` becomes `a | b & c`), or replace the OR combining the product terms with XOR.
bug_categories.applicability: The next-state logic is a sum of three three-input product terms with `&`, `|`, and `~`. Swapping operators alters the truth table (the cellular-automaton rule) while remaining syntactically valid.

bug_categories.description: Remove or add a `~` on one of the literals in a product term, or remove the outer `~` that inverts the whole result.
bug_categories.applicability: The three product terms use specific negation patterns on each neighbor, and the whole expression is negated. Dropping or adding a single `~` changes one minterm of the rule or complements the entire next state.

bug_categories.description: Alter grouping so precedence changes the result, e.g., move the outer `~` to apply only to the first term, or add parentheses that change how `&` and `|` combine across the three terms.
bug_categories.applicability: The expression relies on `&` binding tighter than `|` and on the leading `~` applying to the parenthesized sum. Changing grouping subtly shifts which terms are negated while the code remains legal.

bug_categories.description: Change the non-blocking assignment to a blocking one, remove the else branch update so q holds its value, or change the clock edge to negedge, altering timing and state-update behavior.
bug_categories.applicability: q is updated in a single clocked always block using `<=`. Using negedge clk, dropping the else update, or mixing blocking assignments changes when and whether q evolves relative to load and data.

bug_categories.bug_type: Case item value swap (wrong output constant)
bug_categories.description: Flip the constant assigned in one of the defined case items, e.g. changing 4'h3 from 1 to 0, or 4'h5 from 0 to 1, so the truth table no longer matches the specification.
bug_categories.applicability: The design is a pure 16-entry truth table, so each case arm directly determines the output; flipping one arm such as 4'hc: out = 1 to 0 changes the function for exactly one input combination.

bug_categories.bug_type: Don't-care (X) output replaced with a defined value
bug_categories.description: Replace the 1'bx assignments with 0 or 1, removing the intentional unknown/don't-care behavior for those inputs.
bug_categories.applicability: Entries 4'h4, 4'hd and 4'h9 drive out to 1'bx. Changing e.g. 4'h4: out = 1'bx to out = 0 alters X-propagation behavior and would be caught by 4-state simulation or equivalence checks that treat X specially.

bug_categories.description: Change a deterministic case arm into 1'bx so that the output becomes unknown for an input combination that should be well defined.
bug_categories.applicability: For example, 4'hf: out = 1 changed to 1'bx or 4'h0: out = 0 changed to 1'bx introduces unknown outputs in otherwise defined states, corrupting downstream logic.

bug_categories.description: Permute the concatenation order in the case expression, e.g. {a,b,c,d} becomes {b,a,c,d} or {d,c,b,a}, so every case label maps to a different input combination.
bug_categories.applicability: The case label values (4'h0..4'hf) are interpreted relative to the {a,b,c,d} concatenation; reordering bits remaps the whole truth table, e.g. a becomes the second MSB, changing the function for many inputs at once.

bug_categories.bug_type: Case selector bit omitted / width mismatch
bug_categories.description: Drop one input from the concatenation or replace it with a constant, e.g. case({a,b,c}) with 3-bit labels or {a,b,c,1'b0}, making the output independent of one input.
bug_categories.applicability: Using {a,b,c,1'b0} or ignoring d means the 4-bit labels no longer match uniquely; odd-valued entries become unreachable and out depends on only three inputs, breaking the function.

bug_categories.description: Change one case label to another existing value (e.g. 4'h7 changed to 4'h6, or 4'ha to 4'hb) so one input combination is covered twice and another is left uncovered.
bug_categories.applicability: Because the case statement lists all 16 values explicitly with no default, relabeling an arm leaves one input pattern unassigned and the first matching duplicate wins, giving wrong output for the displaced pattern.

bug_categories.bug_type: Incomplete case coverage causing latch inference
bug_categories.description: Delete one case arm (e.g. 4'hb or 4'h8) or leave the combinational block without a default, so out retains its previous value for the missing input combination and a latch is inferred.
bug_categories.applicability: The always @(*) block has no default assignment; removing any of the 16 arms makes out hold its old value for that input, creating unintended sequential behavior in a combinational design.

bug_categories.description: Replace the blocking assignments with non-blocking ones, or change the sensitivity list from @(*) to a partial list such as @(a or b or c), so out fails to update on changes of some inputs.
bug_categories.applicability: With a restricted sensitivity list omitting d, out does not re-evaluate when only d toggles, producing stale outputs in simulation for pairs like 4'h2/4'h3 or 4'h8/4'h9 that differ only in d.

mutants.bug_type: Case item value swap (wrong output constant)

bug_categories.description: A single bit of one of the 16-bit ROM constants is flipped, e.g. changing 44768 to 44769 or 23054 to 23055, so the output for that input differs by one bit.
bug_categories.applicability: The design is a pure 8-entry lookup table, so any single-bit error in a constant changes the output for exactly one address and is hard to spot without exhaustive testing.

bug_categories.description: Two case entries have their values exchanged, e.g. a=2 returns 25806 and a=5 returns 10196, so the set of values is intact but the address mapping is wrong.
bug_categories.applicability: All values are valid elements of the table, so range or value-set checks would pass. Only per-address checking catches the error.

bug_categories.description: A case label is changed so that two branches share the same address (e.g. label 6 changed to 5) and one address is left uncovered. The first matching branch wins and the uncovered address falls through.
bug_categories.applicability: The case(a) statement has no default and covers all 8 values of the 3-bit input. A duplicated label leaves one address unassigned and creates an unintended latch or hold of the previous value.

bug_categories.description: One case entry (e.g. a=7) is removed. Because the combinational always block has no default assignment, q is not assigned for that address and a latch is inferred that holds the previous output.
bug_categories.applicability: The block is always @(*) with no default or pre-assignment of q, so any missing branch produces latch behavior and a stateful output in a purely combinational design.

bug_categories.description: A constant is changed to a value that is truncated or altered by width, or the output is narrowed, e.g. a sized literal like 8'd44768 truncates to the low 8 bits, or the upper bits of q are forced to zero.
bug_categories.applicability: Many constants exceed 8 bits (e.g. 44768, 50470, 25806). Any narrowing of a literal or of q loses upper bits, which corrupts the output for those addresses.

bug_categories.bug_type: Address bit ordering / input index error
bug_categories.description: The case selector is permuted or partially used, e.g. case({a[0],a[1],a[2]}) or case({1'b0,a[1:0]}), so the lookup address is bit-reversed or the MSB is ignored.
bug_categories.applicability: The input a is 3 bits wide and indexes all 8 entries. Bit-reversal remaps addresses 1<->4 and 3<->6, and ignoring a[2] aliases entries 4-7 onto 0-3.

bug_categories.description: The case labels are shifted so that each value is returned for a+1 (or a-1) modulo 8, e.g. case(a+3'd1) or labels renumbered 1..7,0.
bug_categories.applicability: The table is indexed by a contiguous 0-7 range, so a rotation of the index keeps all values present but shifts every output, and wraps around at the 3-bit boundary.

bug_categories.description: One branch is replaced by a constant such as 0 or 16'hFFFF, or a stuck bit is introduced on q (e.g. q[15] forced to 0 after the case), which hides the real table value for one or more addresses.
bug_categories.applicability: Each branch is a direct constant assignment to q, so replacing a value or masking a bit on the output is easily implemented and changes behavior for specific inputs while remaining valid Verilog.

bug_categories.description: Swap the data sources assigned in two case branches, e.g. case 0 selects e instead of b, or cases 1 and 2 exchange e and a.
bug_categories.applicability: The mux maps c=0->b, 1->e, 2->a, 3->d in a non-alphabetical order, making it easy to introduce a plausible mix-up of inputs that still compiles and produces valid but wrong outputs.

bug_categories.description: Change the default assignment from 4'hf to another constant such as 4'h0, or to a data input like a, so out-of-range selects no longer return all ones.
bug_categories.applicability: Default branch covers c = 4..15 and returns 4'hf; altering the constant silently changes behavior for 12 of 16 select values.

bug_categories.description: Remove one case item (e.g. case 3: q = d) so that select value falls through to the default branch and returns 4'hf.
bug_categories.applicability: Each of the four explicit cases is independent; deleting one makes that select value return 4'hf instead of the proper input.

bug_categories.description: Change a case label constant so it duplicates or shifts another, e.g. label 3 becomes 4 or label 2 becomes 1, leaving one input unreachable.
bug_categories.applicability: Labels 0-3 are decimal literals for the 4-bit selector c; altering one makes input a or d unreachable, or shadows a later item since the first matching case wins.

bug_categories.description: Use a different input as the case expression, such as case(d) or case(b), instead of c.
bug_categories.applicability: All inputs are 4-bit wide so any can be used as the select without width errors, making this a syntactically valid but functionally broken design.

bug_categories.description: Restrict the case expression to a subset of c's bits, e.g. case(c[1:0]) or case(c[2:0]), so upper bits are ignored.
bug_categories.applicability: c is 4 bits but only 0-3 are used; truncating to c[1:0] makes the default branch unreachable and aliases c=4..15 onto valid inputs instead of returning 4'hf.

bug_categories.description: Apply a bit reversal, inversion, or partial-bit assignment on one branch, e.g. q = ~b, q = {b[0],b[1],b[2],b[3]}, or q[2:0] = a leaving q[3] unassigned.
bug_categories.applicability: All data inputs and q are 4 bits, so bit-level mutations compile cleanly; partial assignment can also infer an unintended latch in the combinational always block.

bug_categories.description: Replace @(*) with an incomplete sensitivity list such as @(c) or @(a or b or c), or remove the default branch so that q holds its previous value.
bug_categories.applicability: q depends on a, b, d, e and c; an incomplete list means changes in unlisted data inputs do not update q in simulation, and removing the default would infer a latch for c = 4..15.

bug_categories.description: Remove the inversion on y so the expression becomes z = x | y, changing the function from implication-like (x OR NOT y) to a plain OR.
bug_categories.applicability: The only inversion in the design is ~y; dropping it yields a valid assign that fails when x=0,y=1 (expected 0, gets 1) and when x=0,y=0 (expected 1, gets 0).

bug_categories.description: Move the inversion from y to x, producing z = ~x | y, which swaps the roles of the two inputs.
bug_categories.applicability: Output differs from the original when x != y: for x=1,y=0 original gives 1 but buggy gives 0; for x=0,y=1 original gives 0 but buggy gives 1.

bug_categories.description: Replace the bitwise OR with AND, giving z = x & ~y.
bug_categories.applicability: The single binary operator is |; changing it to & makes the output 1 only for x=1,y=0, breaking the cases x=0,y=0 and x=1,y=1.

bug_categories.description: Replace | with ^, giving z = x ^ ~y, which is equivalent to XNOR(x,y).
bug_categories.applicability: Matches the original except when x=1,y=0 (original 1, buggy 0), so it is a subtle single-vector corruption that tests may miss without exhaustive stimulus.

bug_categories.description: Use logical operators such as z = x || !y or mixed forms like z = x | !y; with 1-bit signals these are equivalent, so pair with a further change such as z = x ^ !y or z = x && !y to produce a functional difference.
bug_categories.applicability: Because all ports are 1-bit, the bitwise/logical swap is mostly benign by itself; a bug is only introduced when the logical operator also replaces OR with AND, giving z = x && !y.

bug_categories.description: Force the output to a constant, e.g., assign z = 1'b1 or z = 1'b0, ignoring the inputs.
bug_categories.applicability: A constant 1 passes 3 of 4 truth-table rows (fails only x=0,y=1); a constant 0 fails 3 rows. This models a stuck-at output or tie-off error.

bug_categories.description: Remove one operand so z depends on only one input, such as z = x or z = ~y.
bug_categories.applicability: z = x fails at x=0,y=0 (expected 1); z = ~y fails at x=1,y=1 (expected 1). Models a missing connection or lost term in a minimal two-input function.

bug_categories.bug_type: Extra inversion on output or double inversion error
bug_categories.description: Invert the whole result (z = ~(x | ~y)) or add an extra inversion to x (z = ~x | ~y), changing polarity.
bug_categories.applicability: z = ~(x | ~y) inverts every truth-table row (equals ~x & y); z = ~x | ~y is NAND and differs at x=0,y=1 (expected 0, gets 1) and at x=1,y=1 (expected 1, gets 0). Models polarity/active-level mistakes.

bug_categories.description: Invert the polarity of the cpu_overheated check so shut_off_computer is asserted when the CPU is not overheated.
bug_categories.applicability: In the first always block, change 'if(cpu_overheated)' to 'if(~cpu_overheated)' or swap the assigned values 1 and 0, causing the computer to shut off when cool and keep running when overheated.

bug_categories.description: Change the arrived gating condition so driving logic is evaluated in the wrong state.
bug_categories.applicability: In the second always block, change 'if(~arrived)' to 'if(arrived)', so the vehicle keeps driving based on gas level only after arrival and is forced to stop while en route.

bug_categories.description: Remove the logical negation on gas_tank_empty so keep_driving follows the empty signal rather than its complement.
bug_categories.applicability: Change 'keep_driving = !gas_tank_empty' to 'keep_driving = gas_tank_empty', so the car keeps driving only when the tank is empty and stops when it has gas.

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong constant value in else branch
bug_categories.description: Change the default value assigned when the vehicle has arrived so it no longer stops driving.
bug_categories.applicability: Change 'keep_driving = 1'b0' to 'keep_driving = 1'b1' in the arrived case, so the vehicle continues driving after arrival; similarly set shut_off_computer to constant 1 in the else branch so it is always asserted.

bug_categories.description: Remove an else branch or assignment path so the output is not assigned in all conditions, creating an unintended latch.
bug_categories.applicability: Delete the 'else shut_off_computer = 0;' clause or the 'else keep_driving = 1'b0;' clause so the output holds its previous value, inferring a latch and causing state retention when inputs change.

bug_categories.description: Replace the logical/bitwise operator or combine conditions incorrectly, changing the Boolean function.
bug_categories.applicability: Alter the keep_driving expression to something like '!gas_tank_empty | arrived' or '!gas_tank_empty & arrived', or merge cpu_overheated into keep_driving, so the combinational function no longer matches the spec.

bug_categories.description: Use the wrong input signal in a condition so the output depends on an unrelated input.
bug_categories.applicability: Change 'if(cpu_overheated)' to 'if(gas_tank_empty)' for shut_off_computer, or change 'if(~arrived)' to 'if(~cpu_overheated)' for keep_driving, creating incorrect cross-dependencies between the two independent functions.

bug_categories.bug_type: Blocking/nonblocking assignment misuse and sequential-style conversion
bug_categories.description: Change combinational assignments to nonblocking or convert to clocked-like behavior that alters timing and simulation semantics.
bug_categories.applicability: Replace '=' with '<=' in the always @(*) blocks, or alter the sensitivity list to a specific signal such as 'always @(cpu_overheated)' or 'always @(arrived)' omitting gas_tank_empty, so keep_driving fails to update when gas_tank_empty changes.

mutants.bug_type: Blocking/nonblocking assignment misuse and sequential-style conversion

bug_categories.description: Change the reset constant 25'h0120000 so the clock resets to the wrong time, e.g. 25'h1120000 (pm=1) or 25'h0000000 (hh=00), or 25'h0130000.
bug_categories.applicability: The reset branch loads {pm,hh,mm,ss} with 25'h0120000 (12:00:00 AM). Any altered constant starts the clock at an invalid or wrong time and breaks the 12-hour sequence from the first cycle.

bug_categories.bug_type: Incorrect comparison constant in carry-enable logic
bug_categories.description: Alter a constant in the enable vector, e.g. change ss[7:0]==8'h59 to 8'h58 or 8'h60, or mm/ss compare 16'h5959 to 16'h5958.
bug_categories.applicability: enable[1], enable[3] and enable[5] are generated by comparing BCD digits against 59/9 patterns. A wrong constant makes minutes, hours tens or the next digit increment at the wrong moment.

bug_categories.bug_type: Bit width / slice mismatch in enable comparison
bug_categories.description: Change a slice width or index in the enable expression, e.g. use hh[3:0] with 20'h95959 replaced by hh[7:0], or mm[3:0] replaced with mm[7:4] in the 12'h959 compare.
bug_categories.applicability: The enable bits compare concatenations of differing widths (24, 20, 16, 12, 8, 4 bits). Selecting the wrong slice changes which digit state triggers the carry, so ripple carries misfire or never fire.

bug_categories.description: Use the wrong enable bit in an update block, e.g. mm[3:0] gated by enable[3] instead of enable[2], or hh[7:4] gated by enable[4] instead of enable[5].
bug_categories.applicability: Each digit update uses enable[0..6] to select its carry condition. Shifting an index makes a digit increment at the wrong rate, or in a hh/mm/ss cascade, skip or double-count.

bug_categories.description: Change a digit wrap threshold: ss[3:0]==9 to 8 or 10, ss[7:4]==5 to 6 or 4, mm[7:4]==5 to 6, hh[3:0]==9 to 8.
bug_categories.applicability: BCD digits wrap at 9 (ones) and 5 (tens). Wrong thresholds yield non-BCD values (e.g. 0x0A) or premature wrap, so seconds/minutes show invalid counts.

bug_categories.description: Change the hour rollover: hh==8'h12 to 8'h11 or 8'h13, the reload value 8'h1 to 8'h0 or 8'h10, or remove the enable[4] term from that condition.
bug_categories.applicability: At 12 the hours must reload to 01 rather than increment to 13. A wrong compare or reload constant gives hours of 00, 13, or skips 12, breaking the 12-hour format.

bug_categories.description: Move the pm toggle to the wrong event: change enable[6] to enable[5] or enable[4], change the 24'h115959 compare to 24'h125959 or 24'h115958, or replace ~pm with a constant assignment.
bug_categories.applicability: pm should flip only on the 11:59:59 to 12:00:00 transition, encoded by enable[6]. A wrong trigger makes AM/PM flip at the wrong hour or every rollover, or never toggle.

bug_categories.description: Alter the control structure: make reset asynchronous (posedge clk or posedge reset), invert ena (if(!ena)), drop the ena gating, or give reset lower priority than ena.
bug_categories.applicability: The always block uses synchronous reset with priority over ena. Changing polarity, priority, or sensitivity makes the clock count while paused, ignore ena, or reset at the wrong time or on the wrong edge.

mutant_rejections.bug_type: Incorrect comparison constant in carry-enable logic
Bit width / slice mismatch in enable comparison

bug_categories.description: In next_state[0], the expression '!in && |state[4:0] | state[7] | state[8] | state[9]' relies on precedence of && versus |. Changing the grouping or replacing && with & (or | with ||) alters which terms are gated by !in, e.g. making state[7], state[8], state[9] also require !in.
bug_categories.applicability: next_state[0], next_state[1] and next_state[7] mix && with | without parentheses. Changing the implicit grouping (e.g., in && (state[0] | state[8] | state[9])) would change the transitions out of states 8 and 9 and the self-loop of state 7.

bug_categories.description: Invert the sense of 'in' in one or more next_state assignments (e.g., replace in with !in or !in with in), so a transition fires on the wrong input value.
bug_categories.applicability: The chain next_state[2..6] uses 'in && state[k]' while next_state[8] and [9] use '!in && state[k]'. Flipping the polarity in next_state[4] or next_state[8] makes the sequence advance on the wrong bit and breaks the counting/detection pattern.

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong state index (off-by-one) in source state
bug_categories.description: A next_state bit is driven from the wrong predecessor state bit, such as next_state[5] = in && state[3] instead of state[4].
bug_categories.applicability: The shift-chain structure next_state[k] = in && state[k-1] for k=2..6 is highly regular, so an off-by-one index in any of these skips or repeats a state in the chain, and the 1s-counting sequence is corrupted.

bug_categories.bug_type: Part-select range error in reduction OR
bug_categories.description: Change the range of the reduction OR in next_state[0] from state[4:0] to state[3:0], state[5:0], or state[4:1], so that some states no longer (or additionally do) return to state 0 upon !in.
bug_categories.applicability: next_state[0] uses |state[4:0]. Dropping state[0] or state[4], or extending to state[5], changes which states return to the idle/start state on a 0 input; state[5] has its own !in transition to state 8, so including it would create a double-successor (non-one-hot) condition.

bug_categories.bug_type: Output term omission / wrong state in output equation
bug_categories.description: Change the output logic by dropping a term or substituting a different state bit, e.g., out1 = state[8] only, or out2 = state[7] | state[8].
bug_categories.applicability: out1 = state[8] | state[9] and out2 = state[7] | state[9] are short OR functions of specific one-hot bits. Swapping state[7] for state[6], or removing state[9] from either output, produces wrong output values in the corresponding states.

bug_categories.bug_type: Operator substitution (OR to AND / AND to OR)
bug_categories.description: Replace a | with & or an && with || in the next_state or output expressions, converting a union of source states into an intersection (which is never true in one-hot encoding) or making a transition unconditional.
bug_categories.applicability: out1 = state[8] & state[9] would be constant 0 for one-hot states; next_state[7] = in && state[6] & state[7] would never set or hold state 7; next_state[1] with || would fire regardless of the input.

bug_categories.bug_type: Missing or dropped term in next-state equation
bug_categories.description: Remove one of the OR'd terms so a state loses a transition, such as deleting '| state[7]' from next_state[7] (removing the hold/self-loop) or '| state[9]' from next_state[1] or next_state[0].
bug_categories.applicability: State 7 is meant to hold via the '| state[7]' term in next_state[7], and states 8/9 return into the chain via next_state[0] and [1]. Removing these terms causes states to drop out or become stuck/dead, so the FSM never reaches the expected loop or return transitions.

bug_categories.description: Swap the targets or sources between related bits, e.g., exchange the logic of next_state[8] and next_state[9] (state[5] vs state[6]) or exchange next_state[2] and next_state[3].
bug_categories.applicability: next_state[8] = !in && state[5] and next_state[9] = !in && state[6] are structurally identical except for the source index, so swapping them (or swapping out1/out2 equations) yields a plausible-looking but functionally wrong FSM that routes the 0-input branch to the wrong terminal states.

mutants.bug_type: Output term omission / wrong state in output equation
Missing or dropped term in next-state equation
Operator substitution (OR to AND / AND to OR)

bug_categories.description: Change the q register's trigger from negedge clock to posedge clock, so q samples a on the rising edge instead of the falling edge.
bug_categories.applicability: The always @(negedge clock) q <= a; block is the only sequential element; switching to posedge changes the sampling instant and the timing relationship between p and q.

bug_categories.description: Invert the condition in the combinational latch so p follows a when clock is low (if(!clock)) instead of when clock is high.
bug_categories.applicability: The always @(*) if(clock) p = a; latch is transparent during clock high; inverting makes it transparent during the opposite phase, so p and q no longer relate as intended (p would then be stable when q updates).

bug_categories.description: Replace the non-blocking assignment in the q flop with a blocking assignment (q = a), or the blocking assignment in the latch with non-blocking (p <= a).
bug_categories.applicability: Both p and q are reg outputs driven from a; changing assignment type alters scheduling/race behavior relative to input a and clock edges in simulation, especially for the latch where p <= a delays the update by a delta cycle.

bug_categories.description: Replace always @(*) with an incomplete sensitivity list such as always @(clock) or always @(a), so the latch no longer reacts to all relevant input changes.
bug_categories.applicability: With always @(clock) p only updates on clock transitions and misses changes of a while clock is high; with always @(a) p misses the clock rising edge, so the latch no longer behaves transparently.

bug_categories.description: Change the latch into an edge-triggered register, e.g., always @(posedge clock) p <= a;, removing transparency.
bug_categories.applicability: The design's distinguishing feature is a level-sensitive latch for p; making it edge-triggered changes p to only update at the rising edge rather than tracking a throughout the high phase.

bug_categories.description: Invert the data captured by one of the storage elements, e.g., q <= ~a or p = ~a.
bug_categories.applicability: Both p and q capture the single input a; inverting one makes the outputs disagree in value, breaking the expected p/q equivalence at the sampling points.

bug_categories.bug_type: Added/removed else branch in latch (incorrect latch inference)
bug_categories.description: Add an else branch such as else p = 1'b0 (or else p = a) to the latch conditional, turning it from a latch that holds its value into combinational logic that either clears p or passes a continuously.
bug_categories.applicability: The missing else in if(clock) p = a; is what infers the latch and holds p during clock low; adding an else eliminates the hold behavior, so p no longer retains its last value when clock is low.

bug_categories.bug_type: Incorrect gating condition on storage elements
bug_categories.description: Add an extra qualifying condition so updates occur only under additional circumstances, e.g., if(clock && a) p = a; or q only updated when a is high (if(a) q <= a).
bug_categories.applicability: Because both p and q are directly loaded from a, adding a dependency on a in the enable prevents them from ever being updated to 0, leaving the outputs stuck high after the first 1 is captured.

mutants.bug_type: Added/removed else branch in latch (incorrect latch inference)

bug_categories.description: Change one of the AND terms in the carry/majority expression, e.g. 'a & b | a & c | b & c' becomes 'a & b | a & c | b | c' or one product term is dropped (a & b | a & c), so the next-state carry no longer computes majority(a,b,c).
bug_categories.applicability: The next-state logic of c is a 3-input majority (full-adder carry); removing or altering any term produces wrong carry in specific input combinations such as a=0,b=1,c=1.

bug_categories.description: Swap an AND with OR (or OR with AND) in the carry equation, e.g. 'a | b & a | c & b | c' or 'a & b & a & c | b & c', changing the carry-generation behavior.
bug_categories.applicability: The expression relies on the precise mix of & and | with precedence; replacing one operator yields a still-valid but functionally different carry function.

bug_categories.description: Change the sum output from 'a ^ b ^ c' to 'a ^ b' or 'a ^ b | c' or 'a ^ b ^ ~c', so q no longer reflects the full-adder sum with the stored carry.
bug_categories.applicability: q is the sum bit of a serial adder; dropping c or replacing XOR with OR/AND causes the sum to be wrong whenever c=1.

bug_categories.description: Invert one of the inputs or the result in the carry update, e.g. 'c <= ~(a & b | a & c | b & c)' or use '~a' in one term, flipping the carry polarity.
bug_categories.applicability: The registered carry c feeds both q and state; inverting it corrupts the carry chain from the first cycle on.

bug_categories.description: Replace the feedback c with a or b in one product term, e.g. 'a & b | a & a | b & c', or use the wrong input pair in a product term (a & b -> a & a).
bug_categories.applicability: The terms a&c and b&c depend on the registered state; mis-wiring them breaks carry propagation across cycles while the design remains syntactically valid.

bug_categories.description: Change 'c <= ...' to a blocking assignment 'c = ...' in the clocked always block, altering simulation ordering between the register update and the combinational outputs q and state.
bug_categories.applicability: q and state are continuous assignments derived from c; blocking assignment in the sequential block can cause race conditions/different sampling versus testbench inputs at the clock edge.

bug_categories.description: Change 'always @(posedge clk)' to 'always @(negedge clk)' or to a level-sensitive/combinational sensitivity list such as 'always @(*)', changing when carry is updated or creating a combinational loop through c.
bug_categories.applicability: The single sequential element c is clocked on posedge; switching edge shifts timing by half a cycle, while '@(*)' makes c depend combinationally on itself, destroying the registered-state behavior.

bug_categories.description: Swap or miswire outputs, e.g. 'assign state = a ^ b' or 'assign state = ~c', or 'assign q = c' instead of the XOR sum, so the exposed state does not correspond to the internal carry register.
bug_categories.applicability: The design exposes c directly as 'state'; changing this assignment makes the observable state diverge from the actual internal carry while q still uses the true c.

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong state index in one-hot transition
bug_categories.description: B3_next is driven from the wrong state bit (e.g., state[B1] or state[B3]) instead of state[B2], breaking the B0->B1->B2->B3 shift sequence.
bug_categories.applicability: assign B3_next = state[B2]; changing the index skips a bit-shift cycle or stalls the shift sequence, so shift_ena is asserted for the wrong number of cycles.

bug_categories.description: The polarity of the data input d is flipped or the negation is removed in one of the product terms, so the sequence detector reacts to the wrong bit value.
bug_categories.applicability: S_next uses ~d for state[S], state[S1], state[S110]; S1_next uses d from state[S]. Flipping one (e.g., state[S1] & d, or S1_next = state[S] & ~d) makes the 1101 pattern detection wrong.

bug_categories.description: An AND is replaced by OR (or vice versa) in a next-state equation, causing spurious or missed transitions.
bug_categories.applicability: Count_next = state[B3] | state[Count] & ~done_counting could become state[B3] & state[Count]..., or Wait_next = state[Count] & done_counting | state[Wait] & ~ack could use & between the terms, so the counting/wait states never properly entered or held.

bug_categories.description: One of the OR'd product terms is dropped from a next-state equation, removing a legal transition.
bug_categories.applicability: Removing state[S110] & ~d or state[Wait] & ack from S_next means the FSM never returns to S from S110 or Wait, causing it to hang; removing state[Count] & ~done_counting breaks the hold in Count.

bug_categories.description: done_counting and ack are swapped or one is negated/ignored, so the Count->Wait and Wait->S transitions respond to the wrong control input.
bug_categories.applicability: Wait_next uses done_counting for entry and ack for exit; swapping them, or using ack instead of ~ack in state[Wait] & ~ack, makes the Wait state exit immediately or never exit, corrupting done.

bug_categories.bug_type: Output decode error (wrong state mapped to output)
bug_categories.description: done or counting is assigned from the wrong state bit, so outputs don't reflect the actual FSM phase.
bug_categories.applicability: done = state[Wait] and counting = state[Count]; swapping them (done = state[Count]) or pointing one to state[B3] gives incorrect status outputs to downstream logic.

bug_categories.bug_type: Part-select range / reduction operator error in shift_ena
bug_categories.description: The slice bounds or reduction operator for shift_ena are altered, so the shift enable covers the wrong set of states or requires all of them simultaneously.
bug_categories.applicability: shift_ena = |state[B3:B0]; changing to state[B3:B1] or state[B2:B0] drops a shift cycle, using &state[B3:B0] makes it never assert in one-hot operation, or extending to include state[Count] enables shifting during counting.

bug_categories.description: One of the state index parameters is assigned a wrong or duplicate value, so multiple state names alias to the same bit or are out of order.
bug_categories.applicability: Changing e.g. parameter B2 = 6 to 5 or Wait = 9 to 8 makes B3_next/done alias to other states, and reordering B0..B3 breaks the B3:B0 range used by shift_ena, or Count = 8 changes counting/Count_next behavior.

mutants.bug_type: Part-select range / reduction operator error in shift_ena
Output decode error (wrong state mapped to output)

bug_categories.description: A single hex digit or bit in one of the 64 SHA-256 round constants is altered, e.g., changing case 17 from 32'hefbe4786 to 32'hefbe4787, so one round produces a wrong K value.
bug_categories.applicability: The design is a pure lookup table of 64 32-bit constants, so any single-entry corruption silently produces an incorrect hash only for that round index and is hard to detect without exhaustive testing.

bug_categories.description: The constants for two round indices are exchanged, e.g., case 12 returns 32'h80deb1fe and case 13 returns 32'h72be5d74.
bug_categories.applicability: All values are individually valid SHA-256 constants, so the output looks plausible, but the round-to-constant mapping is wrong for two indices.

bug_categories.description: A case label is changed to a duplicate or wrong index, e.g., two entries labelled 31 so index 32 has no match, or label 45 changed to 54 so the first matching branch wins and the intended entry is unreachable.
bug_categories.applicability: The case statement has 64 labelled entries with decimal literals; duplicating or shifting a label makes one round fall through and the duplicated label's later item dead.

bug_categories.description: One case item is deleted and there is no default, so the combinational block does not assign tmp_K for that round value, inferring a latch that holds the previous K value.
bug_categories.applicability: The always @(*) block has no default assignment and no default branch; removing any of the 64 items (e.g., round 63) creates unintended storage and stale outputs.

bug_categories.bug_type: Bit width mismatch on input port
bug_categories.description: The round input is narrowed or its bits are truncated, e.g., declared as input wire [4:0] round or the case uses round[4:0], so rounds 32-63 alias onto rounds 0-31.
bug_categories.applicability: round is a 6-bit selector needed to address all 64 entries; reducing it to 5 bits makes the upper half of the table unreachable.

bug_categories.description: A literal's size is changed, e.g., 32'h... replaced with 28'h... or 16'h..., causing zero-extension and loss of the upper bits of K for that round.
bug_categories.applicability: Each entry is a sized 32-bit hex literal assigned to a 32-bit tmp_K; shrinking a size specifier alters the upper bits while remaining valid Verilog.

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong radix or number-base in case label
bug_categories.description: A decimal label is rewritten as an octal/hex or otherwise misinterpreted value, e.g., 10 written as 'h10 (16) or 08/09 handled via a different base, so the entry matches a different round index.
bug_categories.applicability: Labels like 00-09 and 10-63 are unsized decimal literals; changing a base prefix shifts which round selects that constant and collides with other entries.

bug_categories.description: The continuous assignment is altered, e.g., assign K = ~tmp_K, assign K = {tmp_K[15:0], tmp_K[31:16]}, or K driven from a bit-reversed tmp_K, corrupting every returned constant.
bug_categories.applicability: K is a direct wire copy of tmp_K via assign; modifying this one statement affects all 64 rounds uniformly (inversion, byte/halfword swap, or bit-slice drop).

mutants.bug_type: Wrong radix or number-base in case label

bug_categories.description: The device address match compares shift_reg[6:0] to DEV_ADDR. A bug could compare the wrong slice (e.g., shift_reg[7:1]) or use != instead of ==, so the slave either never ACKs its address or ACKs the wrong addresses.
bug_categories.applicability: STATE_ADDRESS, final-bit branch where bit_count_reg == 0 and shift_reg[6:0] == DEV_ADDR decides between STATE_ACK and STATE_IDLE.

bug_categories.description: mode_read_reg is latched from sda_i_reg after the 7 address bits. Inverting the sampled value or sampling the wrong signal swaps read and write behavior, so a master write triggers a read transfer and vice versa.
bug_categories.applicability: STATE_ADDRESS assignment to mode_read_reg and the later branch in STATE_ACK that selects STATE_READ_1 vs STATE_WRITE_1.

bug_categories.description: bit_count_reg is loaded with 4'd7 on start and after ACK, and the transfer ends when it reaches 0. Loading 4'd6 or 4'd8, or changing the comparison from > 0 to > 1 or >= 0, causes one bit too few or too many to be shifted per byte, corrupting data and address framing.
bug_categories.applicability: Start-bit handler, STATE_ACK reload, STATE_READ_3 reload, and the 'bit_count_reg > 0' checks in STATE_ADDRESS, STATE_WRITE_2 and STATE_READ_1.

bug_categories.description: start_bit and stop_bit are derived from sda edges while scl_i_reg is high. Swapping sda_negedge and sda_posedge, or dropping the scl_i_reg qualification, makes the design start/stop on data transitions or misdetect bus conditions, breaking transaction framing.
bug_categories.applicability: Wire assignments for start_bit and stop_bit, and their priority ahead of the state case in the main always block.

bug_categories.description: Data is sampled on scl_posedge and driven on scl_negedge. Swapping them (e.g., sampling address bits on scl_negedge or updating sda_o_reg on scl_posedge) violates I2C timing and yields misaligned or glitched data and ACK.
bug_categories.applicability: scl_posedge/scl_negedge usage in STATE_ADDRESS, STATE_ACK, STATE_WRITE_1/2, STATE_READ_1/2/3.

bug_categories.description: Bytes are shifted in MSB-first via {shift_reg[6:0], sda_i_reg}. Reversing the concatenation order, shifting the wrong bits, or truncating the captured value stores bit-reversed or corrupted data in data_reg, and read data is output in the wrong order.
bug_categories.applicability: STATE_WRITE_2 shift and data_reg <= {shift_reg[6:0], sda_i_reg} update, STATE_ADDRESS shift, and the STATE_READ_1 {sda_o_reg, shift_reg} = {shift_reg, sda_i_reg} shift.

bug_categories.description: The filters require FILTER_LEN consecutive identical samples before updating scl_i_reg/sda_i_reg. Changing the all-ones/all-zeros comparisons, shifting in the wrong direction, or swapping the filter assignments between SCL and SDA changes debounce behavior and can cause missed or spurious edges.
bug_categories.applicability: scl_i_filter_reg and sda_i_filter_reg updates and the comparisons against {FILTER_LEN{1'b1}} / {FILTER_LEN{1'b0}} that update scl_i_reg and sda_i_reg.

bug_categories.description: Master ACK/NACK handling in STATE_READ_3 decides whether to continue or go idle, and slave ACK is driven low in STATE_ACK. Inverting the sda_i_reg check, failing to drive sda_o_reg low for ACK, or going to the wrong next state causes reads to stop early or continue after NACK, and writes to be unacknowledged. A reset-logic variant, such as removing the rst override of state_reg or sda_o_reg, would also leave the FSM in an undefined state.
bug_categories.applicability: STATE_READ_3 branch on sda_i_reg, STATE_ACK sda_o_reg <= 1'b0 assignment, STATE_WRITE_2 -> STATE_ACK transition, and the rst block at the end of the always block.

bug_categories.description: Change the full-detection MSB inversion so the wrap bit is not flipped, e.g. full = (wr_ptr_reg == rd_ptr_reg) or compare only the lower ADDR_WIDTH bits with the MSB XOR dropped.
bug_categories.applicability: The full, full_cur and full_wr wires use wr_ptr == (rd_ptr ^ {1'b1,{ADDR_WIDTH{1'b0}}}). Removing or altering the XOR makes full coincide with empty, or fires full at the wrong occupancy, causing s_axis_tready to deassert incorrectly or the FIFO to overwrite unread data.

bug_categories.description: Omit a register from the synchronous reset block or reset it to a wrong value, e.g. remove rd_ptr_reg reset, leave wr_ptr_cur_reg unreset, or reset only part of m_axis_tvalid_pipe_reg.
bug_categories.applicability: The reset blocks clear wr_ptr_reg, wr_ptr_cur_reg, drop_frame_reg, overflow_reg, bad_frame_reg, good_frame_reg and rd_ptr_reg/m_axis_tvalid_pipe_reg. Dropping wr_ptr_cur_reg or drop_frame_reg from reset leaves stale frame state after reset, so the next frame is stored at the wrong location or dropped.

bug_categories.description: Change the committed write pointer update at end-of-frame from wr_ptr_cur_reg + 1 to wr_ptr_cur_reg (or +2), or change the read pointer increment.
bug_categories.applicability: In the FRAME_FIFO branch with tlast, wr_ptr_reg <= wr_ptr_cur_reg + 1 commits the frame. Using wr_ptr_cur_reg omits the last beat from the readable region, while +2 exposes an uninitialized entry, so frames lose or gain a word.

bug_categories.description: Invert or alter the bad-frame test, e.g. remove the ~ in USER_BAD_FRAME_MASK & ~(s_axis_tuser ^ USER_BAD_FRAME_VALUE), use | instead of &, or XOR without inversion.
bug_categories.applicability: When DROP_BAD_FRAME is set, a frame is dropped if tuser matches USER_BAD_FRAME_VALUE under the mask. Inverting the test drops good frames and passes bad frames, and status_bad_frame/status_good_frame are asserted on the wrong frames.

bug_categories.description: On drop, rewind wr_ptr_cur_reg to the wrong pointer (e.g. leave it unchanged, or set it to rd_ptr_reg instead of wr_ptr_reg), or clear drop_frame_reg at the wrong time/not set overflow_reg.
bug_categories.applicability: In the overflow branch, wr_ptr_cur_reg <= wr_ptr_reg on tlast discards the partial frame. Wrong rollback leaves partial frame data in the committed region or corrupts the next frame, and a missing overflow_reg pulse hides the overflow from status_overflow.

bug_categories.bug_type: Bit slice/offset mismatch in packed word
bug_categories.description: Use wrong slice bounds or offsets when packing/unpacking the memory word, e.g. swap the LAST_OFFSET and ID_OFFSET, compute LAST_OFFSET without KEEP_WIDTH, or use [OFFSET+WIDTH-1:OFFSET] on one side only.
bug_categories.applicability: s_axis and m_axis_pipe_reg[...] use KEEP_OFFSET, LAST_OFFSET, ID_OFFSET, DEST_OFFSET and USER_OFFSET. A mismatch between the write-side packing and read-side extraction scrambles tkeep, tlast, tid, tdest or tuser, or overlaps adjacent fields, so metadata is corrupted at the output.

bug_categories.description: Modify the pipeline advance condition, e.g. use m_axis_tready && ~valid instead of ||, or drop the m_axis_tready clearing of the final valid bit, or shift stages in the wrong order.
bug_categories.applicability: The m_axis_tvalid_pipe_reg stage logic uses (m_axis_tready || ~m_axis_tvalid_pipe_reg) to advance and read from mem. Altering it makes data be duplicated or lost under backpressure, or causes the final stage to keep tvalid high after a transfer, producing repeated beats.

bug_categories.description: Change s_axis_tready or status logic, e.g. drop the DROP_WHEN_FULL term, use full instead of full_cur, swap && and || in the FRAME_FIFO expression, or make status_empty use the wrong pointer pair.
bug_categories.applicability: s_axis_tready = FRAME_FIFO ? !full_cur || full_wr || DROP_WHEN_FULL : !full, and status_full/status_empty are derived from the same flags. A wrong term causes the FIFO to stall when it should drop, accept data when full, or report incorrect full/empty status.

bug_categories.description: Reset value of txd_reg changed from 1 to 0 (or txd_reg omitted from reset), so the UART line is not idle-high after reset.
bug_categories.applicability: In the rst branch, 'txd_reg <= 1' is replaced with 'txd_reg <= 0'. The receiver sees a false start bit after reset, and the idle-line state is violated.

bug_categories.description: The baud-period reload value loses or gains one clock, changing the bit duration.
bug_categories.applicability: Change '(prescale << 3) - 1' to '(prescale << 3)' or '(prescale << 3) - 2' in the start-bit load or data-bit shift branch. Every bit period becomes one cycle too long or short, causing baud-rate drift and sampling errors.

bug_categories.description: The prescale multiplier is altered, so the bit period no longer equals prescale*8 clocks.
bug_categories.applicability: Replace 'prescale << 3' with 'prescale << 2' or 'prescale << 4' in one or more of the three reload sites. Baud rate becomes 2x/0.5x of expected, or inconsistent between start, data and stop bits if only one site is changed.

bug_categories.description: bit_cnt is loaded with the wrong frame length, so too many or too few bits are sent.
bug_categories.applicability: Change 'bit_cnt <= DATA_WIDTH + 1' to 'DATA_WIDTH' or 'DATA_WIDTH + 2'. The frame truncates the last data bit / stop bit or inserts an extra bit; the (bit_cnt > 1) and (bit_cnt == 1) comparisons then misalign.

bug_categories.description: The shift direction or fill bit in data_reg is changed, altering transmitted data order or the stop bit.
bug_categories.applicability: Change '{ data_reg, txd_reg } <= { 1'b0, data_reg }' to shift in 1'b1, or swap to MSB-first by reversing the concatenation, or load 'data_reg <= { 1'b0, s_axis_tdata }'. Data is transmitted in the wrong order, or bits are corrupted.

bug_categories.description: s_axis_tready is asserted or deasserted at the wrong time, breaking AXI-Stream handshake.
bug_categories.applicability: Change 's_axis_tready_reg <= !s_axis_tready_reg' to 's_axis_tready_reg <= 1' (tready stays high after accepting data, causing duplicate/dropped data), or remove 's_axis_tready_reg <= 0' in the 'prescale_reg > 0' branch so tready is asserted while busy.

bug_categories.description: Relational or equality operators in the FSM conditions are altered, changing state transitions.
bug_categories.applicability: Change 'bit_cnt > 1' to 'bit_cnt >= 1' or 'bit_cnt > 2', or 'prescale_reg > 0' to 'prescale_reg > 1'. The stop-bit branch ('bit_cnt == 1') is never reached or reached early, and the frame timing breaks.

bug_categories.description: busy_reg is set or cleared at the wrong time, so it no longer reflects transmission activity.
bug_categories.applicability: Remove 'busy_reg <= 1' from the start-of-frame branch, or clear busy in the idle branch before the stop bit completes (e.g., set 'busy_reg <= 0' in the 'bit_cnt == 1' branch). Upstream logic may then see the transmitter idle during transmission or busy while idle.

bug_categories.description: Change the shift-register update from { rxd_reg, data_reg[DATA_WIDTH-1:1] } (LSB-first, shift right) to { data_reg[DATA_WIDTH-2:0], rxd_reg } (shift left), so received bytes come out bit-reversed.
bug_categories.applicability: Affects the data_reg update in the 'bit_cnt > 1' branch; the UART receives LSB first, so the output tdata is bit-reversed relative to the transmitted byte while valid/ready handshaking still looks normal.

bug_categories.bug_type: Prescale shift amount / half-bit sampling error
bug_categories.description: Change the start-bit prescale load from (prescale << 2) - 2 to (prescale << 3) - 2 (or << 2 for the data bits), so the initial delay no longer equals half a bit time and sampling is no longer at mid-bit.
bug_categories.applicability: Affects the idle branch where a falling edge on rxd_reg is detected, and the data-bit reload (prescale << 3) - 1. Samples drift toward bit edges, causing corrupted data or frame errors at higher baud rates or with jitter.

bug_categories.description: Change the start-bit/data-bit/stop-bit boundary conditions, e.g. 'bit_cnt > DATA_WIDTH + 1' to '>= DATA_WIDTH + 1', or 'bit_cnt > 1' to '>= 1', or initialize bit_cnt to DATA_WIDTH + 1 instead of DATA_WIDTH + 2.
bug_categories.applicability: bit_cnt encodes start bit (DATA_WIDTH+2..DATA_WIDTH+1), data bits, and stop bit (1). Shifting a boundary causes the start bit to be shifted into data, one data bit to be lost, or the stop-bit check to be skipped, producing wrong data or frame errors.

bug_categories.description: Change overrun_error_reg <= m_axis_tvalid_reg to use m_axis_tready, remove it, or assert it unconditionally when a frame completes; alternatively, always overwrite tdata even when the previous word is still pending, or conversely drop the new word when overrun.
bug_categories.applicability: In the bit_cnt == 1 branch with valid stop bit. Overrun should flag only when a new byte arrives while the previous tvalid is still unconsumed; the bug yields false or missed overrun flags.

bug_categories.description: Invert the stop-bit check from 'if(rxd_reg)' to 'if(!rxd_reg)', or swap the actions so valid data is flagged as a frame error and bad frames are delivered to the AXI stream.
bug_categories.applicability: In the bit_cnt == 1 branch. Correct frames would be discarded with frame_error asserted, and frames with a low stop bit would be output as valid data.

bug_categories.description: Change the tvalid clear condition from (m_axis_tvalid && m_axis_tready) to just m_axis_tready or m_axis_tvalid, or move/reorder it so that it clears a tvalid that was set in the same cycle, or never clears it.
bug_categories.applicability: The if at the top of the non-reset branch. tvalid could drop before the consumer accepts, never deassert (producing duplicate data and spurious overruns), or a newly set tvalid could be lost depending on assignment ordering.

bug_categories.bug_type: Reset logic omission / wrong reset value
bug_categories.description: Remove a register from the reset block (e.g. data_reg, rxd_reg) or change reset values, such as rxd_reg <= 0 instead of 1, busy_reg <= 1, or leaving bit_cnt unreset.
bug_categories.applicability: In the rst branch. rxd_reg reset to 0 would make the receiver falsely detect a start bit right after reset; unreset bit_cnt or prescale_reg may leave the FSM in an arbitrary state, and busy would be wrong.

bug_categories.bug_type: Busy flag / start-bit detection logic error
bug_categories.description: Change the start-detect condition from '!rxd_reg' to 'rxd_reg' or to use raw rxd, or alter when busy_reg is set/cleared (e.g. clear busy at the stop bit rather than in idle, or never set it in the start branch).
bug_categories.applicability: In the final else (idle) branch: wrong polarity makes the receiver trigger on idle-high line; using rxd instead of rxd_reg bypasses the synchronizer; busy mis-timed would misreport receiver activity and could fail to reflect an in-progress frame.

mutant_rejections.bug_type: Reset logic omission / wrong reset value

bug_categories.bug_type: Incorrect rotation amount in sigma0 function
bug_categories.description: Change one of the rotate-right amounts in the d0 (small sigma0) computation, e.g. replace the ROTR 7 term { w_1[6:0], w_1[31:7] } with ROTR 8 { w_1[7:0], w_1[31:8] }, or change the ROTR 18 term to ROTR 17.
bug_categories.applicability: d0 is computed from w_1 using rotations of 7 and 18 plus a shift of 3. Any altered constant produces a wrong schedule word w_new for all rounds >= 16 while still being valid Verilog.

bug_categories.bug_type: Rotate replaced by shift (or shift replaced by rotate) in sigma1
bug_categories.description: In d1, replace the logical right shift { 10'b0000000000, w_14[31:10] } with a rotate { w_14[9:0], w_14[31:10] }, or replace a rotate term with a zero-padded shift.
bug_categories.applicability: d1 mixes two rotates (17, 19) and one shift (10) on w_14. Swapping the shift for a rotate keeps the bit widths correct (32 bits) but changes the result, so the bug is subtle and only appears in rounds >= 16.

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong word index in message schedule recurrence
bug_categories.description: Use the wrong memory entries in the W[t] = sigma1(W[t-2]) + W[t-7] + sigma0(W[t-15]) + W[t-16] computation, e.g. w_9 = w_mem[8] instead of w_mem[9], w_14 = w_mem[13] instead of w_mem[14], or w_1 = w_mem[2].
bug_categories.applicability: The design latches w_0, w_1, w_9 and w_14 from fixed w_mem indices. Off-by-one indices produce valid but incorrect schedule words that only diverge once expansion starts.

bug_categories.bug_type: Arithmetic operator error in w_new sum
bug_categories.description: Replace one of the additions in w_new = d1 + w_9 + d0 + w_0 with a subtraction or XOR, or drop one operand (e.g. omit w_0 or w_9).
bug_categories.applicability: w_new is a four-operand modulo-2^32 sum. Changing an operator or omitting a term still yields a 32-bit value but breaks the SHA-256 schedule expansion.

bug_categories.description: Corrupt the sliding window update in the next branch: e.g. w_mem14_new = w_mem[14] instead of w_mem[15], swap two entries, or load w_mem15_new with w_mem[15] or w_mem[0] instead of w_new.
bug_categories.applicability: On next && round>15 each entry shifts down by one and the new word enters at index 15. A single wrong assignment out of 16 corrupts the history used in later rounds while earlier rounds remain correct.

bug_categories.description: Change the thresholds in select_w or in the next condition, e.g. round < 16 to round <= 16 or round < 15, or round > 15 to round >= 15 or round > 16 for the shift update.
bug_categories.applicability: The design switches from direct w_mem output to w_new at round 16 and starts shifting at round > 15. Off-by-one thresholds cause the wrong word to be output at the boundary, or an early or late first shift, shifting the whole window.

bug_categories.description: Swap or misslice the block input mapping during init, e.g. w_mem00_new = block[31:0] (reversed word order), swap two adjacent words, or use an incorrect slice such as block[510:479].
bug_categories.applicability: init loads 16 32-bit words from the 512-bit block with word 0 from the MSBs. Reordered or misaligned slices produce wrong initial W[0..15] words and thus wrong outputs for the first 16 rounds and all expansions.

bug_categories.bug_type: Reset / write-enable and priority logic error
bug_categories.description: Break control logic: make reset synchronous-only or use posedge reset_n, reset to a nonzero value, remove w_mem_we = 1 from one branch, or give init priority incorrectly (e.g. change the second if to else-if or remove the round > 15 condition so next shifts at any round).
bug_categories.applicability: w_mem is updated only when w_mem_we is set, with init and next blocks both writing the same signals so the later block overrides. Changing reset behavior, enable assertion or branch priority alters state loading and shifting, such as shifting during rounds < 16 and destroying unread initial words.
